sanskrit: स ह क्षत्तान्विष्य नाविदमिति प्रत्येयाय तं होवाच यत्रारे ब्राह्मणस्यान्वेषणा तदेनमर्च्छेति
transliteration: sa ha kṣattānviṣya nāvidamiti pratyeyāya taṃ hovāca yatrāre brāhmaṇasyānveṣaṇā tadenamarccheti
translation: [Jānaśruti asked his attendant to go and look for Raikva.] Having looked for him, the attendant thought, ‘I can’t find him, ’ and returned to his master. Jānaśruti then said to him: ‘Well, why don’t you go to places where brāhmins are to be found—in forests and solitary places? Look for him there’.
word_meaning: Saḥ ha kṣattā, that attendant; anviṣya, having looked [for Raikva]; na avidam iti, thought ‘I have not found him’; pratyeyāya, came back; tam ha uvāca, [then Jānaśruti] said to him; are yatra brāhmaṇasya anveṣaṇā, well, wherever brāhmins are to be found [i.e., in
commentary: Jānaśruti’s attendant looked for Raikva in many places, but obviously they were unlikely places. Raikva could be found only in a quiet place, such as a forest or by the side of a river. It would be there that such a person would prefer to stay. So Jānaśruti asked the attendant to search in those places.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
claim_candidates: The realization of a sage is more likely to be found in natural, solitary environments than in populated or ritualistic settings
The instruction to search for Brahmins in forests implies that true spiritual knowledge is associated with renunciation of social life
The attendant’s failure to locate Raikva in ordinary places suggests that conventional searching methods are insufficient for discovering the self
Jānaśruti’s guidance reflects a pedagogical principle that seekers must adjust their search strategies based on the nature of the object sought
objection_hooks: The claim that realization is tied to forests may be culturally specific and not universally valid
The inference that renunciation is necessary for spiritual knowledge overlooks examples of realized individuals in societal contexts
The attendant’s failure could be due to his own lack of discernment rather than the inadequacy of ordinary places
The instruction might be pragmatic rather than doctrinal, thus not establishing a general principle about search strategies

sanskrit: सोऽधस्ताच्छकटस्य पामानं कषमाणमुपोपविवेश तं हाभ्युवाद त्वं नु भगवः सयुग्वा रैक्व इत्यहं ह्यरा३ इति ह प्रतिजज्ञे स ह क्षत्ताविदमिति प्रत्येयाय
transliteration: so'dhastācchakaṭasya pāmānaṃ kaṣamāṇamupopaviveśa taṃ hābhyuvāda tvaṃ nu bhagavaḥ sayugvā raikva ityahaṃ hyarā3 iti ha pratijajñe sa ha kṣattāvidamiti pratyeyāya
translation: The attendant noticed a man sitting under a cart, scratching a rash on his body. Sitting down close to him, the attendant asked, ‘Sir, are you Raikva with the cart?’ The man answered, ‘Well, yes, I am.’ The attendant thought, ‘I have found him, ’ and returned.
word_meaning: Saḥ, he [the attendant]; śakaṭasya adhastāt, [noticed a man sitting] under a cart; pāmānam, with a rash on his skin; kaṣamāṇam, scratching; upa upaviveśa, he sat close to him; tam ha abhyuvāda, he said to him; tvam nu bhagavaḥ sayugvā raikva iti, Sir, are you Raikva with the cart; aham hi arā iti, well, yes, I am the same; pratijajñe, he admitted [rather contemptuously]; saḥ ha kṣattā, that attendant; avidam iti, thought ‘I have found him’; pratyeyāya, came back.
claim_candidates: Recognition of one's true identity is essential for knowledge
The act of naming affirms an individual's essential self
Social recognition validates a person's status within the community
Physical imperfections do not obscure the underlying identity
objection_hooks: The identification based on an external label may be superficial and not reveal deeper self
The attendant's conclusion could be biased; the individual might have misrepresented himself
Physical conditions such as a rash might affect perception, questioning the reliability of recognition
The assumption that a name intrinsically defines self is philosophically contestable

sanskrit: तदु ह जानश्रुतिः पौत्रायणः षट्शतानि गवां निष्कमश्वतरीरथं तदादाय प्रतिचक्रमे तं हाभ्युवाद
transliteration: tadu ha jānaśrutiḥ pautrāyaṇaḥ ṣaṭśatāni gavāṃ niṣkamaśvatarīrathaṃ tadādāya praticakrame taṃ hābhyuvāda
translation: Then Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa went to that place, taking with him six hundred cows, a gold necklace, and a chariot drawn by mules. He said to him [Raikva]:
word_meaning: Tat u ha, next; jānaśrutiḥ pautrāyaṇaḥ, the great-grandson of Janaśruta; ṣaṭ śatāni gavām, six hundred cows; niṣkam, a gold necklace; aśvatarīratham, a chariot drawn by mules; tat ādāya, that with him; praticakrame, went [there]; tam ha abhyuvāda, he said to him.
commentary: Hearing the report from his attendant, and thinking that Raikva might be poor and in need of money, Jānaśruti went with some gifts to offer Raikva, so that Raikva would teach him.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: Offering material wealth to a sage is justified as a means to acquire spiritual knowledge
The act of giving gifts implies that spiritual instruction can be obtained through reciprocal exchange rather than solely through ascetic merit
The seeker’s willingness to travel with wealth indicates that he values the teacher’s instruction above material possession
The narrative suggests that generosity (dana) is a prerequisite for receiving higher knowledge
objection_hooks: Does offering gifts truly guarantee spiritual instruction, or does it risk commodifying sacred knowledge
Could the narrative be describing a pragmatic social custom rather than a doctrinal principle about generosity
Is the assumption that material sacrifice substitutes for ritual supported elsewhere, or is this an isolated example
Might the teacher’s acceptance be motivated by material need, undermining the purity of the teaching relationship

sanskrit: रैक्वेमानि षट्शतानि गवामयं निष्कोऽयमश्वतरीरथोऽनु म एतां भगवो देवतां शाधि यां देवतामुपास्स इति
transliteration: raikvemāni ṣaṭśatāni gavāmayaṃ niṣko'yamaśvatarīratho'nu ma etāṃ bhagavo devatāṃ śādhi yāṃ devatāmupāssa iti
translation: ‘O Raikva, all these—six hundred cows, a gold necklace, and a chariot drawn by mules—are for you. Please tell me about the god you worship’.
word_meaning: Raikva, O Raikva; imāni, all these; ṣaṭ śatāni gavām, six hundred cows; ayam niṣkaḥ, this gold necklace; ayam aśvatarīrathaḥ, this chariot drawn by mules; bhagavaḥ, sir; anuśādhi me, please teach me; etām devatām, about the god; yām devatām upāsse iti, that god which you worship.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: Material offerings such as cows, gold, and a chariot are presented as appropriate means to inquire about the divine, implying that external wealth can serve as a conduit for spiritual knowledge
The request for instruction about the deity presupposes that the deity worshipped by Raikva embodies a knowledge that can be communicated verbally
The verse suggests that the identity of the deity is linked to the material gifts offered, indicating a possible symbolic equivalence between wealth and divine attributes
By addressing Raikva directly, the speaker acknowledges the priest's authority to convey true knowledge of the divine, reflecting a hierarchical transmission of spiritual insight
objection_hooks: The assumption that material offerings facilitate spiritual insight may be challenged, as true knowledge of the divine is said to be independent of external wealth in Upanishadic teachings
The idea that a deity can be fully described verbally may be contested, given the Upanishadic emphasis on the ineffable nature of Brahman
Interpreting the gifts as symbolic of divine attributes could be seen as reading metaphor where the text merely lists material items without symbolic intent
The claim of priestly authority might be questioned, as the Upanishads often promote direct self‑realization over reliance on intermediaries

sanskrit: तमु ह परः प्रत्युवाचाह हारेत्वा शूद्र तवैव सह गोभिरस्त्विति तदु ह पुनरेव जानश्रुतिः पौत्रायणः सहस्रं गवां निष्कमश्वतरीरथं दुहितरं तदादाय प्रतिचक्रमे
transliteration: tamu ha paraḥ pratyuvācāha hāretvā śūdra tavaiva saha gobhirastviti tadu ha punareva jānaśrutiḥ pautrāyaṇaḥ sahasraṃ gavāṃ niṣkamaśvatarīrathaṃ duhitaraṃ tadādāya praticakrame
translation: Raikva said to him, ‘You śūdra, the necklace and chariot along with the cows—let all these be yours.’ Jānaśruti left and then again came back—this time with one thousand cows, a gold necklace, a chariot drawn by mules, and his own daughter.
word_meaning: Tam u, to him [Jānaśruti]; ha paraḥ, the other [i.e., Raikva]; pratyuvāca, replied; aha śūdra, O you śūdra; hāra -itvā, the necklace and chariot; saha gobhiḥ, along with the cows; tava eva astu iti, they may be with you; tat u ha jānaśrutiḥ pautrāyaṇaḥ, then Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa; punaḥ eva, again; sahasram gavām, one thousand cows; niṣkam, a gold necklace; aśvatarīratham, a chariot drawn by mules; duhitaram, his own daughter; tat ādāya, taking that with him; praticakrame, he went back.
commentary: Jānaśruti was a kṣatriya . Why then did Raikva address him as a śūdra? Because Jānaśruti thought he could tempt Raikva to teach him Brahmavidyā, the knowledge of Brahman, through wealth. He did not understand
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: A kṣatriya who attempts to purchase spiritual knowledge demonstrates misunderstanding of the nature of Brahmavidyā
Raikva’s address of Jānaśruti as śūdra indicates that material social status is irrelevant to the transmission of spiritual insight
Jānaśruti’s repeated offering of greater wealth reflects a belief that generosity can substitute for proper spiritual discipline
The dialogue shows that true knowledge of Brahman is not attainable through transactional exchange of material gifts
objection_hooks: One might argue that material offerings (dāna) are a legitimate means to support a teacher and can facilitate learning, challenging the claim that they cannot compel teaching
The designation of śūdra may simply reflect prevailing social hierarchy rather than a philosophical statement about status irrelevance
The narrative may be a historical anecdote without intending to convey a doctrinal principle about wealth substituting for discipline
The text does not explicitly state that Raikva refused to teach, so asserting that transactional exchange cannot yield knowledge may be unwarranted

sanskrit: तं हाभ्युवाद रैक्वेदं सहस्रं गवामयं निष्कोऽयमश्वतरीरथ इयं जायायं ग्रामो यस्मिन्नास्सेऽन्वेव मा भगवः शाधीति
transliteration: taṃ hābhyuvāda raikvedaṃ sahasraṃ gavāmayaṃ niṣko'yamaśvatarīratha iyaṃ jāyāyaṃ grāmo yasminnāsse'nveva mā bhagavaḥ śādhīti
translation: He said to Raikva: ‘I am giving you these thousand cows, this gold necklace, this chariot drawn by mules, this daughter of mine to be your wife, and also this village in which you live. Now, sir, please teach me’.
word_meaning: Tam, to him [Raikva]; ha abhyuvāda, [Jānaśruta] said; raikva, O Raikva; idam sahasram gavām, these thousand cows; ayam niṣkaḥ, this gold necklace; ayam aśvatarīrathaḥ, this chariot drawn by mules; iyam jāyā, this wife [my daughter]; ayam grāmaḥ, this village; yasmin āsse, where you live; [I am presenting all these to you]; bhagavaḥ, sir; eva anuśādhi iti, now please teach me.
commentary: Jānaśruti offered Raikva many things, but most important, he offered his daughter in marriage and
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: Offering material wealth to a teacher is presented as a legitimate means to obtain spiritual instruction
The verse implies that the teacher's willingness to teach is contingent upon the student's generosity
The inclusion of a daughter as a marital gift suggests that social bonds are employed to secure spiritual knowledge
The act of giving a whole village indicates that even communal assets can be offered for personal enlightenment
The verse reflects a transactional view of spiritual instruction, where knowledge is exchanged for material offerings
objection_hooks: The transaction may undermine the notion of knowledge as a divine, gratuitous gift, contradicting Upanishadic teachings that Brahman knowledge is not for sale
The teacher's acceptance of gifts could be seen as compromising spiritual integrity, suggesting moral compromise
Offering a daughter as a wife may reflect patriarchal social norms rather than a genuine spiritual strategy, raising ethical concerns
The idea that a village can be transferred overlooks the communal nature of dharma, questioning the legitimacy of such a transaction

sanskrit: तस्या ह मुखमुपोद्गृह्णन्नुवाचाजहारेमाः शूद्रानेनैव मुखेनालापयिष्यथा इति ते हैते रैक्वपर्णा नाम महावृषेषु यत्रास्मा उवास स तस्मै होवाच
transliteration: tasyā ha mukhamupodgṛhṇannuvācājahāremāḥ śūdrānenaiva mukhenālāpayiṣyathā iti te haite raikvaparṇā nāma mahāvṛṣeṣu yatrāsmā uvāsa sa tasmai hovāca
translation: Lifting the face of the princess, Raikva said: ‘You have brought me many things [but they are not making me speak]. It is this face that is making me speak.’ The villages in the Mahāvṛṣa province, where Raikva lived, were known thenceforth as Raikvaparṇā. It was here Raikva taught Jānaśruti. Raikva said to him:
word_meaning: Tasyāḥ ha mukham upodgṛhṇan, lifting her face; uvāca, [Raikva] said; śūdra, O śūdra; ajahāra, you have brought; imāḥ, all these; anena eva mukhena, by this face [or, mouth]; ālāpayiṣyathā iti, you will make me speak; te ha ete raikvaparṇāḥ nāma, these [villages] known as Raikvaparṇā; mahāvṛṣeṣu, in the province of Mahāvṛṣa; yatra, where; uvāsa, [Raikva] lived; asmai, [and where Raikva taught] him [i.e., Jānaśruti]; tasmai ha uvāca, he said to him.
commentary: Raikva was a brahmacārin . He had no home, and he lived an austere life. He had, however, attained Self-knowledge. When Jānaśruti approached him for spiritual instructions, he was unwilling. He did not like Jānaśruti’s offering him wealth. This is why he called him a śūdra. But When Jānaśruti offered him his daughter in marriage, Raikva was impressed by his keenness. He then agreed to teach him.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: Material offerings cannot elicit true spiritual speech; only the inner self (face) can.
A seeker’s conduct, such as rejecting wealth and offering sincere devotion, determines the guru’s willingness to teach.
Self‑knowledge is attainable by a brahmacārin who lives an austere life, independent of social status.
The guru’s labeling of a seeker as śūdra reflects an ethical judgment rather than a fixed caste hierarchy.
Offering a daughter in marriage can serve as a valid substitute for material gifts in the context of spiritual instruction.
objection_hooks: How can we be certain that material offerings are ineffective rather than simply unappreciated by this particular guru?
The claim that a seeker’s conduct determines teaching may overlook the guru’s autonomous authority to teach or withhold instruction irrespective of behavior.
While this passage suggests self‑knowledge transcends caste, other scriptural passages emphasize caste duties as essential for spiritual progress.
Equating the offering of a daughter with a spiritual gift could be challenged as endorsing a transactional view of marriage that may conflict with ethical principles.

sanskrit: वायुर्वाव संवर्गो यदा वा अग्निरुद्वायति वायुमेवाप्येति यदा सूर्योऽस्तमेति वायुमेवाप्येति यदा चन्द्रोऽस्तमेति वायुमेवाप्येति
transliteration: vāyurvāva saṃvargo yadā vā agnirudvāyati vāyumevāpyeti yadā sūryo'stameti vāyumevāpyeti yadā candro'stameti vāyumevāpyeti
translation: The air swallows everything. When fire is extinguished, it disappears into the air. When the sun sets, it disappears into the air. And when the moon sets, it disappears into the air.
word_meaning: Vāyuḥ vāva samvargaḥ, the air swallows everything; yadā vai agniḥ udvāyati, when fire is extinguished; vāyum eva apyeti, it disappears into the air; yadā sūryaḥ astam eti, when the sun sets; vāyum eva apyeti, it disappears into the air; yadā candraḥ astam eti, when the moon sets; vāyum eva apyeti, it disappears into the air.
commentary: Earlier, the question of imparting spiritual instructions has been discussed. Here, how the instruction is given is being shown. The instruction begins with the forces of nature ( adhidaivata )—by stressing the importance of air. Air can overcome everything, including even the sun, the moon, and fire.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
sub_concepts: Brahman as Cosmological and Physical Principle
claim_candidates: Air (Vāyu) is the ultimate substratum that absorbs all elements, including fire, sun, and moon
The transient disappearance of celestial bodies into air indicates that air underlies and sustains all visible phenomena
Since air can overcome fire, sun, and moon, it functions as a universal principle beyond the apparent hierarchy of elements
The instruction that begins with forces of nature implies that understanding the nature of air is prerequisite for spiritual insight
The verse suggests that the material world is ultimately reducible to a single element, air, reflecting a monistic view
objection_hooks: The claim that air is the ultimate substratum may be challenged by the presence of other essential elements such as earth and water, questioning the exclusivity of air
Interpreting the disappearance of the sun and moon into air as evidence of air's primacy could be a poetic metaphor rather than a literal ontological statement
The assertion that understanding air is prerequisite for spiritual insight assumes a causal link not established in the text; the commentary only notes importance, not necessity
Reducing the material world to air may conflict with other Upanishadic teachings that identify Brahman with consciousness rather than a material element

sanskrit: यदाप उच्छुष्यन्ति वायुमेवापियन्ति वायुर्ह्येवैतान्सर्वान्संवृङ्क्त इत्यधिदैवतम्
transliteration: yadāpa ucchuṣyanti vāyumevāpiyanti vāyurhyevaitānsarvānsaṃvṛṅkta ityadhidaivatam
translation: When water dries up, it disappears into the air. The air swallows all these. This is the worship of the forces of nature ( adhidaivata ).
word_meaning: Yadā āpaḥ ucchuṣyanti, when water dries up; vāyum eva apiyanti, it goes into the air; vāyuḥ hi etān sarvān saṃvṛṅkte, the air swallows all these; iti adhidaivatam, this is the worship of the forces of nature.
commentary: This is to show that air is supreme. It can even destroy such a powerful thing as fire.
contextual_topics: Being as the Source of All
sub_concepts: Brahman as Cosmological and Physical Principle
claim_candidates: The air (Vayu) is portrayed as the ultimate element that subsumes all other elements, indicating its supremacy among natural forces
Worship of natural forces (adhidaivatam) is presented as a valid form of devotion, implying that reverence of elemental powers constitutes religious practice
The process of water evaporating into air demonstrates the transient nature of material forms, suggesting that all phenomena are subject to dissolution into a more subtle principle
The commentary’s statement that air can destroy fire indicates that even the most potent elements can be overcome by a subtler element, challenging the hierarchy of elemental powers
objection_hooks: The verse merely describes a physical process of evaporation and does not explicitly assert the ontological supremacy of air over other elements
It is unclear whether worship of natural forces equates to worship of Brahman or merely acknowledges material powers without deeper metaphysical significance
The claim that all material forms are transient extrapolates beyond the specific observation of water and lacks explicit scriptural support for universal impermanence
The commentary’s remark about air destroying fire may be metaphorical, so asserting a literal elemental hierarchy could be overstating the text’s intent

sanskrit: अथाध्यात्मं प्राणो वाव संवर्गः स यदा स्वपिति प्राणमेव वागप्येति प्राणं चक्षुः प्राणं श्रोत्रं प्राणं मनः प्राणो ह्येवैतान्सर्वान्संवृङ्क्त इति
transliteration: athādhyātmaṃ prāṇo vāva saṃvargaḥ sa yadā svapiti prāṇameva vāgapyeti prāṇaṃ cakṣuḥ prāṇaṃ śrotraṃ prāṇaṃ manaḥ prāṇo hyevaitānsarvānsaṃvṛṅkta iti
translation: Next is the worship concerning the body. Prāṇa swallows everything. When a person sleeps, speech, the eyes, the ears, and the mind—all these go into prana . Prāṇa swallows all these.
word_meaning: Atha adhyātmam, now, that relating to the body; prāṇaḥ vāva samvargaḥ, prāṇa [the vital force] swallows everything; saḥ yadā svapiti, when a person is sleeping; prāṇam eva vāk apyeti, speech disappears into prāṇa; prāṇam cakṣuḥ, the eyes [disappear] into prāṇa; prāṇam śrotram, the ears [disappear] into prāṇa; prāṇam manaḥ, the mind [disappears] into prāṇa; prāṇaḥ hi eva etān sarvān saṃvṛṇkte iti, prāṇa swallows all these.
commentary: When a person falls asleep, the sense organs stop working. They retire into prāṇa, as if they have been swallowed by it.
contextual_topics: In Sleep One Reaches Being
claim_candidates: The vital force prāṇa temporarily incorporates speech, sight, hearing, and mind during sleep
During sleep the senses are subsumed into prāṇa rather than destroyed
Prāṇa functions as a unifying principle of bodily activities
Consciousness remains sustained by prāṇa even when external faculties are inactive
Prāṇa is the primary agent governing the operation and cessation of the sense organs
objection_hooks: How can we know that senses merge into prāṇa rather than simply cease activity, given the verse uses metaphorical language
If prāṇa contains the senses during sleep, does this imply prāṇa is identical to the self, contradicting teachings that distinguish prāṇa from Atman
The claim that consciousness is sustained by prāṇa during sleep may conflict with the view that consciousness arises from the mind alone

sanskrit: तौ वा एतौ द्वौ संवर्गौ वायुरेव देवेषु प्राणः प्राणेषु
transliteration: tau vā etau dvau saṃvargau vāyureva deveṣu prāṇaḥ prāṇeṣu
translation: These two swallow everything: air among the gods and prāṇa among the organs.
word_meaning: Tau vai etau dvau, these are those two; samvargau, all-swallowing; vāyuḥ eva deveṣu, the air among the gods; prāṇaḥ prāṇeṣu, prāṇa [the vital breath] among the organs.
commentary: Briefly, vāyu, air, is the source of fire, the sun, the moon, and water. Therefore one should worship vāyu as outside, in nature ( adhidaivata ). Likewise, prāṇa, the vital breath, is the source of speech, the eyes, the ears, and the mind, and therefore one should worship this prāṇa as within oneself ( adhyātma ).
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
Progressive Worship of Brahman up to the Universal Self
Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
claim_candidates: Vayu and prana are described as all‑swallowing indicating they embody the totality of cosmic and individual life
Worship of Vayu should be directed outward toward nature whereas worship of prana should be directed inward toward the self
The identification of Vayu with the gods and prana with the organs suggests a hierarchical correspondence between macrocosm and microcosm
By equating Vayu and prana with the source of fire sun speech and mind the verse implies that these forces are manifestations of the same underlying reality Brahman
The instruction to worship Vayu externally and prana internally serves as a substitute for external sacrificial rites
objection_hooks: If Vayu and prana are both all‑swallowing how can they be distinguished as separate objects of worship
The claim that worship of Vayu must be external may conflict with the Advaita view that all worship is ultimately internal
Equating cosmic forces with the organs could be seen as metaphorical rather than ontological weakening the assertion of a single underlying reality

sanskrit: अथ ह शौनकं च कापेयमभिप्रतारिणं च काक्षसेनिं परिविष्यमाणौ ब्रह्मचारी बिभिक्षे तस्मा उ ह न ददतुः
transliteration: atha ha śaunakaṃ ca kāpeyamabhipratāriṇaṃ ca kākṣaseniṃ pariviṣyamāṇau brahmacārī bibhikṣe tasmā u ha na dadatuḥ
translation: Once Śaunaka, the son of Kapi, and Abhipratārin, the son of Kakṣasena, were being served their meals when a brahmacārin appeared and begged for some food. They, however, refused to give him any.
word_meaning: Atha ha, once; śaunakam kāpeyam ca abhipratāriṇam kākṣasenim ca pariviṣyamāṇau, food was being served to Śaunaka, the son of Kapi, and Abhipratārin, the son of Kaksasena; brahmacārī bibhikṣe, a brahmacārin
commentary: Śaunaka and Abhipratārin were having their meals, and the cook was serving. Just then a brahmacārin came to them for some food. He was one who had attained the knowledge of Brahman . Śaunaka and Abhipratārin, however, wanted to see if the brahmacārin’s knowledge was genuine, so they did not give him anything.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Refusing food to a brahmacārin demonstrates that true knowledge of Brahman must be evidenced through conduct rather than mere declaration
Possession of Brahman knowledge does not automatically secure material generosity or social acceptance from others
Denial of hospitality to a spiritual seeker serves as a pedagogical method for verifying the authenticity of claimed Brahmanic insight
The context of a shared meal illustrates how the duty of giving (dāna) intersects with the assessment of inner spiritual realization
objection_hooks: Denying food to a seeker may violate the dharma of generosity, raising ethical concerns about the test's moral validity
If Brahman knowledge is self‑evident and beyond external validation, testing it through material means is conceptually inappropriate
The passage may be symbolic rather than literal, so deriving concrete ethical rules from it could misinterpret its intent
The refusal could reflect personal bias of Śaunaka and Abhipratārin rather than a universal principle about Brahman knowledge

sanskrit: स होवाच महात्मनश्चतुरो देव एकः कः स जगार भुवनस्य गोपास्तं कापेय नाभिपश्यन्ति मर्त्या अभिप्रतारिन्बहुधा वसन्तं यस्मै वा एतदन्नं तस्मा एतन्न दत्तमिति
transliteration: sa hovāca mahātmanaścaturo deva ekaḥ kaḥ sa jagāra bhuvanasya gopāstaṃ kāpeya nābhipaśyanti martyā abhipratārinbahudhā vasantaṃ yasmai vā etadannaṃ tasmā etanna dattamiti
translation: The brahmacārin said: ‘One god has swallowed four sages. Who is he who protects this world? O Kāpeya, O Abhipratārin, that god exists in many forms, but human beings cannot see him. The food is meant for him, but you are not giving it to him’.
word_meaning: Saḥ ha uvāca, he [the brahmacārin] said; ekaḥ devaḥ, one god; mahātmanaḥ caturaḥ, four sages; jagāra, swallowed; kaḥ saḥ, who is that [god]; bhuvanasya gopāḥ, the guardian of the world; kāpeya abhipratārin, O Kāpeya, O Abhipratārin; martyāḥ tam na abhipaśyanti, human beings cannot see him; bahudhā vasantam, existing in many forms; yasmai, for whom; vai etat annam, this food; tasmai, to him; etat na dattam iti, did not give it.
commentary: Fire, the sun, the moon, and water—these are said to be four sages. Air controls all these, and air is called the god Prajāpati . Similarly, prāṇa is also the god Prajāpati, and the sages are speech, the eyes, the ears, and the mind. Prajāpati is the protector of all, and he resides in diverse forms—sometimes within the human body ( ādhyātmika ), Sometimes in the forces of nature ( ādhidaivika ), and sometimes within other living beings ( ādhibautika ). People are ignorant about him and do not recognize him. They prepare food for him but do not know it, and they refuse to give it to him.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The divine Prajapati manifests as both the subtle breath (prana) and the macrocosmic elements, indicating that the deity pervades all levels of reality
Human ignorance prevents recognition of the divine presence in everyday phenomena, leading to misdirected offerings
The multiplicity of forms of the divine (internal, divine, external) does not contradict its unity but illustrates Brahman's immanence in all categories of existence
The act of preparing food without awareness of the recipient reflects a ritual substitution where the material offering replaces direct communion with the divine
The swallowing of the four sages (fire, sun, moon, water) by the god signifies that the divine subsumes the sensory and elemental aspects of existence
objection_hooks: If the divine manifests as both subtle breath and macro elements, how can we differentiate the deity from the physical phenomena without circular reasoning
The claim that ignorance prevents recognition may overlook the possibility that the divine intentionally remains hidden, questioning whether knowledge alone is sufficient
Asserting unity despite apparent multiplicity could be a semantic gloss; does the text provide explicit justification for a non‑dual interpretation
Interpreting food offerings as a substitution for communion assumes a ritual logic not explicit in the verse; could the food simply be a metaphor for sustenance

sanskrit: तदु ह शौनकः कापेयः प्रतिमन्वानः प्रत्येयायात्मा देवानां जनिता प्रजानां हिरण्यदंष्ट्रो बभसोऽनसूरिर्महान्तमस्य महिमानमाहुरनद्यमानो यदनन्नमत्तीति वै वयं ब्रह्मचारिन्नेदमुपास्महे दत्तास्मै भिक्षामिति
transliteration: tadu ha śaunakaḥ kāpeyaḥ pratimanvānaḥ pratyeyāyātmā devānāṃ janitā prajānāṃ hiraṇyadaṃṣṭro babhaso'nasūrirmahāntamasya mahimānamāhuranadyamāno yadanannamattīti vai vayaṃ brahmacārinnedamupāsmahe dattāsmai bhikṣāmiti
translation: After thinking this over, Śaunaka Kāpeya went to the brahmacārin and said, ‘He who is the self of all the gods and goddesses, the creator of all things moveable and immoveable, who eats with his golden [i.e., firm] teeth, who is intelligent, whom others cannot eat, who eats things which are not food, whose greatness wise people think highly of—O brahmacārin, we worship him.’ After this he said, ‘Give this man alms’.
word_meaning: Tat u ha, that [statement]; śaunaka kāpeyaḥ pratimanvānaḥ, thought over; pratyeyāya, [and then] went to him; ātmā devānām, the self of all the gods and goddesses; janitā, the creator; prajānām, of all things [moving or unmoving]; hiraṇyadaṃstraḥ, with teeth made of gold; babhasaḥ, the eater; anasūriḥ, intelligent; mahāntam, great; asya, its; mahimānam, greatness; āhuḥ, is so described; anadyamānaḥ, uneatable; yat, that; anannam, no food; atti, eats; brahmacārin, O brahmacārin; vayam, we; idam vai ā-upāsmahe iti, worship this one; datta asmai bhikṣām iti, give alms to him.
commentary: Śaunaka told the brahmacārin: ‘It is not correct that we do not know him. We do know him. He is Prajāpati . He creates and also destroys everything. He is the self of all, and he is also the destṛoyer of all. He is supreme. All wise people worship him as such.’ Śaunaka then told his servant to give the brahmacārin some food.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The self of all gods is identical with the ultimate creator Prajapati
The supreme self possesses golden teeth and consumes that which is not food, indicating its transcendence beyond ordinary nourishment
The supreme self functions both as creator and destroyer of all beings, showing a unity of generative and destructive powers
Wise people worship this supreme self, suggesting that recognition of its nature leads to reverence
Almsgiving to a brahmacārin follows the recognition of the supreme self, linking ethical action to spiritual insight
objection_hooks: The description of golden teeth and eating non‑food may be metaphorical, making the claim of transcendence ambiguous
Identifying the individual self with the supreme creator raises a conflict between personal differentiation and universal identity
The assertion that wise people universally worship the supreme self overlooks possible dissenting traditions
Equating almsgiving with recognition of the supreme self could be a social prescription rather than a necessary metaphysical consequence

sanskrit: तस्म उ ह ददुस्ते वा एते पञ्चान्ये पञ्चान्ये दश सन्तस्तत्कृतं तस्मात्सर्वासु दिक्ष्वन्नमेव दश कृतं सैषा विराडन्नादी तयेदं सर्वं दृष्टं सर्वमस्येदं दृष्टं भवत्यन्नादो भवति य एवं वेद य एवं वेद
transliteration: tasma u ha daduste vā ete pañcānye pañcānye daśa santastatkṛtaṃ tasmātsarvāsu dikṣvannameva daśa kṛtaṃ saiṣā virāḍannādī tayedaṃ sarvaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ sarvamasyedaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ bhavatyannādo bhavati ya evaṃ veda ya evaṃ veda
translation: Then they gave him alms. The first five [ Vāyu, etc.] and the second five [ prāṇa, etc.] together make ten. That is kṛta [the throw of dice of the highest denomination]. These ten are the ten directions, and they are the food. This kṛta is Virāṭ . As Virāṭ is all-pervasive, everything is its food. By that Virāṭ all this is seen. He who knows this Virāṭ becomes Virāṭ himself. He becomes all-pervasive and everything becomes his food.
word_meaning: Tasmai, to him [the brahmacārin ]; u ha daduḥ, they gave [alms]; te vai ete, all these; pañca anye, five other [i.e., air, plus the four others (fire, the sun, the moon, and water) constituting its food]; pañca anye, five other [i.e., prāṇa, plus the four others (speech, the eyes, the ears, and the mind) constituting its food]; daśa santaḥ, make ten; tat kṛtam, that is kṛta [the turn of the dice that swallows all others]; tasmāt, therefore; sarvāsu dikṣu daśa, these which are in the ten directions; annam eva, are the food; kṛtam, [and also] kṛta; sā eṣā virāṭ, that is Virāṭ; annādi, that which swallows; tayā, by that [Virāṭ]; sarvam idam dṛṣṭam, all this is seen; yaḥ evam veda, he who knows thus; asya sarvam idam dṛṣṭam bhavati, all this to him becomes seen; annādaḥ bhavati, [and] he becomes an eater of food.
commentary: Prāṇa (the vital force), speech, the eyes, the ears, and the mind—these five represent our physical ( adhyātmika ) self. Air, fire, the sun, the moon, and water—these five represent nature ( adhidaivika ), which surrounds us. These ten together are compared to the dice throw called kṛta . Being the highest number, kṛta ‘swallows’ the other throws of dice, adds their numbers to itself, and then becomes ten. (Kṛta is 4, so the other numbers are 3, 2, and 1; therefore 4+3+2+1 = 10.) Then if is said that the adhyātmika and adhidaivika elements together are the ten quarters. They represent the whole world, so they are Virāṭ. This Virāṭ is both the eater and the food. The person who knows this then becomes Virāṭ.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The ten combined elements of the internal faculties and external nature constitute the totality of existence as symbolized by the dice throw kṛta
Virāṭ identified with the ten directions functions simultaneously as both the eater and the food of the universe
Knowing Virāṭ transforms the knower into Virāṭ indicating that realization of the universal self leads to identity with the all‑pervasive reality
The dice analogy shows that the highest principle subsumes all lower principles implying a hierarchical absorption within the cosmic order
The internal adhyātmika and external adhidaivika fivefold groups together are sufficient to represent the whole world leaving no need for additional categories
objection_hooks: The enumeration of five internal and five external elements may not exhaust all aspects of existence as Vedantic thought includes subtle elements beyond these ten
Describing Virāṭ as both eater and food appears contradictory raising questions about how a principle can be its own sustenance
The claim that the knower becomes Virāṭ could be metaphorical rather than literal challenging the ontological status of such identity
Using a dice throw as an analogy may be insufficient to capture the complexity of cosmic hierarchy since a dice is a human construct and may not map onto metaphysical realities

sanskrit: सत्यकामो ह जाबालो जबालां मातरमामन्त्रयांचक्रे ब्रह्मचर्यं भवति विवत्स्यामि किंगोत्रो न्वहमस्मीति
transliteration: satyakāmo ha jābālo jabālāṃ mātaramāmantrayāṃcakre brahmacaryaṃ bhavati vivatsyāmi kiṃgotro nvahamasmīti
translation: Once Satyakāma Jābāla said to his mother Jabālā: ‘Revered mother, I would like to live with a teacher as a celibate student. What is my lineage?’.
word_meaning: Satyakāmaḥ jābālaḥ ha, once Satyakāma Jābāla; jabālām mātaram āmantrayāñcakre, said to his mother Jabālā; brahmacaryam bhavati vivatsyāmi, O revered mother, I want to live as a brahmacārin [with a teacher]; kim gotraḥ nu aham asmi iti, what is my lineage?
commentary: To attain Self-realization, one has to practise austerities, study the scriptures, and live a life of self-discipline. The story of Satyakāma illustrates this.
contextual_topics: The Story of Jabala, a Brahmin
Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: The aspiration to adopt brahmacarya indicates that renunciation is viewed as essential for Self‑realization.
Inquiry about one's gotra before entering ascetic life shows that lineage is considered a prerequisite for spiritual discipline.
The mother’s guidance is portrayed as a legitimate source of instruction for initiating a brahmacārin path.
The narrative of Satyakāma Jābāla is employed as a didactic example that the pursuit of Self‑realization begins with a conscious decision to live celibately.
According to the commentary, practicing austerities, studying scriptures, and maintaining self‑discipline are presented as sufficient means to attain Self‑realization.
objection_hooks: One might argue that self‑realization can be achieved without renunciation, as many traditions accept household life.
The requirement of knowing one's gotra could be challenged as a social convention rather than a spiritual necessity.
The reliance on maternal advice may be questioned since ultimate guidance is traditionally sought from a qualified guru.
Claiming that austerities and study alone guarantee Self‑realization may be disputed because direct insight or grace is also emphasized in other teachings.

sanskrit: तस्य ये प्राञ्चो रश्मयस्ता एवास्य प्राच्यो मधुनाड्यः । ऋच एव मधुकृत ऋग्वेद एव पुष्पं ता अमृता आपस्ता वा एता ऋचः
transliteration: tasya ye prāñco raśmayastā evāsya prācyo madhunāḍyaḥ | ṛca eva madhukṛta ṛgveda eva puṣpaṃ tā amṛtā āpastā vā etā ṛcaḥ
translation: The rays of the sun in the east are the eastern honey-cells [of the beehive]. The Ṛk mantras are the bees, and the Ṛg Veda is the flower. The water [from the sacrifice, such as the soma juice and other things] is the nectar [of the flower]. These Ṛk mantras—
word_meaning: Tasya, of that [sun]; ye, those which are; prāñcaḥ raśmayaḥ, the rays in the east; tāḥ eva, they all; asya prācyaḥ madhunāḍyaḥ, are its eastern honey-cells; ṛcaḥ eva madhukṛtaḥ, the Ṛk mantras are the bees; ṛgvedaḥ eva puṣpam, the Ṛg Veda is the flower; tāḥ āpaḥ amṛtāḥ, the water [of the soma and other things offered as oblations] is the nectar; tāḥ vai etāḥ ṛcaḥ, these Ṛks—
commentary: The first rays of the sun seen in the east are like the honey cells of a beehive. In these cells are the bees, which are compared to the Ṛk mantras. The sun in the morning is red, like honey. The Ṛk mantras are called bees because bees produce honey, and the Ṛg Veda is called the flower because that is where the bees get the nectar to make the honey. Here, the term Ṛg Veda does not mean words. It means work—that is, the rituals prescribed in the Veda. It is the result of the rituals that is described as honey. Just as the bees collect the juice from the flowers and change it into honey, so the Ṛks seem to collect from the sacrificial fire the liquid, consisting of the soma juice, butter, etc., from the oblations. This is called nectar because after the ingredients have been in the fire, they are transformed into the sweetest and purest thing possible. The result of the sacrificial ritual is the nectar ( amṛta ), because it leads to immortality. The word amṛta means both ‘nectar’ and ‘immortality.’
claim_candidates: The eastern rays of the sun are metaphorically described as honey cells of a beehive
The Ṛk mantras function as bees that collect nectar from the sacrificial fire
The Ṛg Veda, understood as ritual work, is likened to a flower that provides nectar
The offerings transformed in the fire become amrita, which is said to confer immortality
objection_hooks: How can a physical sun ray be equated with a honey cell without literal basis
Does the metaphor imply that mantras possess intrinsic power or is it merely poetic imagery
Is the identification of amrita with literal immortality justified or is it symbolic
Does the analogy conflate ritual efficacy with natural processes, leading to logical inconsistency

sanskrit: अथ यदवोचंस्वः प्रपद्य इत्यृग्वेदं प्रपद्ये यजुर्वेदं प्रपद्ये सामवेदं प्रपद्य इत्येव तदवोचं तदवोचम्
transliteration: atha yadavocaṃsvaḥ prapadya ityṛgvedaṃ prapadye yajurvedaṃ prapadye sāmavedaṃ prapadya ityeva tadavocaṃ tadavocam
translation: Then, when I said, “I take refuge in svaḥ, ” what I meant was that I take refuge in the Ṛg Veda, I take refuge in the Yajur Veda, and I take refuge in the Sāma Veda . It is this that I meant.
word_meaning: Atha, next; yat avocam, when I said; svaḥ prapadye iti, I take refuge in svaḥ [heaven]; iti eva tat avocam, it is this that I meant; ṛg vedam prapadye, I take refuge in the Ṛg Veda; yajur vedam prapadye, I take refuge in the Yajur Veda; sāma vedam prapadye, I take refuge in the Sāma Veda; tat avocam tat avocam, it is this that I meant, this that I meant.
commentary: One should first meditate on the immortal chest, and then repeat the mantras following the meditation. To emphasize the importance of the worship, the mantras are repeated again and again.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
Progressive Worship of Brahman up to the Universal Self
claim_candidates: The speaker equates taking refuge in svaḥ with taking refuge in each of the three Vedas
The inclusion of all three Vedas indicates that complete spiritual protection requires engagement with the entire Vedic corpus
The commentary suggests that meditating on the immortal chest precedes the verbal refuge, implying that inner contemplation is prerequisite to scriptural devotion
Repeating the mantras multiple times is presented as a method to intensify the worship of the Vedas
objection_hooks: The equivalence between svaḥ and the Vedas may be metaphorical rather than literal, challenging the claim of direct substitution
Asserting that all three Vedas are necessary for complete protection may overlook the sufficiency of a single Veda for certain seekers
The commentary’s instruction to repeat mantras could reflect ritual emphasis rather than evidence of increased efficacy, questioning the claim about intensifying worship

The requirement of meditating on the immortal chest before taking refuge might be a later interpretive addition not present in the original verse, casting doubt on the claim about prerequisite contemplation

sanskrit: पुरुषो वाव यज्ञस्तस्य यानि चतुर्विंशति वर्षाणि तत्प्रातःसवनं चतुर्विंशत्यक्षरा गायत्री गायत्रं प्रातःसवनं तदस्य वसवोऽन्वायत्ताः प्राणा वाव वसव एते हीदंसर्वं वासयन्ति
transliteration: puruṣo vāva yajñastasya yāni caturviṃśati varṣāṇi tatprātaḥsavanaṃ caturviṃśatyakṣarā gāyatrī gāyatraṃ prātaḥsavanaṃ tadasya vasavo'nvāyattāḥ prāṇā vāva vasava ete hīdaṃsarvaṃ vāsayanti
translation: The human body is like a sacrifice, and the first twenty-four years are like the morning libation. The gāyatrī has twenty-four syllables, and the morning libation is accompanied by the gāyatrī. The Vasus reside in this morning libation. The Vasus are the vital breaths and the sense organs, for the word vasu means those who make others live and who live themselves.
word_meaning: Puruṣaḥ vāva yajñaḥ, the human body is like a sacrifice; tasya yāni cāturviṃśati varṣāṇi, its first twenty-four years; tat, that; prātaḥ savanam, is the morning libation; gāyatrī caturviṃśati akṣarā, the gāyatrī is constituted of twenty-four syllables; gāyatram prātaḥ savanam, the morning libation is accompanied by the gāyatrī; asya, of this [i.e., this sacrifice of the human body]; tat, it [the morning libation covering the first twenty-four years]; vasavaḥ, the deities called Vasus; anvāyattāḥ, are connected; prāṇāḥ vāva vasavaḥ, the prāṇas [together with the sense organs] are the Vasus; hi, for; ete, these [Vasus]; idam sarvam, everything in this [world]; vāsayanti, cause to live [and they themselves also live (vasu)].
commentary: In the previous section, meditation and repetition of certain mantras was recommended for the long life of one’s children. The same thing is being recommended now for one’s own life. Here the meditation is that one’s life is a sacrifice, and that the first twenty-four years are the morning offering. This offering is connected with the gāyatrī, which has twenty-four syllables. The Vasus are also connected with this offering, and they are thought of as the organs, which abide ( vasu ) and which also make others abide.
contextual_topics: Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The human body functions as a sacrificial offering, with its early years constituting a prime offering analogous to a morning libation
The Gayatri mantra, composed of twenty-four syllables, is intrinsically linked to the first twenty-four years of life, serving as a ritual accompaniment to that period
The Vasus, identified with the vital breaths and sense organs, are the animating forces that sustain both individual life and the broader existence
Meditating on the equivalence of the body to a sacrifice and the alignment of the Gayatri with early life can extend longevity, implying that ritual symbolism directly influences lifespan
The identification of sense organs with Vasus suggests a non‑dual view where the material and divine are coextensive
objection_hooks: How can the metaphor of the body as a sacrifice be taken literally to affect lifespan, given that physical aging is a biological process
Does the identification of sense organs with Vasus imply that all sensory experience is divine, or is this merely symbolic, and what evidence supports the literal equivalence
The Gayatri's twenty‑four syllables may be a structural observation, but does the text assert a causal relationship between reciting Gayatri and the first twenty‑four years of life
If the early twenty‑four years are a "morning libation," what about the subsequent years—does the text provide guidance, or does this framework leave later life unaddressed

sanskrit: सा हैनमुवाच नाहमेतद्वेद तात यद्गोत्रस्त्वमसि बह्वहं चरन्ती परिचारिणी यौवने त्वामलभे साहमेतन्न वेद यद्गोत्रस्त्वमसि जबाला तु नामाहमस्मि सत्यकामो नाम त्वमसि स सत्यकाम एव जाबालो ब्रवीथा इति
transliteration: sā hainamuvāca nāhametadveda tāta yadgotrastvamasi bahvahaṃ carantī paricāriṇī yauvane tvāmalabhe sāhametanna veda yadgotrastvamasi jabālā tu nāmāhamasmi satyakāmo nāma tvamasi sa satyakāma eva jābālo bravīthā iti
translation: Jabālā said to him: ‘My son, I don’t know what your lineage is. I was very busy serving many people when I was young, and I had you. As this was the situation, I know nothing about your lineage. My name is Jabālā, and your name is Satyakāma. When asked about your lineage, say, “I am Satyakāma Jābāla .”’.
word_meaning: Sā, she [Jabālā]; ha enam uvāca, said to him; na aham etat veda, I don’t know this; tāta, my son; yat gotraḥ tvam asi, what your lineage is; bahu aham carantī paricāriṇī, I was busy serving many people; yauvane tvām alabhe, I had you when I was young; sā etat, for this reason; aham yat gotraḥ tvam asi na veda, I know nothing about what your lineage is; jabālā tu nāma aham asmi, but my name is Jabālā; satyakāmaḥ nāma tvam asi, your name is Satyakāma; saḥ satyakāmaḥ eva jābālaḥ bruvīthāḥ iti, [when asked about your lineage] say this that you are Satyakāma Jābāla.
contextual_topics: The Story of Jabala, a Brahmin
claim_candidates: The speaker asserts that one may truthfully identify oneself by a conventional name despite lacking knowledge of true lineage
The speaker claims ignorance of the son's gotra, indicating that lineage knowledge is not essential for self-identification
The instruction to use a prescribed verbal formula suggests that verbal identity can serve as a substitute for factual genealogical knowledge
The narrative implies that social duties such as serving many people can preclude acquisition of personal lineage knowledge
The naming of the son as Satyakāma reflects an ascribed moral quality, indicating that names convey ethical identity
objection_hooks: The proposed naming without factual basis may be considered dishonest and undermine truthfulness
The importance of gotra in Vedic tradition suggests that lineage knowledge is essential for ritual eligibility, so ignorance is problematic
A verbal formula cannot replace actual knowledge of lineage and may cause confusion in social contexts
Assigning moral qualities via a name does not guarantee that the individual will embody those qualities

sanskrit: स ह हारिद्रुमतं गौतममेत्योवाच ब्रह्मचर्यं भगवति वत्स्याम्युपेयां भगवन्तमिति
transliteration: sa ha hāridrumataṃ gautamametyovāca brahmacaryaṃ bhagavati vatsyāmyupeyāṃ bhagavantamiti
translation: Satyakāma went to Gautama, the son of Haridrumata, and said: ‘Revered sir, I wish to live with you as a celibate. I have come, revered sir, to be your disciple’.
word_meaning: Saḥ ha hāridmmatam gautamam etya, he went to Gautama, the son of Haridrumata; uvāca, [and] said; brahmacaryam bhagavati vatsyāmi, revered sir, I wish to live [with you] as a celibate student; upeyām bhagavantam iti, I have come to you, revered sir, [as a disciple].
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty
Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: Seeking brahmacarya under a guru is presented as a legitimate path to spiritual progress
Celibacy is implied as a prerequisite for authentic discipleship in this context
Hierarchical respect expressed as “revered sir” is essential for the transmission of spiritual knowledge
The act of approaching a teacher indicates that liberation requires guidance rather than solitary effort
objection_hooks: The requirement of celibacy may not be universally necessary for spiritual advancement, as other traditions allow married life
The emphasis on hierarchical respect could be a cultural construct rather than a spiritual necessity
Some schools argue that self‑realization can occur without a guru, challenging the claim that guidance is essential
The notion that brahmacarya is a legitimate path may be questioned given the validity of other ashramas such as grihastha or sannyasa

sanskrit: तं होवाच किंगोत्रो नु सोम्यासीति स होवाच नाहमेतद्वेद भो यद्गोत्रोऽहमस्म्यपृच्छं मातरं सा मा प्रत्यब्रवीद्बह्वहं चरन्ती परिचरिणी यौवने त्वामलभे साहमेतन्न वेद यद्गोत्रस्त्वमसि जबाला तु नामाहमस्मि सत्यकामो नाम त्वमसीति सोऽहं सत्यकामो जाबालोऽस्मि भो इति
transliteration: taṃ hovāca kiṃgotro nu somyāsīti sa hovāca nāhametadveda bho yadgotro'hamasmyapṛcchaṃ mātaraṃ sā mā pratyabravīdbahvahaṃ carantī paricariṇī yauvane tvāmalabhe sāhametanna veda yadgotrastvamasi jabālā tu nāmāhamasmi satyakāmo nāma tvamasīti so'haṃ satyakāmo jābālo'smi bho iti
translation: Gautama asked him, ‘O Somya, what is your lineage?’ Satyakāma said: ‘Sir, I do not know what my lineage is. When I asked my mother, she said to me: “I was very busy serving many people when I was young, and I had you. As this was the situation, I know nothing about your lineage. My name is Jabālā, and your name is Satyakāma.” So, sir, I am Satyakāma Jābāla ’.
word_meaning: Tam ha uvāca, he [Gautama] said to him; kim gotraḥ nu somya asi iti, O Somya, what is your lineage; saḥ ha uvāca, he [Satyakāma] said; na aham etat veda bhoḥ, I do not know this, sir; yat gotraḥ aham asmi, of what lineage I am; apṛccham mātaram, I asked my mother; sā mā pratyabravīt, she said to me; bahu aham carantī paricāriṇī, I was busy serving many people; yauvane tvām alabhe, I had you when I was young; sā etat, for this reason; aham yat gotraḥ tvam asi na veda, I know nothing about what your lineage is; jabālā tu nāma aham asmi, but my name is Jabālā; satyakāmaḥ nāma tvam asi, your name is Satyakāma; saḥ aham satyakāmaḥ jābālaḥ asmi bhoḥ iti, so I am Satyakāma Jābāla, sir.
commentary: Jabālā told Satyakāma the truth and, should anyone ask him, she told him to tell the truth also—irrespective
contextual_topics: The Story of Jabala, a Brahmin
claim_candidates: The speaker admits ignorance of his lineage, indicating that lineage knowledge is not essential for personal identity
The mother's explanation that she was busy serving many people suggests that social duty can take precedence over genealogical knowledge
The identification by name (Jabala, Satyakāma) is presented as sufficient self-definition, implying that personal naming can substitute for gotra knowledge
The instruction to always tell the truth, irrespective of circumstance, establishes truthfulness as a universal ethical imperative
objection_hooks: How can identity be claimed without knowledge of gotra when lineage traditionally determines ritual and social status
Does emphasizing service over lineage risk neglecting the dharma associated with family obligations
Is a mere name sufficient for self-definition, or does it ignore a deeper metaphysical self beyond nomenclature
Is the command to always tell the truth realistic, given situations where truth may cause harm or conflict

sanskrit: तं होवाच नैतदब्राह्मणो विवक्तुमर्हति समिधं सोम्याहरोप त्वा नेष्ये न सत्यादगा इति तमुपनीय कृशानामबलानां चतुःशता गा निराकृत्योवाचेमाः सोम्यानुसंव्रजेति ता अभिप्रस्थापयन्नुवाच नासहस्रेणावर्तेयेति स ह वर्षगणं प्रोवास ता यदा सहस्रं सम्पेदुः
transliteration: taṃ hovāca naitadabrāhmaṇo vivaktumarhati samidhaṃ somyāharopa tvā neṣye na satyādagā iti tamupanīya kṛśānāmabalānāṃ catuḥśatā gā nirākṛtyovācemāḥ somyānusaṃvrajeti tā abhiprasthāpayannuvāca nāsahasreṇāvarteyeti sa ha varṣagaṇaṃ provāsa tā yadā sahasraṃ sampeduḥ
translation: Gautama said to him: ‘No non-brāhmin could speak like this. [Therefore, you must be a brāhmin.] O Somya, go and get me some fuel [for the sacrificial fire]. I will initiate you [as a brāhmin by presenting you with the sacred thread], as you have not deviated from truth.’ After the initiation, he selected four hundred feeble and famished cows. Addressing Satyakāma, Gautama said, ‘O Somya, take these cows away [and look after them].’ As. Satyakāma was taking them away, he said, ‘I will not come back until there are a thousand of them.’ He lived away for many years until they had become a thousand.
word_meaning: Tam ha uvāca, he [Gautama] said to him; na etat abrāhmaṇaḥ vivaktum arhati, no non-brāhmin could speak like this; samidham āhara, get some fuel; somya, O Somya; tvā upaneṣye, I shall initiate you; na satyāt agāḥ iti, you have not deviated from truth; tam upanīya, having initiated him; kṛśānām abalānām catuḥśatāḥ gāḥ, four hundred thin and famished cows; nirākṛtya uvāca, having chosen, he said; somya, O Somya; anusaṃvraja iti, take these away; tāḥ abhiprasthāpayan, as he was leaving with them; uvāca, he [Satyakāma] said; na āvarteya asahasreṇa, I will not come back until they are a thousand in number; saḥ ha varṣagaṇam provāsa, he lived away for a long time; tāḥ yadā sahasram sampeduḥ, until they were a thousand.
commentary: The point is, no matter what Satyakāma’s birth was, he had the qualities of a brāhmin—love of truth and learning. Though he had to suffer much hardship living in the forest looking after the cows, he was more concerned with keeping his word than with seeking physical comforts.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: Truthfulness and dedication qualify a person as a Brahmin irrespective of birth
The sacred thread initiation confers Brahminical status, indicating ritual acts can transform social‑spiritual identity
A vow to increase the herd to a thousand demonstrates that ethical resolve outweighs material comfort in spiritual progress
Enduring hardship to keep one’s word is presented as a higher virtue than seeking physical comfort
Caring for cows after initiation symbolizes the performance of sacrificial duties as a path to Brahminical identity
objection_hooks: The claim that truthfulness alone makes one a Brahmin ignores the traditional varna system based on birth, creating a logical inconsistency
Asserting that a ritual thread can change one’s essential nature may be challenged as merely symbolic, lacking ontological transformation
Emphasizing hardship over comfort could be questioned as promoting asceticism without clarifying its relevance to dharma
Interpreting cow care as a symbolic representation of sacrificial duty may overextend the metaphor beyond the textual evidence

sanskrit: अथ हैनमृषभोऽभ्युवाद सत्यकाम३ इति भगव इति ह प्रतिशुश्राव प्राप्ताः सोम्य सहस्रं स्मः प्रापय न आचार्यकुलम्
transliteration: atha hainamṛṣabho'bhyuvāda satyakāma3 iti bhagava iti ha pratiśuśrāva prāptāḥ somya sahasraṃ smaḥ prāpaya na ācāryakulam
translation: Then a bull called to Satyakāma, saying, ‘O Satyakāma!’ He replied, ‘Yes, lord.’ [The bull then said: ] ‘We are now a thousand. Take us to the teacher’s house’.
word_meaning: Atha, then; ha enam ṛṣabhaḥ abhyuvāda iti, a bull called to him [Satyakāma] saying; satyakāma, O Satyakāma; bhagavaḥ iti ha pratiśuśrāva, he replied, ‘Yes, lord’; prāptāḥ somya sahasram smaḥ, we are now a thousand; prāpaya naḥ ācāryakulam, lead us to the teacher’s house.
commentary: Vāyu (air) is the presiding deity of the quarters (the directions). Being pleased with Satyakāma for the way he fulfilled his promise to his teacher, Vāyu entered the body of a bull and spoke to Satyakāma in a very heavy voice. Satyakāma recognized the deity, and so he addressed him as ‘lord.’
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: Vāyu rewards Satyakāma for fulfilling his promise to his teacher, showing divine favor depends on ethical conduct
The deity Vāyu can assume the form of a bull, indicating fluidity between divine and material realms
Satyakāma’s address of Vāyu as ‘lord’ demonstrates reverence for divine authority regardless of external appearance
The request to be taken to the teacher’s house highlights the central role of the guru in spiritual progress
objection_hooks: How can we be sure that Vāyu’s favor is based on ethical conduct rather than arbitrary divine whim, given the text does not explicitly link the reward to the promise fulfillment?
The notion that a deity can assume animal form may be metaphorical rather than literal; could the bull represent a symbolic vehicle of instruction rather than an actual transformation?
Addressing the deity as ‘lord’ might be a conventional honorific rather than an indication of recognized divine authority, questioning the claim about reverence irrespective of form
The request to go to the teacher’s house could simply reflect a narrative device rather than a doctrinal emphasis on the guru, so the claim about centrality of teacher may be overstated

sanskrit: स य एतमेवं विद्वांश्चतुष्कलं पादं ब्रह्मणः प्रकाशवानित्युपास्ते प्रकाशवानस्मिँल्लोके भवति प्रकाशवतो ह लोकाञ्जयति य एतमेवं विद्वांश्चतुष्कलं पादं ब्रह्मणः प्रकाशवानित्युपास्ते
transliteration: sa ya etamevaṃ vidvāṃścatuṣkalaṃ pādaṃ brahmaṇaḥ prakāśavānityupāste prakāśavānasmim̐lloke bhavati prakāśavato ha lokāñjayati ya etamevaṃ vidvāṃścatuṣkalaṃ pādaṃ brahmaṇaḥ prakāśavānityupāste
translation: ‘He who knows this foot of Brahman, which has four parts and is called “the Shining, ” and worships it as such becomes famous in this world. He who knows this foot of Brahman, which has four parts and is called “the Shining, ” and worships it as such attains other worlds which are luminous’.
word_meaning: Saḥ yaḥ etam evam vidvān, he who knows this thus; catuṣkalam pādam brahmaṇaḥ, one foot [or quarter] of Brahman having four parts; prakāśavān iti, known as the shining; upāste, [and] meditates on it; prakāśavān asmin loke bhavati, becomes famous in this world; yaḥ etam evam vidvān, he who knows this thus; catuṣkalam pādam brahmaṇaḥ, one foot of Brahman having four parts; prakāśavān iti, known as the shining; upāste, [and] meditates on it; prakāśavataḥ ha lokān jayati, wins luminous worlds after death.
commentary: If you worship Brahman as luminous, you yourself become luminous—that is, you become famous. But not only that, after your death you go to those luminous worlds where gods and goddesses live.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
Progressive Worship of Brahman up to the Universal Self
claim_candidates: Knowing and meditating on the luminous foot of Brahman guarantees fame in this world
Worship of the shining aspect of Brahman results in attainment of luminous afterlife realms
The four‑part foot of Brahman represents a specific manifestation of Brahman that can be objectified in worship
Spiritual illumination (prakāśa) is both a cause and effect of devotion to Brahman
The text suggests that knowledge of Brahman's foot is sufficient for liberation from ordinary existence
objection_hooks: The claim that fame in this world follows from worship may conflate worldly reputation with spiritual merit, raising logical tension
The assertion that worship guarantees luminous worlds assumes a deterministic afterlife, which may be challenged by epistemic doubt about scriptural authority
Identifying a “foot” of Brahman as a distinct object could conflict with the non‑dual doctrine that Brahman is indivisible, causing ontological confusion
The idea that knowledge alone leads to liberation overlooks the role of ethical conduct, questioning the completeness of the claim

sanskrit: अग्निष्टे पादं वक्तेति स ह श्वोभूते ग आभिप्रस्थापयांचकार ता यत्राभि सायं बभूवुस्तत्राग्निमुपसमाधाय गा उपरुध्य समिधमाधाय पश्चादग्नेः प्राङुपोपविवेश
transliteration: agniṣṭe pādaṃ vakteti sa ha śvobhūte ga ābhiprasthāpayāṃcakāra tā yatrābhi sāyaṃ babhūvustatrāgnimupasamādhāya gā uparudhya samidhamādhāya paścādagneḥ prāṅupopaviveśa
translation: [Then the bull said, ] ‘ Agni [fire] will tell you about another foot of Brahman .’ The next day Satyakāma collected the cows and drove them towards his teacher’s house. At dusk they arrived at a place [where they halted for the night]. Having confined the cows and collected some fuel, he lit a fire and sat down just behind it facing east.
word_meaning: Agniḥ te pādam vaktā iti, Agni [fire] will tell you about [another] foot; saḥ ha śvaḥ-bhūte gāḥ abhiprasthāpayāñcakāra, the next day he led the cows [towards his teacher’s house]; yatra sāyam, when it was dusk; tāḥ abhi-babhūvuḥ, they arrived at a place; tatra agnim upasamādhāya, having made a fire there; gāḥ uparudhya, keeping the cows confined; samidham ādhāya, having collected fuel; paścāt agneḥ, behind the fire; prāk upa-upaviveśa, sat facing the east.
commentary: The next day Satyakāma finished his morning rites and then started for the teacher’s house with the cows. They halted for the night at a suitable spot, and after gathering the cows together, Satyakāma lit a fire and sat by it facing east. The bull had told him that Agni (fire) would teach him about another foot of Brahman. He began to wonder what Agni would say and when he would say it. He could not think of anything else.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The fire Agni functions as an autonomous teacher capable of revealing a distinct aspect of Brahman
Brahman possesses multiple feet or aspects, indicating that the ultimate reality can be apprehended through successive revelations
Sitting by the fire facing east is prescribed as an appropriate posture for receiving divine instruction about Brahman
Non-human entities such as a bull can convey legitimate spiritual guidance concerning the nature of Brahman
The ritual act of gathering cows and preparing fire serves as a necessary preparatory condition for the transmission of Brahman knowledge
objection_hooks: How can an inanimate element like fire possess the agency to teach, suggesting the claim may be metaphorical rather than literal
Describing Brahman as having multiple feet implies a part‑whole relation that conflicts with the non‑dual assertion of Brahman's indivisibility
The requirement to sit facing east before fire may reflect cultural convention rather than an essential condition for spiritual insight
Relying on a bull’s message could undermine the primacy of rational inquiry, raising epistemic doubt about the authority of such revelations

sanskrit: तमग्निरभ्युवाद सत्यकाम३ इति भगव इति ह प्रतिशुश्राव
transliteration: tamagnirabhyuvāda satyakāma3 iti bhagava iti ha pratiśuśrāva
translation: Fire called to him, ‘O Satyakāma.’ He replied, ‘Yes, lord’.
word_meaning: Agniḥ, fire; tam abhyuvāda, called to him; satyakāma iti, O Satyakāma; bhagavaḥ iti ha pratiśuśrāva, he replied, ‘Yes, lord.’
claim_candidates: The fire (Agni) is addressed as a lord, indicating its divine authority in the dialogue
The individual Satyakāma acknowledges the fire's address with a respectful affirmation, showing reverence to elemental divinity
The name Satyakāma, meaning truth‑desiring, suggests that the seeker aligns truth with the divine fire
The exchange exemplifies a reciprocal recognition between the seeker and the divine, where the seeker affirms the divine summons
objection_hooks: The title “lord” may be a conventional honorific rather than an assertion of actual divinity, questioning the claim of divine authority
The respectful reply could be a ritualistic formality, not genuine reverence, challenging the claim of sincere acknowledgment
The etymology of Satyakāma does not necessarily imply a philosophical link to fire, undermining the claim of truth being associated with fire
The brief interaction may not constitute a full reciprocal recognition of divinity, disputing the claim of mutual acknowledgment

sanskrit: ब्रह्मणः सोम्य ते पादं ब्रवाणीति ब्रवीतु मे भगवानिति तस्मै होवाच पृथिवी कलान्तरिक्षं कला द्यौः कला समुद्रः कलैष वै सोम्य चतुष्कलः पादो ब्रह्मणोऽनन्तवान्नाम
transliteration: brahmaṇaḥ somya te pādaṃ bravāṇīti bravītu me bhagavāniti tasmai hovāca pṛthivī kalāntarikṣaṃ kalā dyauḥ kalā samudraḥ kalaiṣa vai somya catuṣkalaḥ pādo brahmaṇo'nantavānnāma
translation: [Fire said, ] ‘O Somya, let me tell you about one foot of Brahman .’ [Satyakāma replied, ] ‘Yes, lord, please tell me.’ [Fire] said to him: ‘The earth is one part, the mid-region is another part, heaven is a third part, and the ocean is a fourth part. O Somya, these are the four parts that make up a foot of Brahman. This foot is named Anantavān, the Unlimited’.
word_meaning: Somya, O Somya; brahmaṇaḥ te pādam bravāṇi iti, I will now tell you about a foot of Brahman; bravītu me bhagavān iti, yes, lord, please tell me; tasmai ha uvāca, [fire] said to him; pṛthivī kalā, the earth is one part; antarikṣam kalā, the space between heaven and earth is one part; dyauḥ kalā, heaven is one part; samudraḥ kalā, the ocean is one part; eṣaḥ vai somya catuṣkalaḥ pādaḥ brahmaṇaḥ, O Somya, these are the four parts that make up one foot of Brahman; anantavān nāma, named Anantavān, the Unlimited.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The four macrocosmic divisions—earth, antariksha, heaven, and ocean—collectively constitute a single foot of the infinite Brahman, indicating that Brahman pervades all realms
Naming this foot Anantavān (the Unlimited) implies that even a limited portion of Brahman is itself infinite, suggesting that any part of Brahman embodies its totality
The fire (Agni) acting as speaker demonstrates that elemental forces can convey authoritative knowledge of Brahman's structure, positioning fire as a conduit of divine revelation
The foot metaphor provides a pedagogical framework whereby the infinite Brahman can be approached through comprehensible partial representations, facilitating realization of the universal self
objection_hooks: If a foot of Brahman is limited to four parts, how can it be accurately described as unlimited without contradiction?
Can the testimony of fire be considered a reliable source for doctrinal truth, or is it merely symbolic language?
Does asserting that any part of Brahman is infinite not imply a division within Brahman, conflicting with the principle of its indivisibility?
Is the identification of earth, space, heaven, and ocean as a foot of Brahman universally valid, or does it reflect a culturally specific cosmology?

sanskrit: स य एतमेवं विद्वांश्चतुष्कलं पादं ब्रह्मणोऽनन्तवानित्युपास्तेऽनन्तवानस्मिँल्लोके भवत्यनन्तवतो ह लोकाञ्जयति य एतमेवं विद्वांश्चतुष्कलं पादं ब्रह्मणोऽनन्तवानित्युपास्ते
transliteration: sa ya etamevaṃ vidvāṃścatuṣkalaṃ pādaṃ brahmaṇo'nantavānityupāste'nantavānasmim̐lloke bhavatyanantavato ha lokāñjayati ya etamevaṃ vidvāṃścatuṣkalaṃ pādaṃ brahmaṇo'nantavānityupāste
translation: ‘He who knows this foot of Brahman, which has four parts and is known as “the Unlimited, ” and worships it as such becomes long-lived in this world. He who knows this foot of Brahman, which has four parts and is known as “the Unlimited, ” and worships it as such attains worlds which are long-lasting’.
word_meaning: Saḥ yaḥ etam evam vidvān, he who knows this thus; catuṣkalam pādam brahmaṇaḥ, one foot of Brahman having four parts; anantavān iti, known as the Unlimited; upāste, [and] meditates on it; anantavān asmin loke bhavati, becomes long-lived in this world; yaḥ etam evam vidvān, he who knows this thus; catuṣkalam pādam brahmaṇaḥ, one foot of Brahman having four parts; anantavān iti, known as the Unlimited; upāste, [and] meditates on it; anantavataḥ ha lokān jayati, wins long-lasting worlds after death.
contextual_topics: Progressive Worship of Brahman up to the Universal Self
The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
claim_candidates: He who knows the four‑part foot of Brahman called the Unlimited and worships it attains an extended lifespan in this world
The same worship of the Unlimited foot of Brahman leads to the acquisition of long‑lasting worlds after death
By naming Brahman's foot as having four parts and as the Unlimited, the text uses this aspect as a symbol of Brahman's infinite nature
The passage presents knowledge and worship of this Brahman‑symbol as sufficient for both worldly longevity and post‑mortem cosmic reward without mentioning other rites
objection_hooks: The link between a symbolic foot and physical longevity may be metaphorical rather than literal, challenging the factual claim
Claiming that worship of a single aspect of Brahman guarantees post‑death worlds may conflict with other Upanishadic teachings that stress complete self‑realization
Describing a foot as Unlimited appears contradictory, raising ontological confusion about how a limited part can represent infinity
Asserting that this practice alone ensures longevity and cosmic reward overlooks the importance of ethical conduct emphasized elsewhere

sanskrit: हंसस्ते पादं वक्तेति स ह श्वोभूते गा अभिप्रस्थापयांचकार ता यत्राभि सायं बभूवुस्तत्राग्निमुपसमाधाय गा उपरुध्य समिधमाधाय पश्चादग्नेः प्राङुपोपविवेश
transliteration: haṃsaste pādaṃ vakteti sa ha śvobhūte gā abhiprasthāpayāṃcakāra tā yatrābhi sāyaṃ babhūvustatrāgnimupasamādhāya gā uparudhya samidhamādhāya paścādagneḥ prāṅupopaviveśa
translation: [Then the fire said, ] ‘The swan will tell you about another foot of Brahman .’ The next day Satyakāma collected the cows and drove them towards his teacher’s house. At dusk they arrived at a place [where they halted for the night]. Having confined the cows and collected some fuel, he lit a fire and sat down just behind it facing east.
word_meaning: Haṃsaḥ te pādam vaktā iti, the swan will tell you about [another] foot; saḥ ha śvaḥ-bhūte gāḥ abhiprasthāpayāñcakāra, the next day he led the cows [towards his teacher’s house]; yātra sāyam, when it was dusk; tāḥ abhi-babhūvuḥ, they arrived at a place; tatra agnim upasamādhāya, having made a fire there; gāḥ uparudhya, keeping the cows confined; samidham ādhāya, having collected fuel; paścāt agneḥ, behind the fire; prāk upa-upaviveśa, sat facing the east.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The fire functions as a didactic medium that conveys knowledge of Brahman
The swan is presented as a symbolic messenger revealing a further aspect of Brahman
The ritual act of lighting a fire and sitting behind it facing east is prescribed for approaching knowledge of Brahman

objection_hooks: The fire's speech may be metaphorical rather than an actual teaching medium, questioning the claim that fire serves as a didactic entity

The described ritual actions could be routine duties without inherent spiritual significance, undermining the claim that they are prescribed methods for attaining knowledge of Brahman
The mention of cows may be a narrative detail unrelated to spiritual integration, making the claim that material duties are integrated with spiritual inquiry speculative

sanskrit: तंहंस उपनिपत्याभ्युवाद सत्यकाम३ इति भगव इति ह प्रतिशुश्राव
transliteration: taṃhaṃsa upanipatyābhyuvāda satyakāma3 iti bhagava iti ha pratiśuśrāva
translation: The swan came flying to him and said, ‘O Satyakāma.’ Satyakāma replied, ‘Yes, lord’.
word_meaning: Haṃsaḥ upanipatya, the swan flew near; tam abhyuvāda satyakāma iti, [and] called to him, ‘O Satyakāma’; bhagavaḥ iti ha pratiśuśrāva, he replied, ‘Yes, lord.’
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The swan addresses Satyakāma with the title ‘lord’, indicating that the bird recognizes a divine authority
Satyakāma’s reply ‘Yes, lord’ shows his acceptance of being spoken to as a deity
The interaction suggests that the divine can manifest in the form of a swan

sanskrit: ब्रह्मणः सोम्य ते पादं ब्रवाणीति ब्रवीतु मे भगवानिति तस्मै होवाचाग्निः कला सूर्यः कला चन्द्रः कला विद्युत्कलैष वै सोम्य चतुष्कलः पादो ब्रह्मणो ज्योतिष्मान्नाम
transliteration: brahmaṇaḥ somya te pādaṃ bravāṇīti bravītu me bhagavāniti tasmai hovācāgniḥ kalā sūryaḥ kalā candraḥ kalā vidyutkalaiṣa vai somya catuṣkalaḥ pādo brahmaṇo jyotiṣmānnāma

commentary: The swan is speaking here of luminous things, such as fire, the sun, etc. Its partiality for luminous things gives rise to the suspicion that it is itself something luminous. It is, in fact, Āditya, the sun.

sanskrit: स य एतमेवं विद्वांश्चतुष्कलं पादं ब्रह्मणो ज्योतिष्मानित्युपास्ते ज्योतिष्मानस्मिँल्लोके भवति ज्योतिष्मतो ह लोकाञ्जयति य एतमेवं विद्वांश्चतुष्कलं पादं ब्रह्मणो ज्योतिष्मानित्युपास्ते

sanskrit: मद्गुष्टे पादं वक्तेति स ह श्वोभूते गा अभिप्रस्थापयांचकार ता यत्राभि सायं बभूवुस्तत्राग्निमुपसमाधाय गा उपरुध्य समिधमाधाय पश्चादग्नेः प्राङुपोपविवेश

commentary: The madgu, or diver-bird, is most of the time in water. Because of its close connection with water, and because water sustains life, the diver-bird stands for life ( prāṇa ).

sanskrit: ब्रह्मणः सोम्य ते पादं ब्रवाणीति ब्रवीतु मे भगवानिति तस्मै होवाच प्राणः कला चक्षुः कला श्रोत्रं कला मनः कलैष वै सोम्य चतुष्कलः पादो ब्रह्मण आयतनवान्नाम
transliteration: brahmaṇaḥ somya te pādaṃ bravāṇīti bravītu me bhagavāniti tasmai hovāca prāṇaḥ kalā cakṣuḥ kalā śrotraṃ kalā manaḥ kalaiṣa vai somya catuṣkalaḥ pādo brahmaṇa āyatanavānnāma
translation: [The madgu said, ] ‘O Somya, let me tell you about one foot of Brahman .’ [Satyakāma replied, ] ‘Yes, lord, please tell me.’ [The madgu] said to him: ‘ Prāṇa is one part, the eyes are another part, the ears are a third part, and the mind is a fourth part. O Somya, these are the four parts that make up a foot of Brahman. This foot is named Āyatanavān, the Support’.
word_meaning: Somya, O Somya; brahmaṇaḥ te pādam bravāṇi iti, I will now tell you about a foot [or quarter] of Brahman; bravītu me bhagavān iti, yes, lord, please tell me; tasmai ha uvāca, [the madgu] said to him; prāṇaḥ kalā, prāṇah [the vital force] is one part; cakṣuḥ kalā, the eyes are one part; śrotram kalā, the ears are one part; manaḥ kalā, the mind is one part; eṣaḥ vai somya catuṣkalaḥ pādaḥ brahmaṇaḥ, O Somya, these are the four parts that make up a foot of Brahman; āyatanavān nāma, named Āyatanavān, the Support.
commentary: This part of the story, about the madgu, is devoted to the teaching of prāṇa. In fact, the madgu represents prāṇa. Here the role of the mind has to be understood. The mind is the fourth part of this foot of Brahman, and it is the repository of all that we experience through our diverse organs. This is why it is called Āyatanavān, the Support.

He who knows this foot of Brahman, which has four parts and is known as “the Support, ” and worships it as such attains worlds which are spacious’.
word_meaning: Saḥ yaḥ etam evam vidvān, he who knows this thus; catuṣkalam pādam brahmaṇaḥ, one foot [or quarter] of Brahman having four parts; āyatanavān iti, known as the Support; upāste, [and] meditates on it; āyatanavān asmin loke bhavati, becomes āyatanavān [i.e., a support to others] in this world; yaḥ etam evam vidvān, he who knows this thus; catuṣkalam pādam brahmaṇaḥ, one foot of Brahman having four parts; āyatanavān iti, known as the Support [i.e., it is spacious and therefore able to support things]; upāste, [and] meditates on it; āyatanavataḥ ha lokān jayati, wins spacious worlds after death.
commentary: If a person worships this foot of Brahman as āyatanavān—that is, as spacious—he himself becomes spacious. Being spacious means that he can give shelter to many. He has this advantage as long as he is alive. Then when he dies he is able to attain many larger worlds.

sanskrit: ब्रह्मविदिव वै सोम्य भासि को नु त्वानुशशासेत्यन्ये मनुष्येभ्य इति ह प्रतिजज्ञे भगवांस्त्वेव मे कामे ब्रूयात्
transliteration: brahmavidiva vai somya bhāsi ko nu tvānuśaśāsetyanye manuṣyebhya iti ha pratijajñe bhagavāṃstveva me kāme brūyāt
translation: The teacher said: ‘Somya, you shine like one who has known Brahman . Who taught you?’ Satyakāma assured him: ‘Certainly no human being. But will you, O Lord, please teach me now about Brahman, the subject closest to my heart?’.
word_meaning: Brahmavit iva vai somya bhāsi, [the teacher, Gautama, said to Satyakāma, ] Somya, you are shining like one who has known Brahman; kaḥ nu tvā anuśaśāsa iti, who taught you; anye manuṣyebhyaḥ, somebody other than a human being; iti ha pratijajñe, he assured him; bhagavān tu eva me kāme bruyāt, but, Lord, teach me now about Brahman, the subject closest to my heart.
commentary: The look on Satyakāma’s face surprised his teacher. He looked like a knower of Brahman. He was shining. What are the signs of a person who has known Brahman? According to Śaṅkara, that person is happy and cheerful, with a smile on his face all the time. His mind is always under control, as are his sense organs. He is also free from desires and therefore from worries. Satyakāma had these signs. This is why his teacher asked him who had taught him. Satyakāma emphatically said that no human being had taught him. He meant thereby that so long as his teacher was there he needed no other human being to teach him. He also assured his teacher that he had now come to him to learn about Brahman, the subject dearest to him.
