transliteration: taṃ jāyovāca tapto brahmacārī kuśalamagnīnparicacārīnmā tvāgnayaḥ paripravocanprabrūhyasmā iti tasmai hāprocyaiva pravāsāṃcakre
translation: Satyakāma’s wife said to him: ‘The brahmacārin is much reduced by austerities and has looked after the fires with great care. Lest the fires blame you, I suggest you teach him.’ But Satyakāma did not teach him. Instead, he left on a journey.

sanskrit: स ह व्याधिनानशितुं दध्रे तमाचार्यजायोवाच ब्रह्मचारिन्नशान किं नु नाश्नासीति स होवाच बहव इमेऽस्मिन्पुरुषे कामा नानात्यया व्याधीभिः प्रतिपूर्णोऽस्मि नाशिष्यामीति
transliteration: sa ha vyādhinānaśituṃ dadhre tamācāryajāyovāca brahmacārinnaśāna kiṃ nu nāśnāsīti sa hovāca bahava ime'sminpuruṣe kāmā nānātyayā vyādhībhiḥ pratipūrṇo'smi nāśiṣyāmīti
translation: Upakosala was upset and started fasting. His teacher’s wife said to him: ‘ Brahmacārin, eat something. Why are you not eating?’ Upakosala said: ‘There are too many desires in me and they are pulling me in different directions. I am like one suffering from many ailments. I don’t want to eat’.
word_meaning: Saḥ, he [Upakosala]; ha vyādhinā, due to mental affliction; anaśitum dadhre, started fasting; tam ācārya - jāyā uvāca, the teacher’s wife said to him; brahmacārin aśāna, brahmacārin, start eatine; kim nu na āśnāsi iti, why are you not eating; saḥ ha uvāca, he [Upakosala] said; bahavaḥ ime asmin puruṣe kāmāḥ there are many desires in this person; nānātyayāḥ, they are pulling me in different directions; vyādhibhiḥ pratipūrṇaḥ asmi, I am full of ailments; na aśiṣyāmi iti, I will not eat anything.

sanskrit: अथ हाग्नयः समूदिरे तप्तो ब्रह्मचारी कुशलं नः पर्यचारीद्धन्तास्मै प्रब्रवामेति तस्मै होचुः प्राणो ब्रह्म कं ब्रह्म खं ब्रह्मेति
transliteration: atha hāgnayaḥ samūdire tapto brahmacārī kuśalaṃ naḥ paryacārīddhantāsmai prabravāmeti tasmai hocuḥ prāṇo brahma kaṃ brahma khaṃ brahmeti
translation: Then the fires—the Dakṣiṇāgni, the Gārhapatya, and the Āhavanīya —began to say to each other: ‘This brahmacārin has become thin from practising austerities. word_meaning: Atha ha agnayaḥ samūdire, then the fires [the Dakṣiṇāgni, the Gārhapatya, and the Āhavanīya] began to say; taptaḥ brahmacārī, the austere brahmacārin; kuśalam, with great care; naḥ paryacārīt, looked after us; hanta asmai prabravāma iti, so we will teach him; tasmai ha ucuḥ, they said to him; prāṇaḥ brahma, prāṇa is Brahman; kam brahma, happiness is Brahman; kham brahma iti, ākāśa [space] is Brahman.
commentary: The three fires that had been so well taken care of by Upakosala were moved to see his condition. They also felt that a great injustice had been done to him by his teacher, Satyakāma. They then decided to take it upon themselves to teach him.

sanskrit: स होवाच विजानाम्यहं यत्प्राणो ब्रह्म कं च तु खं च न विजानामीति ते होचुर्यद्वाव कं तदेव खं यदेव खं तदेव कमिति प्राणं च हास्मै तदाकाशं चोचुः
transliteration: sa hovāca vijānāmyahaṃ yatprāṇo brahma kaṃ ca tu khaṃ ca na vijānāmīti te hocuryadvāva kaṃ tadeva khaṃ yadeva khaṃ tadeva kamiti prāṇaṃ ca hāsmai tadākāśaṃ cocuḥ
translation: Upakosala said: ‘I know that prāṇa is Brahman . But that ka and kha are Brahman I do not know.’ The fires replied, ‘That which is ka is also kha, and that which is kha is also ka .’ Then the fires taught him that Brahman was both prāṇa and ākāśa [space].
word_meaning: Saḥ ha uvāca, he [Upakosala] said; vijānāmi aham yat prāṇa brahma, I know that prāṇa is Brahman; kam ca tu kham ca na vijānāmi iti, but I don’t know that ‘ka’ and ‘kha’ are Brahman; te ha ucaḥ, they [the fires] said; yat vāva kam tat eva kham, that which is ‘ka’ is also ‘kha’; yat eva kham tat eva kam iti, that which is ‘kha’ is also ‘ka’; prāṇam ca ha asmai tat ākāśam ca ucaḥ, then they taught him about prāṇa and ākāśa [space].
commentary: Upakosala had no difficulty accepting that prāṇa was Brahman, for prāṇa is the vital breath and Without the vital breath, life is impossible. In view of its importance it may be conceded that prāṇa is Brahman. But how can ka and kha be Brahman? Upakosala thought to himself: ‘ Ka is happiness, but what kind of happiness? It is happiness born of sense experience. It is therefore transitory. It cannot be the same as Brahman. Similarly, kha is also transitory, for it means ākāśa, space. Ākāśa is material and therefore transitory.’ The fires then said that ka and kha are used as both nouns and adjectives, and sometimes they qualify each other. Kha as an adjective may qualify ka when ka stands for Brahman. What does ka mean here? Here it means Brahman without any attributes. Similarly, when we say kha, we mean ākāśa. When we say ka is kha, we mean ‘pleasure’ is ākāśa. But this is not the material ākāśa. Here it means the ākāśa, space, inside the heart. The idea is that Brahman and joy ( ka ) are both in the space inside the heart ( khā ).

The Universal Self

sanskrit: अथ हैनं गार्हपत्योऽनुशशास पृथिव्यग्निरन्नमादित्य इति य एष आदित्ये पुरुषो दृश्यते सोऽहमस्मि स एवाहमस्मीति
transliteration: atha hainaṃ gārhapatyo'nuśaśāsa pṛthivyagnirannamāditya iti ya eṣa āditye puruṣo dṛśyate so'hamasmi sa evāhamasmīti
translation: Then the Gārhapatya fire said to him [Upakosala]: ‘The earth, fire, food, and the sun—these are all part of my [i.e., part of Brahman ’s] body. The person seen in the solar orb is me. I am that’.
word_meaning: Atha ha enam gārhapatyaḥ anuśaśāsa, next the Gārhapatya fire gave him this instruction; pṛthivī agniḥ annam ādityaḥ iti, the earth, fire, food, and the sun [are all part of me—i.e., of Brahman]; yaḥ eṣaḥ āditye puruṣaḥ dṛśyate, the person seen in the sun; saḥ aham asmi saḥ eva aham asmi iti, I am he, I am he.
commentary: First the fires taught Upakosala together. Now they are teaching him separately. The Gārhapatya fire begins. He said: ‘The earth, fire, food, and the sun—these constitute my body. I divide myself into these things. There in the solar region is a person. That is me. I am known as the Gārhapatya fire and I am also this person in the solar region. Earth and food are both objects of enjoyment and consumption, but fire and the sun are not in this category. They are similar to each other, however, just as food and the earth are similar to each other, being objects that people can enjoy.’

sanskrit: ते होचुरुपकोसलैषा सोम्य तेऽस्मद्विद्यात्मविद्या चाचार्यस्तु ते गतिं वक्तेत्याजगाम हास्याचार्यस्तमाचार्योऽभ्युवादोपकोसल३ इति
transliteration: te hocurupakosalaiṣā somya te'smadvidyātmavidyā cācāryastu te gatiṃ vaktetyājagāma hāsyācāryastamācāryo'bhyuvādopakosala3 iti
translation: The fires said: ‘O Somya Upakosala, we have just told you the knowledge of fire. That is also Self-knowledge. Your teacher will tell you about the way to the next world.’ In due course, his teacher returned, and he called him, saying, ‘Upakosala’.
word_meaning: Te ha ucuḥ, they [the fires] said; upakosala somya, O Somya Upakosala; eṣā te asmat vidyā, this knowledge about us [we have given] to you; ca ātma -vidyā, that is also Self-knowledge; ācāryaḥ tu te gatim vakta iti, but the teacher will tell you about the way [to the next world]; asya ācāryaḥ, his teacher; ājagāma ha, returned; ācāryaḥ abhyuvāda tam upakosala iti, the teacher called him, ‘O Upakosala.’
commentary: What the fire meant was that Upakosala’s teacher would give him the final lesson. He would tell Upakosala what he should do to get the full benefit of what he had learned from the fires.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman

sanskrit: भगव इति ह प्रतिशुश्राव ब्रह्मविद इव सोम्य ते मुखं भाति को नु त्वानुशशासेति को नु मानुशिष्याद्भो इतीहापेव निह्नुत इमे नूनमीदृशा अन्यादृशा इतीहाग्नीनभ्यूदे किं नु सोम्य किल तेऽवोचन्निति
transliteration: bhagava iti ha pratiśuśrāva brahmavida iva somya te mukhaṃ bhāti ko nu tvānuśaśāseti ko nu mānuśiṣyādbho itīhāpeva nihnuta ime nūnamīdṛśā anyādṛśā itīhāgnīnabhyūde kiṃ nu somya kila te'vocanniti
translation: [Upakosala] replied, ‘Yes, lord.’ [His teacher said: ] ‘O Somya, your face is shining like that of a knower of Brahman . Who has taught you?’ ‘Sir, who will teach me?’ He said this as if he was trying to hide the truth. Then, pointing to the fires, he said: ‘Earlier they looked, different. Now they look like this.’ In this way, he indicated the fires. [The teacher asked, ] ‘Somya, what did the fires teach you?’.
word_meaning: Bhagavaḥ iti ha pratiśuśrāva, ‘Yes, lord, ’ he replied; brahmavidaḥ iva somya te mukham bhāti, your face is shining like that of a knower of Brahman; kaḥ nu tvā anuśaśāsa iti, who has taught you; kaḥ nu mā anuśiṣyāt bho iti, who will teach me, sir; iha iva apanihnute, [he said this] as if he was trying to hide [the truth]; ime, these [pointing to the fires]; nūnam īdṛśāḥ, look like this [as if they are frightened]; anyādṛśāḥ iti, looked different before; iha agnīn abhyūde, in this way he spoke about the fires; kim nu somya kila te avocan iti, Somya, what did they teach you?
commentary: Upakosala knew the limitations of the fires, and that is why he did not want to tell his teacher what they had taught him, or that they had taught him anything at all. Further, he noticed that in the presence of his teacher the fires appeared to be frozen with fear. This is why he was vague and evasive in his reply.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman

sanskrit: इदमिति ह प्रतिजज्ञे लोकान्वाव किल सोम्य तेऽवोचन्नहं तु ते तद्वक्ष्यामि यथा पुष्करपलाश आपो न श्लिष्यन्त एवमेवंविदि पापं कर्म न श्लिष्यत इति ब्रवीतु मे भगवानिति तस्मै होवाच
transliteration: idamiti ha pratijajñe lokānvāva kila somya te'vocannahaṃ tu te tadvakṣyāmi yathā puṣkarapalāśa āpo na śliṣyanta evamevaṃvidi pāpaṃ karma na śliṣyata iti bravītu me bhagavāniti tasmai hovāca
translation: Upakosala replied, ‘This is what they said.’ [And he told his teacher all that the fires had taught him.] The teacher said: ‘O Somya, they taught you only about the worlds, but I will teach you about Brahman .
word_meaning: Idam iti ha pratijajñe, ‘This [is what they taught, ]’ he [Upakosala] replied; lokān vāva kila somya te avocan, they have only told you about the worlds, O Somya; aham tu te tat vakṣyāmi, but I will tell you about that [Brahman]; yathā puṣkara -palāśe āpaḥ na śliṣyante, as water does not stick to the lotus leaf; evam, in the same way; vidi, one who knows [Brahman]; evam, thus; pāpam karma na śliṣyate iti, is not tainted by sinful work; bravītu me bhagavān iti, sir, please teach me; tasmai ha uvāca, he said to him.
commentary: Just as water never sticks to a lotus leaf, similarly, sin never sticks to one who knows Brahman thus.’ Upakosala replied, ‘Sir, please teach me about Brahman.’ The teacher said— A person who has known Brahman is always pure. Nothing can taint him. He is incapable of doing anything wrong.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman

sanskrit: य एषोऽक्षिणि पुरुषो दृश्यत एष आत्मेति होवाचैतदमृतमभयमेतद्ब्रह्मेति तद्यद्यप्यस्मिन्सर्पिर्वोदकं वा सिञ्चति वर्त्मनी एव गच्छति
transliteration: ya eṣo'kṣiṇi puruṣo dṛśyata eṣa ātmeti hovācaitadamṛtamabhayametadbrahmeti tadyadyapyasminsarpirvodakaṃ vā siñcati vartmanī eva gacchati
translation: The teacher said: ‘The person seen in the eyes is the Self. It is immortal and fearless. It is Brahman . This is why, if anyone puts clarified butter or water in the eyes, it goes to the corners of the eyes’.
word_meaning: Yaḥ eṣaḥ akṣiṇi puruṣaḥ dṛśyate, this person who is seen in the eyes; eṣaḥ ātmā, this is the Self; iti ha uvāca, he [the teacher] said; etat amṛtam abhayam, this is immortal and fearless; etat brahma iti, this is Brahman; tat, this is why; asmin, into this [eye]; yadi api sarpiḥ vā udakam vā siñcati, if anyone puts clarified butter or water; vartmanī eva gacchati, it goes into the comers [of the eye].
commentary: How do you know the Self? You have to have full self-control. You have to have a gentle nature, and you must withdraw your mind completely from the external world. Then you can see the Self in the eyes. That Self is immortal, fearless, and it is Brahman (literally, ‘the biggest’). As water does not stick to a lotus leaf, so also, if water or something else is put in the eyes, it does not hurt them because the eyelids protect them. This is why the eyelids are called ‘lotuses.’ The eyes are the seat of the Self. What the Upaniṣad is saying is that if the seat of the Self is pure and not susceptible to any impurity, the Self is naturally the same.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
The Universal Self

sanskrit: एतं संयद्वाम इत्याचक्षत एतं हि सर्वाणि वामान्यभिसंयन्ति सर्वाण्येनं वामान्यभिसंयन्ति य एवं वेद

translation: They call him Saṃyadvāma, for everything that is good and beautiful comes to him. One who knows this has everything that is good and beautiful come to him.
word_meaning: Etam saṃyadvāmaḥ iti ācakṣate, they call him Saṃyadvāma [i.e., one in whom everything that is good is concentrated]; hi, because; etam sarvāṇi vāmāni abhisaṃyanti, all good and beautiful things come to him; yaḥ evam veda, he who knows thus; sarvāṇi enam vāmāni abhisaṃyanti, all good and beautiful things come to him.
commentary: The word vāma means ‘attractive, ’ ‘beautiful, ’ or ‘desirable.’ The Self is Saṃyadvāma because all good things become concentrated in it. And one who knows the Self also becomes the receptacle of all good things.

sanskrit: एष उ एव वामनीरेष हि सर्वाणि वामानि नयति सर्वाणि वामानि नयति य एवं वेद

translation: This person in the eyes is Vāmanī, the source of all that is good and pure, for he inspires in people all that is good and pure. One who knows this grants all that is good and pure to others.
word_meaning: Eṣaḥ u eva vāmanīḥ, and this [person in the eyes] is Vāmanī [the source of all that is good and pure]; hi, for; eṣaḥ, this [person in the eyes]; eva, surely; sarvāṇi vāmāni nayati, grants all that is good and pure; yaḥ evam veda, he who knows thus; sarvāṇi vāmāni nayati, grants all that is good and pure.
commentary: The word vāmanī means one who carries the fruits of good work to all beings according to what they deserve. He is the support of all that is good. One who knows this conveys the fruits of good work to others.

sanskrit: एष उ एव भामनीरेष हि सर्वेषु लोकेषु भाति सर्वेषु लोकेषु भाति य एवं वेद

translation: The person in the eyes is Bhāmanī, shining, for he shines in all the worlds [including the sun]. One who knows this shines in all the worlds.

commentary: This person in the eyes is the source of all light. The Kaṭha Upaniṣad [II.2.15] says, ‘All this shines because he shines.’

sanskrit: अथ यदु चैवास्मिञ्छव्यं कुर्वन्ति यदि च नार्चिषमेवाभिसंभवन्त्यर्चिषोऽहरह्न आपूर्यमाणपक्षमापूर्यमाणपक्षाद्यान्षडुदङ्ङेति मासांस्तान्मासेभ्यः संवत्सरं संवत्सरादादित्यमादित्याच्चन्द्रमसं चन्द्रमसो विद्युतं तत् पुरुषोऽमानवः स एनान्ब्रह्म गमयत्येष देवपथो ब्रह्मपथ एतेन प्रतिपद्यमाना इमं मानवमावर्तं नावर्तन्ते नावर्तन्ते
transliteration: atha yadu caivāsmiñchavyaṃ kurvanti yadi ca nārciṣamevābhisaṃbhavantyarciṣo'harahna āpūryamāṇapakṣamāpūryamāṇapakṣādyānṣaḍudaṅṅeti māsāṃstānmāsebhyaḥ saṃvatsaraṃ saṃvatsarādādityamādityāccandramasaṃ candramaso vidyutaṃ tat puruṣo'mānavaḥ sa enānbrahma gamayatyeṣa devapatho brahmapatha etena pratipadyamānā imaṃ mānavamāvartaṃ nāvartante nāvartante
translation: Then, for those who know this, whether proper funeral rites are performed or not, they go after death to the world of light. From the world of light they go to the world of day; from the world of day to the world of the bright fortnight; from the world of the bright fortnight to the six months when the sun moves northward; from there they go to the year; from the year to the sun; from the sun to the moon; and from the moon to lightning. There someone, not human, receives them and leads them to brahmaloka . This is the way of the gods. This is also the way to Brahman . Those who go by this path never return to this mortal world. They never return.
word_meaning: Atha, then; yat, if; u ca eva asmin, in this situation [i.e., for those who know the Self in the eyes]; śavyam, funeral rites; kurvanti, they perform; yadi ca na, or if not; arciṣam, to light; eva abhisambhavanti, they go; arciṣaḥ, from light; ahaḥ, to day; ahnaḥ, from day; āpūryamāṇapakṣam, to the bright fortnight; āpūryamāṇapakṣāt, from the bright fortnight; ṣaṭ māsān, to the six months; yān udan eti, [when the sun] moves to the north; tān, to that; māsebhyaḥ, from those months; saṃvatsaram, to the year; saṃvatsarāt, from the year; ādityam, to the sun; ādityāt, from the sun; candramasam, to the moon; candramasaḥ, from the moon; vidyutam, to lightning; tat, there; puruṣaḥ, a person [existing there]; amānavaḥ, not human; enān, those [human beings]; saḥ gamayati, he leads; brahma, to brahmaloka; eṣaḥ devapathaḥ, this is the path of the gods; brahmapathaḥ, the way to Brahman; etena, by this [path]; pratipadyamānāḥ, those who go; imam mānavam āvartam, to this world of human beings; na āvartante, do not return; na āvartante, do not return.
commentary: Normally when a person dies, his funeral rites should be performed with great care. This, however, does not apply in the case of one who has known Brahman. If the funeral rites are performed for him, it is good. But if for one reason or another they are not, it As regards those who worship the Self in the eyes by attributing to it qualities such as saṃyadvāma, vāmanī, or bhāmanī, or those who worship the fires as earth, water, prāṇa, etc., they go after death to the deity of light. From there they go to the deities of day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice, and so on. Finally they reach a point where someone appears who is higher than a human being. He leads them to satyaloka, which is the realm of Brahmā . This is not, however, Para Brahman (Pure Consciousness). To attain liberation, one must realize one’s identity with Para Brahman, where there is no going or coming from one realm to another.

sanskrit: एष ह वै यज्ञो योऽयं पवते एष ह यन्निदं सर्वं पुनाति यदेष यन्निदं सर्वं पुनाति तस्मादेष एव यज्ञस्तस्य मनश्च वाक्च वर्तनी
transliteration: eṣa ha vai yajño yo'yaṃ pavate eṣa ha yannidaṃ sarvaṃ punāti yadeṣa yannidaṃ sarvaṃ punāti tasmādeṣa eva yajñastasya manaśca vākca vartanī
translation: He who blows [i.e., air] is the sacrifice. While moving, he purifies all this. Since he purifies all this while moving, he is the sacrifice. The mind and speech are both his paths.
word_meaning: Eṣaḥ ha vai yajñaḥ, he is a sacrifice; yaḥ ayam pavate, this one who blows [i.e., air]; eṣaḥ ha, he; yan, while moving; idam sarvam, all this; punāti, purifies; yat, since; eṣaḥ yan idam sarvam punāti, he purifies all this while moving; tasmāt, therefore; eṣaḥ eva yajñaḥ, he is the sacrifice; manaḥ ca vāk ca, mind and speech; tasya vartanī, are his paths.
commentary: Anything that moves can clean or purify things, and this process of cleaning or purifying is a kind of sacrifice. Air is called here a sacrifice because it moves and by moving it purifies. There are two ways by which the air purifies—by speech and by the mind. By speech we utter mantras, and by the mind we understand them. Speech and the mind both operate by the power derived from air.
contextual_topics: The Sacred Syllable Om
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man

sanskrit: तयोरन्यतरां मनसा संस्करोति ब्रह्मा वाचा होताध्वर्युरुद्गातान्यतरांस यत्रौपाकृते प्रातरनुवाके पुरा परिधानीयाया ब्रह्मा व्यवदति
transliteration: tayoranyatarāṃ manasā saṃskaroti brahmā vācā hotādhvaryurudgātānyatarāṃsa yatraupākṛte prātaranuvāke purā paridhānīyāyā brahmā vyavadati
translation: 2-3. The priest called brahmā in a sacrifice purifies one of these two paths [i.e., the path of the mind] by his [discriminating] mind. The hotā, the adhvaryu, and the udgātā priests purify the other [i.e., the path of speech] by [chaste and elegant] speech. If, however, the brahmā priest breaks his silence when the morning anuvāka has begun, before the paridhānīya Ṛk hymn has been read, then only one path [the path of speech] has been purified. The other is ruined. Just as a one-legged person trying to walk, or a one-wheeled chariot trying to move, is doomed, in the same way the sacrifice is ruined. And when the sacrifice is ruined, the sacrificer is also ruined. In fact, the sacrificer is even liable for having committed a sin by performing the sacrifice in that way.

claim_candidates: The brahmā priest must maintain absolute silence during the morning anuvāka to purify the mental path of the sacrifice
If the brahmā priest breaks his silence, the sacrifice is fundamentally ruined and the sacrificer incurs sin
The efficacy of a sacrifice depends on the simultaneous purification of both the mind path and the speech path; neglect of either invalidates the ritual
The failure of a single priest is likened to a one‑legged person attempting to walk, indicating that completeness is essential for ritual success
The brahmā priest’s exclusive role is to purify the mental aspect, while the hotā, adhvaryu, and udgātā priests purify the verbal aspect
objection_hooks: How can mere external silence of a priest guarantee the purification of the inner mind, which may be independent of outward conduct?
The analogy of a one‑legged person may be metaphorical; does it logically entail that the sacrifice is ruined, or could the ritual retain validity despite the priest’s lapse?
If the sacrifice is ruined because the brahmā priest speaks, why is the sacrificer held responsible for the priest’s transgression?
Could the purification performed by the other three priests compensate for the brahmā’s failure, preserving the overall efficacy of the sacrifice?

sanskrit: तयोरन्यतरां मनसा संस्करोति ब्रह्मा वाचा होताध्वर्युरुद्गातान्यतरांस यत्रौपाकृते प्रातरनुवाके पुरा परिधानीयाया ब्रह्मा व्यवदति

contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct

claim_candidates: The purity of the mind path is essential for a successful sacrifice; without it, the sacrifice is ruined
The brahmā priest must remain silent during the anuvāka to purify the mind path
Breaking silence by the brahmā priest contaminates the mind path, making the sacrificer liable for sin
The effectiveness of the speech path alone is insufficient; both mind and speech paths are required for a valid sacrifice
The ruin of the sacrifice entails the ruin of the sacrificer, indicating a direct moral responsibility for ritual conduct
objection_hooks: How can the internal mental purity be objectively assessed if it depends on the priest's silence, which is a subjective state
Does the text imply that the sacrifice is invalid solely due to the brahmā's silence breach, disregarding the other priests' correct performance
The analogy of a one‑legged person may be metaphorical; does it logically entail that the sacrificer is a sinner, or could the sin be limited to the priest
The requirement of silence might be a later ritual addition rather than an essential metaphysical principle, weakening the claim about necessity of mind purification

sanskrit: अथ यत्रोपाकृते प्रातरनुवाके न पुरा परिधानीयाया ब्रह्मा व्यवदत्युभे एव वर्तनी संस्कुर्वन्ति न हीयतेऽन्यतरा
transliteration: atha yatropākṛte prātaranuvāke na purā paridhānīyāyā brahmā vyavadatyubhe eva vartanī saṃskurvanti na hīyate'nyatarā
translation: But in the case of the sacrifice in which the reading of the morning anuvāka has already begun, and the brahmā priest does not break his silence before the paridhānīya has started, then both paths are purified. Neither of them becomes destroyed.
word_meaning: Atha yatra, in the case of that sacrifice; upākṛte prātaḥ anuvāke, in which the reading of the morning anuvāka has begun; purā paridhānīyāyāḥ, before the beginning of the paridhānīya Ṛk hymn; brahmā na vyavavadati, the brahmā priest does not speak; ubhe eva vartanī, both the paths; saṃskurvanti, they purify; na hīyate anyatarā, neither of them is destroyed.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty
Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: The silence of the brahmā priest before the paridhānīya is a necessary condition for the purification of both sacrificial paths
Initiating the morning anuvāka marks the point at which the sacrifice's efficacy becomes dependent on ritual conduct rather than prior intention
When the prescribed sequence of the anuvāka and priestly silence is observed, neither of the two ritual paths suffers destruction
The verse implies that proper ritual performance can preserve both paths without requiring additional sacrificial offerings
objection_hooks: It is unclear how mere silence can effect purification; the mechanism is not explained in the verse
The identity of the two paths is ambiguous; the text does not specify what they refer to
The claim that neither path is destroyed may be limited to this specific sacrifice and not universally applicable
The assertion that ritual conduct alone suffices may overlook the role of inner intention which the verse does not mention

sanskrit: स यथोभयपाद्व्रजन्रथो वोभाभ्यां चक्राभ्यां वर्तमानः प्रतितिष्ठत्येवमस्य यज्ञः प्रतितिष्ठति यज्ञं प्रतितिष्ठन्तं यजमानोऽनुप्रतितिष्ठति स इष्ट्वा श्रेयान्भवति
transliteration: sa yathobhayapādvrajanratho vobhābhyāṃ cakrābhyāṃ vartamānaḥ pratitiṣṭhatyevamasya yajñaḥ pratitiṣṭhati yajñaṃ pratitiṣṭhantaṃ yajamāno'nupratitiṣṭhati sa iṣṭvā śreyānbhavati
translation: Just as a person with two legs can walk, or a chariot with two wheels can move, and attain the goal, so also his sacrifice succeeds. And if the sacrifice succeeds, the sacrificer also succeeds. He attains much greatness through his sacrifice.
word_meaning: Yathā, as; ubhayapāt, a person with both legs; vrajam, walking; vā, or; rathaḥ ubhābhyām cakrābhyām, a chariot with both wheels; vartamānaḥ, moving; pratitiṣṭhati, succeeds; evam, so also; asya yajñaḥ pratitiṣṭhati, his [the sacrificer’s] sacrifice succeeds; yajñam pratitiṣṭhantam yajamānaḥ anupratitiṣṭhati, if the sacrifice succeeds, the sacrificer also succeeds; saḥ, he [the sacrificer]; iṣṭvā śreyān bhavati, becomes greater through his sacrifice.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: The success of a sacrifice is contingent upon its functional completeness, analogous to a bipedal being or a two‑wheeled chariot achieving motion
When a sacrifice succeeds, the sacrificer attains success, implying a direct causal link between ritual outcome and personal attainment
The attainment of greatness by the sacrificer is dependent on the successful performance of the sacrifice
The verse employs the dual‑element analogy to suggest that balanced or dual aspects are necessary for the efficacy of spiritual action
objection_hooks: Does the analogy of legs and wheels adequately justify the claim that ritual success guarantees personal success, or does it merely illustrate functional similarity
How can an external ritual outcome be considered a reliable indicator of internal spiritual achievement, given possible discrepancies between outward performance and inner disposition
Might the assertion that sacrifice leads to greatness overlook situations where sacrifice results in loss or suffering, thereby challenging its universal applicability

sanskrit: प्रजापतिर्लोकानभ्यतपत्तेषां तप्यमानानां रसान्प्रावृहदग्निं पृथिव्या वायुमन्तरिक्षातादित्यं दिवः
transliteration: prajāpatirlokānabhyatapatteṣāṃ tapyamānānāṃ rasānprāvṛhadagniṃ pṛthivyā vāyumantarikṣātādityaṃ divaḥ
translation: Prajāpati worshipped the worlds, and from those which he worshipped he was able to extract their essence. From earth he took fire, from the interspace he took air, and from heaven he took the sun.
word_meaning: Prajāpatiḥ lokān abhyatapat, Prajāpati worshipped the worlds; teṣām tapyamānānām, from those which were worshipped; rasān prāvṛhat, he extracted the essence; agnim pṛthivyāḥ, fire from the earth; vāyum antarikṣāt, air from the space between the earth and heaven; ādityam divaḥ, and the sun from heaven.
commentary: The brahmā priest must observe silence to maintain the sanctity of the sacrifice he is performing. If the sanctity is lost, then the purpose of the sacrifice will be defeated. So if, for some reason or other, the sanctity is lost, due amends have to be made. One way to make amends is to seek the blessings of the lokas, the worlds. You pray to the worlds and then you are able to get their essence to support Your worship of the worlds is the amends you make, and the extracts you get in return are the blessings that protect you.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Worship of the worlds enables the practitioner to obtain their essential qualities as protective blessings
Extracting fire from earth, air from space, and sun from heaven signifies that material elements are manifestations of divine essence accessible through proper ritual
Loss of sanctity in sacrifice requires seeking the worlds' blessings as a corrective measure
Silence of the brahmā priest is a prerequisite for preserving the efficacy of the sacrifice and for divine extraction
objection_hooks: How can worship of external worlds yield internal protective blessings without invoking a personal deity
The extraction metaphor may be symbolic; does it imply literal control over elements, which seems metaphysically untenable
Is the requirement of silence uniquely necessary, or could other forms of reverence achieve the same sanctity
If loss of sanctity can be remedied by seeking blessings, does this not undermine the original importance of maintaining sanctity

sanskrit: स एतास्तिस्रो देवता अभ्यतपत्तासां तप्यमानानां रसान्प्रावृहदग्नेरृचो वायोर्यजूंषि सामान्यादित्यात्
transliteration: sa etāstisro devatā abhyatapattāsāṃ tapyamānānāṃ rasānprāvṛhadagnerṛco vāyoryajūṃṣi sāmānyādityāt
translation: Then he worshipped these three deities. From those which he worshipped he extracted the essence. He got the Ṛk mantras from fire, the Yajuḥ mantras from air, and the Sāma mantras from the sun.
word_meaning: Saḥ etāḥ tisraḥ devatāḥ abhyatapat, [then] he worshipped these three deities [fire, air, and the sun]; tāsām tapyamānānām, from those which he worshipped; rasān prāvṛhat, he extracted the essence; agneḥ ṛcaḥ, the Ṛk mantras from fire; vāyoḥ yajūṃṣi, the Yajuḥ mantras from air; sāmāni ādityāt, the Sāma mantras from the sun.
contextual_topics: Progressive Worship of Brahman up to the Universal Self
claim_candidates: Worship of fire, air, and sun yields distinct classes of Vedic mantras, namely Ṛk from fire, Yajuḥ from air, and Sāma from the sun.
Extracting the essence (rasān) from deities indicates that ultimate reality can be accessed through symbolic mediation of natural elements.
The three deities function as aspects of cosmic order, integrating ritual action with the acquisition of sacred sound.
The sequence of fire, air, and sun reflects an ascending order of spiritual potency in Vedic practice.
Mantras are not merely recited but are distilled from the intrinsic qualities of the elements themselves.
objection_hooks: The verse does not explicitly state a hierarchical potency among fire, air, and sun, so the claim of ascending spiritual order may be unwarranted.
The term rasān could refer to material essence rather than a metaphysical reality, challenging the link to ultimate reality.
Identifying the deities as functional aspects of cosmic order extends beyond the literal enumeration of fire, air, and sun in the text.

sanskrit: स एतां त्रयीं विद्यामभ्यतपत्तस्यास्तप्यमानाया रसान्प्रावृहद्भूरित्यृग्भ्यो भुवरिति यजुर्भ्यः स्वरिति सामभ्यः
transliteration: sa etāṃ trayīṃ vidyāmabhyatapattasyāstapyamānāyā rasānprāvṛhadbhūrityṛgbhyo bhuvariti yajurbhyaḥ svariti sāmabhyaḥ
translation: Then Prajāpati worshipped these three Vedas . And from those Vedas that were worshipped he extracted the essence. From the Ṛg Veda he got ‘bhūḥ, ’ from the Yajur Veda he got ‘bhuvaḥ, ’ and from the Sāma Veda he got ‘svaḥ’.
word_meaning: Saḥ etām trayīm vidyām abhyatapat, [then] he worshipped the knowledge from these three; tasyaḥ tapyamānāyāḥ, from these that he worshipped; rasān prāvṛhat, he extracted the essence; bhūḥ iti ṛgbhyaḥ, ‘bhūḥ’ from the Ṛg Veda; bhuvaḥ iti yajurbhyaḥ, ‘bhuvaḥ’ from the Yajur Veda; svaḥ iti sāmabhyaḥ, ‘svaḥ’ from the Sāma Veda.
contextual_topics: The Sacred Syllable Om
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The three Vedas contain the essential phonemes that constitute the sacred syllable Om, representing the totality of Brahman
Prajapati's worship of the Vedas and extraction of bhū, bhuva, sva demonstrates that ritual knowledge can be reduced to a concise symbolic formula
The identification of bhū, bhuva, sva with the Rig, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas respectively implies a hierarchical relationship among the Vedas, each contributing a specific aspect of cosmic reality
The process described indicates that the ultimate reality Brahman is accessible through contemplation of the syllable Om derived from scriptural essence
objection_hooks: The reduction of each extensive Veda to a single phoneme may oversimplify the richness and diversity of Vedic knowledge
Equating the extraction of essence with a formulaic reduction ignores the contextual and performative dimensions of Vedic rituals
Traditional views treat the Vedas as equally authoritative, so asserting a hierarchy based on phonemic extraction is contestable
A phoneme such as Om may not, by itself, convey the totality of Brahman, raising epistemic doubts about the claim of direct access

sanskrit: तद्यदृक्तो रिष्येद्भूः स्वाहेति गार्हपत्ये जुहुयादृचामेव तद्रसेनर्चां वीर्येणर्चां यज्ञस्य विरिष्टं संदधाति
transliteration: tadyadṛkto riṣyedbhūḥ svāheti gārhapatye juhuyādṛcāmeva tadrasenarcāṃ vīryeṇarcāṃ yajñasya viriṣṭaṃ saṃdadhāti
translation: This is why, if it seems likely that there will be any harm done to the sacrifice because of a mistake in the Ṛk, the priest should offer oblations in the Gārhapatya fire saying, ‘Bhūḥ svāhā .’ Then, by the essence and strength of the Ṛk, any likely harm done to the sacrifice from a mistake in the Ṛk will be averted.
word_meaning: Tat, that is why; yat ṛktaḥ riṣyet, if there should be any harm done [to the sacrifice] because of [a mistake] in the Ṛk; bhūḥ svāhā iti gārhapatye juhuyāt, then he should offer oblations in the Gārhapatya fire saying, ‘Bhūḥ svāhā’; ṛcām eva tat rasena, by that essence of the Ṛk; ṛcām vīryeṇa, by the strength of the Ṛk; ṛcām yajñasya viriṣṭam, the harm done to the sacrifice by the mistake in the Ṛk; sandadhāti, is averted.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: The utterance Bhūḥ svāhā in the Gārhapatya fire can neutralize harm caused by a mistake in the Rig
The essence (rasā) and strength (vīrya) of the Rig function as protective power for the sacrifice
A priest's correct verbal formula is sufficient to avert ritual impurity regardless of a textual error
The efficacy of a sacrifice depends on the intrinsic potency of the sacred text rather than solely on material offerings
objection_hooks: How can a verbal utterance counteract an actual mistake in the sacred text?
Does attributing protective power to the Rig imply the text itself is a deity, conflicting with non‑dual perspectives?
If the priest's formula averts harm, why is textual accuracy emphasized elsewhere in the ritual manuals?
Could reliance on a formula lead to complacency about proper ritual preparation?

sanskrit: स यदि यजुष्टो रिष्येद्भुवः स्वाहेति दक्षिणाग्नौ जुहुयाद्यजुषामेव तद्रसेन यजुषां वीर्येण यजुषां यज्ञस्य विरिष्टं संदधाति
transliteration: sa yadi yajuṣṭo riṣyedbhuvaḥ svāheti dakṣiṇāgnau juhuyādyajuṣāmeva tadrasena yajuṣāṃ vīryeṇa yajuṣāṃ yajñasya viriṣṭaṃ saṃdadhāti
translation: Then if it seems likely that there will be any harm done to the sacrifice because of a mistake in the Yajuḥ, the priest should offer oblations in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire saying, ‘ Bhuvaḥ svāhā .’ Then, by the essence and strength of the Yajuḥ, any likely harm done to the sacrifice from a mistake in the Yajuḥ will be averted.
word_meaning: Atha yadi yajuṣṭaḥ riṣyet, then if there should be any harm done [to the sacrifice] because of [a mistake] in the Yajuḥ; bhuvaḥ svāhā iti dakṣiṇāgnau juhuyāt, then he should offer oblations in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire saying, ‘Bhuvaḥ svāhā’; yajuṣām eva tat rasena, by that essence of the Yajuḥ; yajuṣām vīryeṇa, by the strength of the Yajuḥ; yajuṣām yajñasya viriṣṭam, the harm done to the sacrifice by the mistake in the Yajuḥ; sandadhāti, is averted.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: A corrective oblation Bhuvaḥ svāhā offered in the Dakṣiṇāgni can neutralize any harm caused by a mistake in the primary sacrifice
The ability of the corrective oblation to avert harm depends on the essence (ras) and strength (vīrya) of the original Yajuḥ
Mistakes in the performance of a sacrifice do not irrevocably damage its efficacy if appropriate remedial rites are performed
The priest is instructed to assess potential harm and prescribe specific fire offerings to preserve the integrity of the sacrifice
objection_hooks: How can the verbal formula Bhuvaḥ svāhā physically prevent a mistake from affecting the sacrificial outcome
Does reliance on a remedial rite imply that the initial precise performance of the sacrifice is not essential
Is the notion of the 'essence' of the Yajuḥ an empirically verifiable factor or a symbolic construct
Might this prescription be limited to a particular ritual context, reducing its universal applicability

sanskrit: अथ यदि सामतो रिष्येत्स्वः स्वाहेत्याहवनीये जुहुयात्साम्नामेव तद्रसेन साम्नां वीर्येण साम्नां यज्ञस्य विरिष्टं संदधाति
transliteration: atha yadi sāmato riṣyetsvaḥ svāhetyāhavanīye juhuyātsāmnāmeva tadrasena sāmnāṃ vīryeṇa sāmnāṃ yajñasya viriṣṭaṃ saṃdadhāti
translation: Then if it seems likely that there will be any harm done to the sacrifice because of a mistake in the Sāma, the priest should offer oblations in the Āhavanīya fire saying, ‘svaḥ svāhā .’ Then, by the essence and strength of the Sāma, any likely harm done to the sacrifice from a mistake in the Sāma will be averted.
word_meaning: Atha yadi sāmataḥ riṣyet, then if there should be any harm done [to the sacrifice] because of [a mistake] in the Sāma; svaḥ svāhā iti āhavanīye juhuyāt, then he should offer oblations in the Āhavanīya fire saying, ‘svaḥ svāhā’; sāmnām eva tat rasena, by that essence of the Sāma; sāmnām vīṛyeṇa, by the strength of the Sāma; sāmnām yajñasya viriṣṭam, the harm done to the sacrifice by the mistake in the Sāma; sandadhāti, is averted.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: The intrinsic essence of the Sāma chant possesses the power to neutralize any harm that may arise from a mistake in the chant during a sacrifice.
A priest can avert potential damage to the yajna by reciting ‘svaḥ svāhā’ in the āhavanīya fire, invoking the Sāma’s potency.
The effectiveness of the sacrifice depends more on the inner potency of the sacred chant than on external corrective actions.
Corrective mantra utterance serves as a substitute for physical adjustments when errors occur in the ritual performance.
objection_hooks: How can a verbal utterance, such as the Sāma, exert causal influence over physical mishaps in the sacrificial fire?
Is there empirical evidence that the essence of a chant can reliably prevent material harm, or is this claim based solely on faith?
Might reliance on mantra substitution encourage negligence in maintaining precise ritual procedures?
Does the verse imply that the mantra’s power is independent of the priest’s intention, raising questions about agency?

sanskrit: तद्यथा लवणेन सुवर्णं संदध्यात्सुवर्णेन रजतं रजतेन त्रपु त्रपुणा सीसं सीसेन लोहं लोहेन दारु दारु चर्मणा
transliteration: tadyathā lavaṇena suvarṇaṃ saṃdadhyātsuvarṇena rajataṃ rajatena trapu trapuṇā sīsaṃ sīsena lohaṃ lohena dāru dāru carmaṇā
translation: It is like joining gold with the help of borax, silver with the help of gold, tin with the help of silver, lead with the help of tin, iron with the help of lead, wood with the help of iron, and wood with the help of leather.
word_meaning: Tat yathā, it is like; lavaṇena, with the help of borax; suvarṇam sandadhyāt, one joins gold; suvarṇena rajatam, silver with the help of gold; rajatena trapu, tin with the help of silver; trapuṇā sīsam, lead with the help of tin; sīsena loham, iron with the help of lead; lohena dāru, wood with the help of iron; dāru carmaṇā, [and] wood with the help of leather.
commentary: Two things can join together when the right combination of materials is used. In the same way, if there is
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman

claim_candidates: The verse suggests that the efficacy of spiritual practice depends on the appropriate auxiliary means, analogous to using a specific metal to fuse another metal

The analogy implies that the Self can be united with Brahman only when the correct preparatory conditions are present

The inclusion of wood and leather shows that even the most base elements can be incorporated, implying inclusivity of all aspects of existence in the ultimate union
objection_hooks: The analogy of metals may be purely technical and not intended to convey a spiritual principle, so inferring a doctrine of auxiliary means could be overextension

The claim that the Self can be united with Brahman only with preparatory conditions may conflict with Advaita's assertion of inherent identity, raising ontological inconsistency

sanskrit: एवमेषां लोकानामासां देवतानामस्यास्त्रय्या विद्याया वीर्येण यज्ञस्य विरिष्टं संदधाति भेषजकृतो ह वा एष यज्ञो यत्रैवंविद्ब्रह्मा भवति
transliteration: evameṣāṃ lokānāmāsāṃ devatānāmasyāstrayyā vidyāyā vīryeṇa yajñasya viriṣṭaṃ saṃdadhāti bheṣajakṛto ha vā eṣa yajño yatraivaṃvidbrahmā bhavati
translation: Similarly, by the power of these worlds, these deities, and these three holy scriptures, any flaws in the sacrifice are made up. Where there is a knowledgeable brahmā priest, that sacrifice gets the right medicine.
word_meaning: Evam, in this way; vīryeṇa, by the strength; eṣām lokānām, of these worlds; āsām devatānām, of these deities; asyāḥ trayyāḥ vidyāyāḥ, of these three holy scriptures; yajñasya viriṣṭam sandadhāti, he [the brahmā priest] makes up for the flaws of a sacrifice; yatra evamvit brahmā bhavati, when there is a knowledgeable brahmā priest; eṣaḥ yajñaḥ, this sacrifice; bheṣajakṛtaḥ ha vai, gets the right medicine.
commentary: When a person is sick he must take the appropriate medicine. Similar is the case of a sacrifice that has gotten off to a bad start. If the priest is a knowledgeable one, he will take the right steps to rectify the errors. Like a good doctor, he will apply the right medicine—that is, the combined powers of the worlds, the deities, and the scriptures.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: The efficacy of a sacrifice depends more on the priest's knowledge than on the ritual's material components
The combined powers of worlds, deities, and scriptures function as a therapeutic agent for a flawed sacrifice
A sacrifice performed without a knowledgeable brahmā priest is analogous to a sick person receiving no appropriate medicine
The presence of the three holy scriptures is essential for correcting sacrificial errors
The priest's role is to apply cosmic resources, indicating that ritual success is mediated through divine authority rather than human effort alone
objection_hooks: How can the priest's knowledge alone compensate for fundamental ritual mistakes that violate scriptural injunctions

sanskrit: एष ह वा उदक्प्रवणो यज्ञो यत्रैवंविद्ब्रह्मा भवत्येवंविदं ह वा एषा ब्रह्माणमनुगाथा यतो यत आवर्तते तत्तद्गच्छति
transliteration: eṣa ha vā udakpravaṇo yajño yatraivaṃvidbrahmā bhavatyevaṃvidaṃ ha vā eṣā brahmāṇamanugāthā yato yata āvartate tattadgacchati
translation: That sacrifice which is directed by a capable brahmā priest leads to the uttarāyaṇa [the path of the gods]. There is a verse in praise of such a learned priest: ‘Wherever the sacrifice goes wrong, this priest goes there to set things right’.

commentary: Whenever a sacrifice is to be held, a competent priest should be placed in charge. This will ensure A capable priest is always in demand wherever a sacrifice is being held, because, first, he can avoid mistakes, and second, should there be any mistake, in spite of all the care taken, the priest knows how to correct it.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty

Emphasizing external priestly control may diminish the inner spiritual significance of the sacrifice itself

sanskrit: मानवो ब्रह्मैवैक ऋत्विक्कुरूनश्वाभिरक्षत्येवंविद्ध वै ब्रह्मा यज्ञं यजमानं सर्वांश्चर्त्विजोऽभिरक्षति तस्मादेवंविदमेव ब्रह्माणं कुर्वीत नानेवंविदं नानेवंविदम्
transliteration: mānavo brahmaivaika ṛtvikkurūnaśvābhirakṣatyevaṃviddha vai brahmā yajñaṃ yajamānaṃ sarvāṃścartvijo'bhirakṣati tasmādevaṃvidameva brahmāṇaṃ kurvīta nānevaṃvidaṃ nānevaṃvidam
translation: A good brahmā priest is one who is able to observe silence, or one who is thoughtful. Just as a horse protects the soldiers, a learned brahmā priest protects the sacrifice, the sacrifices, and all the other priests. Therefore, one should appoint only such a learned brahmā for one’s sacrifice. One should not appoint anyone else.
word_meaning: Mānavaḥ brahmā eva ekaḥ ṛtvik, a true brahmā priest is one who is thoughtful [or, is able to observe silence]; kurūn aśvā abhirakṣati, [just as] a horse protects the soldiers; evamvit ha vai brahmā, such a learned brahmā priest; yajñam yajamānam sarvān ca ṛtvijaḥ abhirakṣati, protects the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the other priests; tasmāt, therefore; evam vidam eva brahmāṇam kurvīta, one should appoint only such a learned brahmā priest; na anevam vidam, not one who is otherwise; na anevam vidam, not one who is otherwise.
commentary: When a priest is able to maintain silence and is by nature thoughtful, he may be appointed as the brahmā for a sacrifice. He is the chief priest by virtue of his scholarship and his character. The Upaniṣad compares him to a horse which protects his master when he is in trouble. A good brahmā priest can take care of the sacrifice, the sacrifices, and the subordinate priests. For this reason, only one who is qualified should be appointed. One who is not fit should not be given the honour.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: A brahmā priest who maintains silence and thoughtfulness is essential for the proper protection of the sacrifice

Ritual efficacy depends on the ethical and intellectual qualities of the officiant, not merely on ritual performance

Is the horse analogy sufficient to establish moral qualification for priestly duties?

sanskrit: यो ह वै ज्येष्ठं च श्रेष्ठं च वेद ज्येष्ठश्च ह वै श्रेष्ठश्च भवति प्राणो वाव ज्येष्ठश्च श्रेष्ठश्च
transliteration: yo ha vai jyeṣṭhaṃ ca śreṣṭhaṃ ca veda jyeṣṭhaśca ha vai śreṣṭhaśca bhavati prāṇo vāva jyeṣṭhaśca śreṣṭhaśca
translation: Om. He who knows the oldest and the best himself becomes the oldest and the best. It is prāṇa which is the oldest and the best.
word_meaning: Yaḥ ha vai, he who; jyeṣṭham ca śreṣṭham ca veda, knows the oldest and the best; jyeṣṭhaḥ ca ha vai śreṣṭhaḥ ca bhavati, himself becomes the oldest and the best; prāṇaḥ vāva jyeṣṭhaḥ ca śreṣṭhaḥ ca, prāṇa is indeed the oldest and the best.
commentary: The importance of prāṇa has been mentioned earlier. True, it works in conjunction with the organs of speaking, hearing, seeing, etc., but it is the first and foremost of all of them. Prāṇa is in a child even when it is still in it’s mother’s womb. It is active before the various organs are active. Prāṇa therefore commands respect from all. The reason why so much importance is given to prāṇa is to teach us to show respect where respect is due. We should respect both age and merit. Then we also shall command respect from all because of our age and merit. Indirectly, this is a hint that we should respect knowledge.
contextual_topics: The Sacred Syllable Om
claim_candidates: He who knows the oldest and best becomes the oldest and best
Prana is the primordial principle that operates before the sensory organs become active

The emphasis on prana indirectly instructs us to respect knowledge
objection_hooks: How can mere knowledge of prana cause ontological transformation into being the oldest and best?

Could the instruction to respect knowledge be interpreted as valuing intellectual achievement over spiritual realization?

sanskrit: यो ह वै वसिष्ठं वेद वसिष्ठो ह स्वानां भवति वाग्वाव वसिष्ठः
transliteration: yo ha vai vasiṣṭhaṃ veda vasiṣṭho ha svānāṃ bhavati vāgvāva vasiṣṭhaḥ
translation: He who knows that which is of high standing himself becomes of high standing among his own relatives. Eloquence gives one this high standing [in society].
word_meaning: Yaḥ ha vai, he who; vasiṣṭham veda, knows that which is of high standing; vasiṣṭhaḥ ha svānām bhavati, becomes of high standing among his own relatives; vāk vāva vasiṣṭhaḥ, speech [i.e., eloquence] is surely of high standing [i.e., it is the secret of high standing].
commentary: If a person respects another for his power to influence others, he himself some day has the same power and commands respect from others. It is, in fact, the power of eloquence which is behind this influence.

sanskrit: यो ह वै प्रतिष्ठां वेद प्रति ह तिष्ठत्यस्मिंश्च लोकेऽमुष्मिंश्च चक्षुर्वाव प्रतिष्ठा
transliteration: yo ha vai pratiṣṭhāṃ veda prati ha tiṣṭhatyasmiṃśca loke'muṣmiṃśca cakṣurvāva pratiṣṭhā
translation: He who knows the support attains a support in this world and also in the other world [i.e., heaven]. The eye is indeed the support.

commentary: Good sight is necessary for success in life. A sharp eye is not merely a physical asset; it is also a mental asset. It means a good and sharp sense of judgement. sanskrit: यो ह वै सम्पदं वेद संहास्मै कामाः पद्यन्ते दैवाश्च मानुषाश्च श्रोत्रं वाव सम्पत्

sanskrit: यो ह वा आयतनं वेदायतनं ह स्वानां भवति मनो ह वा आयतनम्
transliteration: yo ha vā āyatanaṃ vedāyatanaṃ ha svānāṃ bhavati mano ha vā āyatanam

commentary: There is something in the body-mind complex of human beings called āyatana . If a person knows this ‘āyatana, ’ it is to be understood that he is a wise person. And such a person is able to serve as an āyatana to his own relatives. That is to say, he is The mind is the āyatana of the body-mind complex. Why? contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct

sanskrit: अथ ह प्राणा अहंश्रेयसि व्यूदिरेऽहंश्रेयानस्म्यहं श्रेयानस्मीति

sanskrit: ते ह प्राणाः प्रजापतिं पितरमेत्योचुर्भगवन्को नः श्रेष्ठ इति तान्होवाच यस्मिन्व उत्क्रान्ते शरीरं पापिष्ठतरमिव दृश्येत स वः श्रेष्ठ इति
transliteration: te ha prāṇāḥ prajāpatiṃ pitarametyocurbhagavanko naḥ śreṣṭha iti tānhovāca yasminva utkrānte śarīraṃ pāpiṣṭhataramiva dṛśyeta sa vaḥ śreṣṭha iti
translation: The organs then went to their father Prajāpati and said, ‘Revered sir, who among us is the best?’ He replied, ‘He is the best among you on whose departure the body becomes totally untouchable’.
word_meaning: Te ha prāṇāḥ, those organs; pitaram prajāpatim etya, coming to their father Prajāpati; ucuḥ, said; bhagavan, revered sir; naḥ, among us; kaḥ śreṣṭhaḥ iti, who is the best; tān ha uvāca, he said to them; vaḥ, among you; yasmin utkrānte, on whose leaving; śarīram pāpiṣṭhataram iva dṛśyeta, the body appears to be untouchable; saḥ vaḥ śreṣṭhaḥ, he is the best among you.
commentary: We all know what happens when life leaves the body. It is not the same body. It shrinks. It becomes ugly. And soon it starts decomposing. No one wants to touch it. The way he changed his voice is called kaku .
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The prāṇa is the supreme organ because its departure renders the body untouchable

sanskrit: सा ह वागुच्चक्राम सा संवत्सरं प्रोष्य पर्येत्योवाच कथमशकतर्ते मज्जीवितुमिति यथा कला अवदन्तः प्राणन्तः प्राणेन पश्यन्तश्चक्षुषा शृण्वन्तः श्रोत्रेण ध्यायन्तो मनसैवमिति प्रविवेश ह वाक्
transliteration: sā ha vāguccakrāma sā saṃvatsaraṃ proṣya paryetyovāca kathamaśakatarte majjīvitumiti yathā kalā avadantaḥ prāṇantaḥ prāṇena paśyantaścakṣuṣā śṛṇvantaḥ śrotreṇa dhyāyanto manasaivamiti praviveśa ha vāk
translation: First speech left the body. After staying away one whole year, he came back and asked the other organs, ‘How did you sustain yourselves in my absence?’ The rest of the organs said: ‘Just as mute people do without speaking, but they are able to survive by breathing, and see with the eyes, hear with the ears, and think with the mind. We did the same.’ Hearing all this, speech re-entered the body.
word_meaning: Sā ha vāk, that speech; ut-cakrāma, left [the body]; saṃvatsaram proṣya, after staying away one year; sā paretya uvāca, he came back and said; mat ṛte, in my absence; katham, how; jīvitum aśakata iti, did you manage to survive; yathā kalāḥ, [the other organs said: ] just as the mute; avadantaḥ, do not speak; praḥantaḥ prāṇena, [but] are able to survive with the help of prāṇa, the vital force; paśyantaḥ cakṣuṣā, to see with the help of the eyes; śṛṇvantaḥ śrotreṇa, to hear with the help of the ears; dhyāyantaḥ manasā, to think with the help of the mind; evam iti, in the same way; vāk praviveśa ha, [hearing this] speech re-entered the body.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Speech (vāk) can temporarily separate from the body without loss of identity

objection_hooks: If speech is merely a function of the mind, how can it exist independently of the body

The text does not explicitly state that hearing the explanation causes speech to re‑enter, so the causal link is uncertain

sanskrit: चक्षुर्होच्चक्राम तत्संवत्सरं प्रोष्य पर्येत्योवाच कथमशकतर्ते मज्जीवितुमिति यथान्धा अपश्यन्तः प्राणन्तः प्राणेन वदन्तो वाचा शृण्वन्तः श्रोत्रेण ध्यायन्तो मनसैवमिति प्रविवेश ह चक्षुः
transliteration: cakṣurhoccakrāma tatsaṃvatsaraṃ proṣya paryetyovāca kathamaśakatarte majjīvitumiti yathāndhā apaśyantaḥ prāṇantaḥ prāṇena vadanto vācā śṛṇvantaḥ śrotreṇa dhyāyanto manasaivamiti praviveśa ha cakṣuḥ
translation: Next the organ of vision left the body. After staying away one whole year, it came back and asked the other organs, ‘How did you sustain yourselves in my absence?’ The rest of the organs said: ‘Just as blind people do without seeing, but they are able to survive by breathing, and speak with the organ of speech, hear with the ears, and think with the mind. We did the same.’ Hearing all this, the organ of vision re-entered the. body.
word_meaning: Cakṣuḥ ha, the organ of vision; ut-cakrāma, left [the body]; saṃvatsaram proṣya, after staying away one year; tat paretya uvāca, it came back and said; mat ṛte, in my absence; katham, how; jīvitum aśakata iti, did you manage to survive; yathā andhāḥ, [the other organs said: ] just as the blind; apaśyantaḥ, do not see; prāṇantaḥ prāṇena, [but] are able to survive with the help of prāṇa, the vital force; vadantaḥ vācā, to speak with the help of the organ of speech; śṛṇvantaḥ śrotreṇa, to hear with the help of the ears; dhyāyantaḥ manasā, to think with the help of the mind; evam iti, in the same way; cakṣuḥ praviveśa ha, [hearing this] the organ of vision re-entered the body.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The vision organ's departure and return illustrates that the self can temporarily withdraw from perception without ceasing existence
The other senses sustain the organism through prana, indicating that life persists independent of visual input
The dialogue among organs suggests that consciousness is a composite of sensory functions rather than a singular faculty
The reintegration of the vision organ after hearing the others' testimony implies that knowledge of interdependence restores wholeness
objection_hooks: How can the self be said to persist without the organ of vision if consciousness is fundamentally visual in Upanishadic thought
Does the verse truly imply a composite consciousness, or is it merely a metaphor for bodily functions, thus weakening the claim of non‑singular consciousness
The claim that knowledge of interdependence restores wholeness assumes a causal link not explicit in the text; the verse may simply narrate a sequence without implying philosophical principle

sanskrit: श्रोत्रं होच्चक्राम तत्संवत्सरं प्रोष्य पर्येत्योवाच कथमशकतर्ते मज्जीवितुमिति यथा बधिरा अशृण्वन्तः प्राणन्तः प्राणेन वदन्तो वाचा पश्यन्तश्चक्षुषा ध्यायन्तो मनसैवमिति प्रविवेश ह श्रोत्रम्
transliteration: śrotraṃ hoccakrāma tatsaṃvatsaraṃ proṣya paryetyovāca kathamaśakatarte majjīvitumiti yathā badhirā aśṛṇvantaḥ prāṇantaḥ prāṇena vadanto vācā paśyantaścakṣuṣā dhyāyanto manasaivamiti praviveśa ha śrotram
translation: Next the organ of hearing left the body. After staying away one whole year, it came back and asked the other organs, ‘How did you sustain yourselves in my absence?’ The rest of the organs said: ‘Just as deaf people do without hearing, but they are able to survive by breathing, and speak with the organ of speech, see with the eyes, and think with the mind. We did the same.’ Hearing all this, the organ of hearing re-entered the body.
word_meaning: Śrotram ha, the organ of hearing; ut-cakrāma, left [the body]; saṃvatsaram proṣya, after staying away one year; tat paretya uvāca, it came back and said; mat ṛte, in my absence; katham, how; jīvitum aśakata iti, did you manage to survive; yathā badhirāḥ, [the other organs said: ] just as the deaf; aśṛṇvantaḥ, do not hear; prāṇantaḥ prāṇena, [but] are able to survive with the help of prāṇa, the vital force; vadantaḥ vācā, to speak with the help of the organ of speech; paśyantaḥ cakṣuṣā, to see with the help of the eyes; dhyāyantaḥ manasā, to think with the help of the mind; evam iti, in the same way; śrotram praviveśa ha, [hearing this] the organ of hearing re-entered the body.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The senses can function independently of each other, indicating that the self is not limited to any single sense organ
The reintegration of the hearing organ after a period of absence symbolizes the restoration of wholeness to the individual self
The ability of deaf people to survive using other faculties suggests that consciousness is not dependent on any particular sensory input
The narrative implies that the body’s vital force (prāṇa) sustains life irrespective of sensory capacities
The organ of hearing’s inquiry about survival reflects a self‑reflective awareness inherent in consciousness
objection_hooks: The claim that senses function independently may ignore the interdependence of sensory perception in integrated experience
The symbolism of hearing re‑entering may be a narrative device rather than a metaphysical statement about wholeness
Asserting that consciousness is independent of sensory input conflicts with empirical evidence that perception shapes awareness
The role of prāṇa as sustaining life independent of senses is not explicitly stated, merely implied, thus the claim may overextend the text

sanskrit: मनो होच्चक्राम तत्संवत्सरं प्रोष्य पर्येत्योवाच कथमशकतर्ते मज्जीवितुमिति यथा बाला अमनसः प्राणन्तः प्राणेन वदन्तो वाचा पश्यन्तश्चक्षुषा शृण्वन्तः श्रोत्रेणैवमिति प्रविवेश ह मनः
transliteration: mano hoccakrāma tatsaṃvatsaraṃ proṣya paryetyovāca kathamaśakatarte majjīvitumiti yathā bālā amanasaḥ prāṇantaḥ prāṇena vadanto vācā paśyantaścakṣuṣā śṛṇvantaḥ śrotreṇaivamiti praviveśa ha manaḥ
translation: Next the mind left the body. After staying away one whole year, he came back and asked the other organs, ‘How did you sustain yourselves in my absence?’ The rest of the organs said: ‘Just as children do without thinking for themselves, but they are able to survive by breathing, and speak with the organ of speech, see with the eyes, and hear with the ears. We did the same.’ Hearing all this, the mind re-entered the body.
word_meaning: Manaḥ ha, the mind; ut-cakrāma, left [the body]; saṃvatsaram proṣya, after staying away one year; tat paretya uvāca, he came back and said; mat ṛte, in my absence; katham, how; jīvitum aśakata iti, did you manage to survive; yathā bālāḥ, [the other organs said: ] just as the children; amanasaḥ, do not receive much support from the mind; prāṇantaḥ prāṇena, [but] are able to survive with the help of prāṇa, the vital force; vadantaḥ vācā, to speak with the help of the organ of speech; paśyantaḥ cakṣuṣā, to see with the help of the eyes; śṛṇvantaḥ śrotreṇa, to hear with the help of the ears; evam iti, in the same way; manaḥ praviveśa ha, [hearing this] the mind re-entered the body.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The mind can exist apart from the body for an extended period, indicating that consciousness is not wholly dependent on bodily organs
The organs continue their functions by means of prana, showing that vital force sustains life independently of the mind
Children survive without mental guidance, suggesting that basic physiological processes do not require the mind
The mind re‑enters the body only after hearing the organs’ report, implying that awareness of their state is required for the mind to reunite with the body
objection_hooks: If the mind is independent, how does it obtain information about the organs without sensory input
The narrative may be metaphorical rather than literal, so claims about disembodied consciousness could be symbolic
A year of separation might represent a deep sleep state, not an actual detachment of mind from body
The claim that prana alone sustains organs overlooks the role of subtle mental factors in regulating functions

sanskrit: अथ ह प्राण उच्चिक्रमिषन्स यथा सुहयः पड्वीशशङ्कून्संखिदेदेवमितरान्प्राणान्समखिदत्तं हाभिसमेत्योचुर्भगवन्नेधि त्वं नः श्रेष्ठोऽसि मोत्क्रमीरिति
transliteration: atha ha prāṇa uccikramiṣansa yathā suhayaḥ paḍvīśaśaṅkūnsaṃkhidedevamitarānprāṇānsamakhidattaṃ hābhisametyocurbhagavannedhi tvaṃ naḥ śreṣṭho'si motkramīriti
translation: Now prāṇa, the vital force, decided to leave. Just as a good horse is able to uproot the pegs to which its feet are tied, similarly, the chief prāṇa was about to carry the other organs away with him. Those other organs then came to him and with great humility said: ‘O lord, be our leader. You are the greatest among us. Please don’t leave us’.
word_meaning: Atha ha saḥ prāṇaḥ, now that prāṇa, the vital force; uccikramiṣan, wishing to go out; yathā, just as; suhayaḥ, a good horse; paḍvīśa-śaṅkūn, the pegs to which his feet are tied; saṃkhidet, uproots; evam, in the same way; itarān prāṇān, the other organs; samakhidat, began to leave with him; tam abhisametya, coming to him [with great humility]; ucuḥ ha, land] said; bhagavan, lord; edhi, be our leader; naḥ tvam śreṣṭhaḥ asi, you are the best among us; mā utkramīḥ iti, please do not leave us.
commentary: The organs, beginning with vāk (speech), left the body one after another. But that made little or no difference to the body or to the rest of the organs. Then prāṇa decided to leave. Just as he started to go, all the other organs felt that they were being forced to leave also. They realized then that they were not free; they were utterly dependent on the chief prāṇa. Coming to him, they showed him respect and said that they now recognized his superiority.
contextual_topics: Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
Being as the Source of All
claim_candidates: The chief prāṇa functions as the governing principle of all bodily organs, implying that without it the organs cannot act independently
The humility expressed by the organs towards prāṇa indicates an inherent hierarchical order within the subtle body
The departure of prāṇa precipitates the dissolution of the body, suggesting that prāṇa is the essential life‑force whose loss results in death
Recognition of dependence on prāṇa by the organs demonstrates that self‑identity is contingent upon the central life principle rather than on individual functions
The analogy of a horse uprooting its pegs illustrates that the vital force can override even the most firmly attached bodily functions
objection_hooks: The heart exhibits autonomous rhythmic activity, which may challenge the claim that all organs are wholly dependent on prāṇa
The text does not explicitly state that death follows prāṇa's departure, leaving the causal link between prāṇa's exit and bodily dissolution ambiguous
Advaita holds that the atman is independent of bodily functions, which contradicts the claim that self‑identity is contingent on prāṇa
The horse metaphor could be interpreted as poetic illustration rather than a literal assertion of hierarchical order, weakening the metaphysical inference

sanskrit: अथ हैनं वागुवाच यदहं वसिष्ठोऽस्मि त्वं तद्वसिष्ठोऽसीत्यथ हैनं चक्षुरुवाच यदहं प्रतिष्ठास्मि त्वं तत्प्रतिष्ठासीति
transliteration: atha hainaṃ vāguvāca yadahaṃ vasiṣṭho'smi tvaṃ tadvasiṣṭho'sītyatha hainaṃ cakṣuruvāca yadahaṃ pratiṣṭhāsmi tvaṃ tatpratiṣṭhāsīti
translation: The organ of speech then said to the chief prāṇa, ‘If I have the quality of high standing, it is because you have that quality.’ Next the organ of vision said to him, ‘True, I have the quality of supporting others, but I owe that quality to you’.
word_meaning: Atha ha enam vāk uvāca, next vāk [speech] said to him [i.e., to prāṇa]; yat aham vasiṣṭhaḥ asmi, I am as much endowed with [the quality of] high standing; tat tvani vasiṣṭhaḥ asi iti, as you are endowed with [the quality of] high standing; atha ha enam cakṣuḥ uvāca, next the organ of vision said to him; yat aham pratiṣṭhā asmi, I am as much endowed with [the quality of] support; tat tvam pratiṣṭhā asi iti, as you are a support.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The quality of high standing attributed to speech is ultimately derived from the chief prana
Vision’s quality of support is derived from speech, indicating interdependence among senses
The organs’ mutual acknowledgment demonstrates that individual functions are not independent but mutually contingent
The dialogue implies that the self is a composite of senses, each reflecting the other's excellence
objection_hooks: If the organ of speech is not a conscious entity, how can it make a claim about its own quality?
Mutual attribution may suggest that qualities are not intrinsic, contradicting the notion of an inherent self
The dependence of vision on speech could be read as poetic exaggeration rather than a doctrinal statement
If each organ depends on another, does this undermine the autonomy of the chief prana?

sanskrit: अथ हैनंश्रोत्रमुवाच यदहं सम्पदस्मि त्वं तत्सम्पदसीत्यथ हैनं मन उवाच यदहमायतनमस्मि त्वं तदायतनमसीति
transliteration: atha hainaṃśrotramuvāca yadahaṃ sampadasmi tvaṃ tatsampadasītyatha hainaṃ mana uvāca yadahamāyatanamasmi tvaṃ tadāyatanamasīti
translation: The organ of hearing then said to the chief prāṇa, ‘If I have the quality of affluence, it is because you have that quality.’ Next the mind said to him, ‘True, I have the quality of being a shelter to many, but that quality is, in fact, yours’.
word_meaning: Atha ha enam śrotram uvāca, next the organ of hearing said to him [i.e., to prāṇa]; yat aham sampat asmi, I am as much endowed with [the quality of] affluence; tat tvam sampat asi iti, as you are endowed with [the quality of] affluence; atha ha enam manaḥ uvāca, next the mind said to him; yat aham āyatanam asmi, I am as much endowed with [the quality of] a shelter; tat tvam āyatanam asi iti, as you are a shelter.
commentary: Tenants may go to their landlord and say many things to please him and exhibit their loyalty. Like that, the various sense organs which had earlier fought among themselves, each claiming superiority, are now, with great humility, declaring that they have nothing of their own—that whatever good qualities they have they owe to their master, the chief prāṇa.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The qualities attributed to the organ of hearing are ultimately derived from the chief prāṇa, not inherent to the organ itself
The mind acknowledges that its function as a shelter is fundamentally the attribute of the chief prāṇa, indicating the mind's dependence on prāṇa
The sense organs, previously in conflict over superiority, demonstrate humility by recognizing the primacy of prāṇa, suggesting a hierarchical ordering of subtle elements
The verse implies that all apparent qualities of the individual self are manifestations of the universal life principle (prāṇa), supporting a non‑dual view of self and Brahman
The dialogue illustrates that the sense organs' self‑identification is an illusion, and true identity lies with the chief prāṇa
objection_hooks: If qualities are derived from prāṇa, how does the verse account for the distinct functional differences among sense organs
The attribution of all qualities to prāṇa may overlook the possibility that sense organs possess intrinsic capacities independent of prāṇa
The claim of a hierarchical ordering may be challenged by the Upanishadic view that all elements are ultimately non‑different; hierarchy could be a provisional teaching
Interpreting the passage as supporting non‑dualism may be an extrapolation beyond the immediate context of sense‑organ humility

sanskrit: न वै वाचो न चक्षूंषि न श्रोत्राणि न मनांसीत्याचक्षते प्राणा इत्येवाचक्षते प्राणो ह्येवैतानि सर्वाणि भवति
transliteration: na vai vāco na cakṣūṃṣi na śrotrāṇi na manāṃsītyācakṣate prāṇā ityevācakṣate prāṇo hyevaitāni sarvāṇi bhavati
translation: Scholars do not call them organs of speech, eyes, ears, or minds. They call them ‘ prāṇas, ’ for prāṇa has become all these organs.
word_meaning: Na vai vācaḥ, not organs of speech; na cakṣūṃṣi, not eyes; na śrotrāṇi, not ears; na manāṃsi, not minds; iti eva ācakṣate, they say; prāṇāḥ iti eva ācakṣate, they say the prāṇas; hi, for; prāṇaḥ bhavati, prāṇa has become; etāni sarvāṇi, all these.
commentary: The Self is the source of everything that exists, living or non-living. The Self manifests itself in many forms—as human beings, animals, plants, etc. And it is because of the Self that we live, speak, and act. Human beings have two sets of organs—organs of perception and organs of action. We also have a mind. These organs are powerful, but the most powerful is the mind. Yet none of these organs is independent. Each one exists and functions only to serve the Self, the master. The Self is within the body as well as without. Within the body it is the Ātman, which functions through prāṇa, the vital breath. As prāṇa, it animates the body and all the organs. Without prāṇa, the body with all its organs is dead, useless.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The prāṇa is the underlying reality that manifests as all sensory and mental organs
The organs of speech, sight, hearing, and mind are expressions of the same prāṇa and are not independent
The Self (Ātman) functions through prāṇa, making prāṇa the animating principle of the body
Identifying organs as prāṇa implies that the distinction between body and Self is ultimately illusory
Knowledge of prāṇa leads to understanding of the Self
objection_hooks: If prāṇa is identical to all organs, how does one account for functional differences among them
The claim that organs are not independent seems to conflict with empirical observation of distinct sensory modalities
Equating the Self with prāṇa may conflate the individual soul with a universal principle, creating ontological confusion
Suggesting that body and Self are illusory could undermine personal moral responsibility

sanskrit: स होवाच किं मेऽन्नं भविष्यतीति यत्किंचिदिदमा श्वभ्य आ शकुनिभ्य इति होचुस्तद्वा एतदनस्यान्नमनो ह वै नाम प्रत्यक्षं न ह वा एवंविदि किंचनानन्नं भवतीति
transliteration: sa hovāca kiṃ me'nnaṃ bhaviṣyatīti yatkiṃcididamā śvabhya ā śakunibhya iti hocustadvā etadanasyānnamano ha vai nāma pratyakṣaṃ na ha vā evaṃvidi kiṃcanānannaṃ bhavatīti
translation: Prāṇa then asked, ‘What will be my food?’ The other organs said: ‘Anything that even dogs, birds, and other animals can eat in this world is your food.’ All that is food for ana. Ana is a name of prāṇa. For one who knows this nothing is uneatable. [That is, he can eat any food that an animal can eat.]
word_meaning: Saḥ ha uvāca, he [prāṇa] asked; kim me annam bhaviṣyati iti, what will be my food; iti ucuḥ ha, [the other organs] replied; ā-śvabhyaḥ ā-śakunibhyaḥ, for dogs as well as birds; yat idam kiñcit, whatever there is; tat vai, all that; etat anasya annam, is this food for prāṇa; anaḥ ha vai nāma pratyakṣam, ‘ana’ is the name of prāṇa itself; ha vai evam vidi, for one who knows thus; kiñcana na anannam bhavati iti, nothing becomes uneatable [i.e., anything an animal can eat is food for him].
commentary: There is some difference between the words prāṇa and ana. Prāṇa has a limited meaning. It refers to something characterized by breathing. It breathes, and in order to keep breathing it needs food. It may be a specific kind of food. It may not eat every kind of food. Ana, however, is that which can eat any kind of food. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (1.5.23) says, ‘The sun rises and sets in prāṇa.’ It also says that the person who knows the true nature of prāṇa is one from whom the sun rises and into whom it sets.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
sub_concepts: Brahman as Cosmological and Physical Principle
claim_candidates: The true nature of prāṇa (ana) is that it can subsist on any material that animals consume, indicating its universal alimentary capacity
Knowing the identity of prāṇa as ana leads to the realization that nothing is uneatable, implying a non-dual understanding of nourishment
The distinction between prāṇa and ana reflects a doctrinal differentiation between a limited life‑force and the universal self, suggesting a hierarchical view of vital principles
The statement that the sun rises and sets in prāṇa indicates that prāṇa is a conduit for cosmic processes, supporting the view that prāṇa embodies Brahman
If prāṇa is identified with ana, then the limitation of prāṇa disappears, implying that the ultimate self is unrestricted in its sustenance
objection_hooks: The claim that ana can eat any food may be challenged by the existence of substances such as poison that are inedible even for animals, questioning the universality of the statement
Equating knowledge of prāṇa with knowledge of Brahman may be an epistemic leap, as the verse only discusses prāṇa's alimentary function, not ultimate reality
The assertion that the sun rises and sets in prāṇa could be metaphorical rather than literal, undermining the claim that prāṇa embodies Brahman
The distinction between prāṇa and ana might be a linguistic nuance rather than a substantive metaphysical hierarchy, weakening the claim of a hierarchical vital principle

sanskrit: स होवाच किं मे वासो भविष्यतीत्याप इति होचुस्तस्माद्वा एतदशिष्यन्तः पुरस्ताच्चोपरिष्टाच्चाद्भिः परिदधति लम्भुको ह वासो भवत्यनग्नो ह भवति
transliteration: sa hovāca kiṃ me vāso bhaviṣyatītyāpa iti hocustasmādvā etadaśiṣyantaḥ purastāccopariṣṭāccādbhiḥ paridadhati lambhuko ha vāso bhavatyanagno ha bhavati
translation: Prāṇa asked, ‘What will be my covering?’ The organs replied, ‘Water.’ This is why, before and after eating their meals, people cover him with water [i.e., they sip water]. He then becomes covered with a cloth and is no longer naked.
word_meaning: Saḥ ha uvāca, he [prāṇa] said; kim me vāsaḥ bhaviṣyati iti, what will be my covering; āpaḥ iti ha ucuḥ, [the other organs] replied, ‘Water’; tasmāt, that is why; vai aśiṣyantaḥ purastāt ca, people before eating; upariṣṭāt ca, and after [eating]; etat adbhiḥ paridadhati, cover him [prāṇa] with water [i.e., they sip water]; lambhukaḥ ha vāsaḥ bhavati, thereby he becomes covered with a cloth; anagnaḥ ha bhavati, he is no longer naked.
commentary: The water that is sipped before the meal is said to be the lower cloth, and that which is sipped afterwards is said to be the upper cloth.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The verse suggests that water functions as a symbolic covering for the vital breath (prāṇa), analogous to a cloth.
The practice of sipping water before and after meals is presented as a ritual substitute for physical clothing of the self.
The dialogue implies that the organs possess agency to answer the prāṇa's query about its covering.
The commentary identifies pre‑meal water as a lower cloth and post‑meal water as an upper cloth, indicating a layered protective process for the self.
objection_hooks: The interpretation that water serves as a symbolic covering may conflate metaphor with literal instruction, lacking explicit textual evidence that water is metaphorical rather than merely physical.
Claim that sipping water substitutes for clothing assumes a ritual equivalence not directly stated; the verse may simply describe a hygienic practice without deeper symbolic meaning.
Attributing agency to the organs may be a poetic device, but the text does not define the organs as sentient beings, so the claim of agency could be overstated.

The commentary's identification of water as lower and upper cloths could be a later interpretive layer, not an inherent meaning of the verse, thus the claim of a layered protective process may be speculative.

sanskrit: तद्धैतत्सत्यकामो जाबालो गोश्रुतये वैयाघ्रपद्यायोक्त्वोवाच यद्यप्येनच्छुष्काय स्थाणवे ब्रूयाज्जायेरन्नेवास्मिञ्छाखाः प्ररोहेयुः पलाशानीति
transliteration: taddhaitatsatyakāmo jābālo gośrutaye vaiyāghrapadyāyoktvovāca yadyapyenacchuṣkāya sthāṇave brūyājjāyerannevāsmiñchākhāḥ praroheyuḥ palāśānīti
translation: Having told this to Vyāghrapada’s son Gośruti, Satyakāma Jābāla said, ‘If a person tells this even to a dry stump [of a tree], branches and leaves will grow off it’.
word_meaning: Tat ha etat, this [teaching]; satyakāmaḥ jābālaḥ, Satyakāma Jābāla; gośrutaye vaiyāhrapadyāya uktva, saying to Vyāghrapada’s son Gośruti; uvāca, he said; yadi api, even if; etat, this [teaching]; śuṣkāya athāṇave brūyāt, a person gives to a dry stump; śākhāḥ praroheyuḥ palāśān, branches and leaves; jāyeran eva asmin, will grow off it.
commentary: This verse is meant to praise the philosophy of prāṇa . Teaching this philosophy to Gośruti, the son of Vyāghrapada, Satyakāma said that this teaching is capable of restoring life to a dead tree. Even if there is only a dry stump of a tree, leaves and branches will begin to sprout from it on hearing this teaching. Imagine then what effect it will produce if it is taught to a living human being.
contextual_topics: Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The teaching of prāṇa possesses the power to animate inert matter.
Hearing the teaching can cause latent life potential to manifest in a dead tree.
The efficacy of the teaching is independent of the receptacle's prior vitality.
If the teaching can revive a dry stump, it can transform a living human being more profoundly.
objection_hooks: How can a verbal teaching cause physical growth without a material cause?
Does the metaphor imply a literal biological effect or a symbolic spiritual awakening?
Is the statement about a dry stump intended as hyperbole rather than a factual claim?
Can the doctrine of prāṇa be substantiated empirically to support the claimed effect?
