sanskrit: वसिष्ठाय स्वाहेत्यग्नावाज्यस्य हुत्वा मन्थे सम्पातमवनयेत्प्रतिष्ठायै स्वाहेत्यग्नावाज्यस्य हुत्वा मन्थे सम्पातमवनयेत्सम्पदे स्वाहेत्यग्नावाज्यस्य हुत्वा मन्थे सम्पातमवनयेदायतनाय स्वाहेत्यग्नावाज्यस्य हुत्वा मन्थे सम्पातमवनयेत्
transliteration: vasiṣṭhāya svāhetyagnāvājyasya hutvā manthe sampātamavanayetpratiṣṭhāyai svāhetyagnāvājyasya hutvā manthe sampātamavanayetsampade svāhetyagnāvājyasya hutvā manthe sampātamavanayedāyatanāya svāhetyagnāvājyasya hutvā manthe sampātamavanayet
translation: Saying, ‘Vasiṣṭhāya svāhā ’ [i.e., svāhā to high standing], one should offer the oblation to the fire and then put whatever is left over in the offering spoon into the homa pot. Saying, ‘Pratiṣṭhāyai svāhā’ [i.e., svāhā to the support], one should offer the oblation to the fire and then put whatever is left over in the offering spoon into the homa pot. Saying, ‘Sampade svāhā’ [i.e., svāhā to affluence], one should offer the oblation to the fire and then put whatever is left over in the offering spoon into the homa pot. Saying, ‘Āyatanāya svāhā’ [i.e., svāhā to the abode], one should offer the oblation to the fire and then put whatever is left over in the offering spoon into the homa pot.
word_meaning: Vasiṣṭhāya svāhā iti, saying ‘Vasiṣṭhāya svāhā’ [i.e., Svāhā to high standing]; agnau ājyasya hutvā, one should offer the oblation to the fire; manthe sampātam avanayet, and put whatever is left over in the offering spoon into the homa pot; pratiṣṭhāyai svāhā iti, saying ‘Pratiṣṭhāyai svāhā’ [i.e., Svāhā to the support]; agnau ājyasya hutvā, one should offer the oblation to the fire; manthe sampātam avanayet, and put whatever is left over in the offering spoon into the homa pot; sampade svāhā iti, saying ‘Sampade svāhā’ [i.e., Svāhā to affluence]; agnau ājyasya hutvā, one should offer the oblation to the fire; manthe sampātam avanayet, and put whatever is left over in the offering spoon into the homa pot; āyatanāya svāhā iti, saying ‘Āyatanāya svāhā’ [i.e., Svāhā to the abode]; agnau ājyasya hutvā, one should offer the oblation to the fire; manthe sampātam avanayet, and put whatever is left over in the offering spoon into the homa pot.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: The repeated invocation of svaha to distinct entities (Vasiṣṭhāya, Pratiṣṭhāyai, Sampade, Āyatanāya) demonstrates that a single ritual utterance can be simultaneously dedicated to multiple divine aspects
The directive to transfer the remaining oblation from the spoon into the homa pot indicates that the material residue of the sacrifice retains sanctified value
The verse positions the fire (agnau) as the essential medium through which the offered oblation is transformed before any residue is handled
By prescribing the same procedural steps for offerings to varied principles, the text suggests an underlying non-dual view that material ritual actions embody spiritual realities
objection_hooks: If svaha is uttered to several different principles, how can the intention be unambiguously directed, or does this not create doctrinal confusion
The claim that leftover oblation remains sanctified may be challenged as merely practical disposal without inherent spiritual potency
Asserting fire as a transformative medium could be seen as symbolic rather than an ontologically effective process
Interpreting the procedural uniformity as evidence of non-dual integration might overread metaphysics into a purely ritual instruction

sanskrit: अथ प्रतिसृप्याञ्जलौ मन्थमाधाय जपत्यमो नामास्यमा हि ते सर्वमिदं स हि ज्येष्ठः श्रेष्ठो राजाधिपतिः स मा ज्यैष्ठ्यं श्रैष्ठ्यं राज्यमाधिपत्यं गमयत्वहमेवेदं सर्वमसानीति
transliteration: atha pratisṛpyāñjalau manthamādhāya japatyamo nāmāsyamā hi te sarvamidaṃ sa hi jyeṣṭhaḥ śreṣṭho rājādhipatiḥ sa mā jyaiṣṭhyaṃ śraiṣṭhyaṃ rājyamādhipatyaṃ gamayatvahamevedaṃ sarvamasānīti
translation: Then, moving some distance from the fire and holding the homa pot in his hands, he keeps repeating the mantra: ‘You are named ama, because all this rests on you. You are the first, the best, outstanding, and supreme. May I also be the first, the best, outstanding, and supreme. May I be all all this.’
word_meaning: Atha, then; pratisṛpya, moving away [from the fire]; añjalau mantham ādhāya, holding the homa pot in his hands; japati, he keeps repeating; amaḥ nāma asi, you are named ‘ama’; amā hi te, because on you [as prāṇa ]; sarvam idam, all this [rests]; saḥ hi jyeṣṭhaḥ śreṣṭhaḥ, he [i.e., prāṇa, called here ‘ama’] is the oldest and the best; rājā, princely; adhipatiḥ, supreme; saḥ, that [prāṇa]; mā gamayatu, make me; jyaiṣṭhyam śraiṣṭhyam rājyam ādhipatyam, the first, the best, outstanding, and supreme; aham eva idam sarvam asāni iti, may I be all this.
commentary: According to Śaṅkara, ama is another name for prāṇa. The whole world rests on prāṇa. This is why prāṇa is also called ama (all). Prāṇa is the best and the highest. Prāṇa is this world.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: Prana, called ama, is the foundational principle upon which the entire manifested world rests
Prana is characterized as the oldest and highest (jyeṣṭha, śreṣṭha) among all entities
The aspirant’s mantra seeks to equate the individual self with prana, thereby aspiring to become the universal first, best, and supreme
Identifying oneself with prana implies that the self can attain the status of the universal ruler (rājādhipati) and encompass all existence
objection_hooks: How can a limited individual consciousness legitimately claim identity with the all-pervading prana without logical contradiction
Does the verse assert an ontological identity between self and prana, or merely a devotional aspiration, and how is this distinction justified
The premise that the world rests on prana may be challenged by alternative cosmological explanations; what scriptural evidence supports this exclusive claim
If prana is the supreme ruler, how does this reconcile with the existence of other deities or principles acknowledged elsewhere in the Upanishads

sanskrit: अथ खल्वेतयर्चा पच्छ आचामति तत्सवितुर्वृणीमह इत्याचामति वयं देवस्य भोजनमित्याचामति श्रेष्ठं सर्वधातममित्याचामति तुरं भगस्य धीमहीति सर्वं पिबति निर्णिज्य कंसं चमसं वा पश्चादग्नेः संविशति चर्मणि वा स्थण्डिले वा वाचंयमोऽप्रसाहः स यदि स्त्रियं पश्येत्समृद्धं कर्मेति विद्यात्
transliteration: atha khalvetayarcā paccha ācāmati tatsaviturvṛṇīmaha ityācāmati vayaṃ devasya bhojanamityācāmati śreṣṭhaṃ sarvadhātamamityācāmati turaṃ bhagasya dhīmahīti sarvaṃ pibati nirṇijya kaṃsaṃ camasaṃ vā paścādagneḥ saṃviśati carmaṇi vā sthaṇḍile vā vācaṃyamo'prasāhaḥ sa yadi striyaṃ paśyetsamṛddhaṃ karmeti vidyāt
translation: Then, while saying this Ṛk mantra foot by foot, he eats some of what is in the homa pot. He says, ‘We pray for that food of the shining deity, ’ and then eats a little of what is in the homa pot. Saying, ‘We eat the food of that deity, ’ he eats a little of what is in the homa pot. Saying, ‘It is the best and the support of all, ’ he eats a little of what is in the homa pot. Saying, ‘We quickly meditate on Bhaga, ’ he eats the rest and washes the vessel or spoon. Then, with his speech and mind under control, he lies down behind the fire, either on the skin of an animal or directly on the sacrificial ground. If he sees a woman in his dream, he knows that the rite has been successful [and that he will succeed in whatever he does].
word_meaning: Atha khalu etayā ṛcā, then while [saying] this Ṛk mantra; pacchaḥ foot by foot; ācāmati, he eats a little [of what is in the homa pot]; tat savituḥ vṛṇīmahe, we pray for that [food] of the shining deity; iti ācāmati, saying this he eats a little [of what is in the homa pot]; vayam devasya bhojanam, we eat the food of the deity; iti ācāmati, saying this he eats a little [of what is in the homa pot]; śreṣṭham sarvadhātamam, it is the best and the support of all; iti ācāmati, saying this he eats a little [of what is in the homa pot]; turam, quickly; bhagasya dhīmahi, we meditate on Bhaga; iti sarvam pibati, saying this he drinks the rest; nirṇijya kaṃsam, [and] washing the vessel [i.e., the homa pot]; vā camasam, or spoon; aprasāhaḥ, with his mind under control; vācaṃyamaḥ, [and] his speech under control; agneḥ paścāt, behind the fire; carmaṇi vā sthaṇḍile vā, on the skin of an animal or directly on the sacrificial ground; saṃviśati, he sleeps; saḥ yadi, if he; striyam paśyet, sees a woman [in his dream]; karma samṛddham, the sacrificial rite is successful; iti vidyāt, he knows that.
commentary: While eating, the sacrificer should repeat the appropriate mantra. That is, he should eat a little and then repeat one foot of the Ṛk mantra; then eat a little more and repeat another foot, and so on. What is this mantra? It is a prayer to Savitā, the sun god. If you repeat this prayer with the appropriate rite, you will become as bright and pure as the sun.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: Repeating the mantra while consuming the sacrificial offering purifies the sacrificer, making him as bright as the sun
The appearance of a woman in the sacrificer's dream is a reliable indicator that the rite has been successful
Eating a portion of the sacrificial offering while reciting the mantra integrates the material and the divine, thereby transforming the food into the deity's sustenance
The sequence of mantra recitation foot by foot corresponds to the incremental consumption of the offering, implying a prescribed ritual rhythm
The ritual's success is measured by internal mental control and dream symbolism rather than external outcomes
objection_hooks: How can a subjective dream be considered an objective proof of ritual success?
The claim that mantra recitation while eating makes one as bright as the sun seems metaphorical; does it imply literal transformation?
Is the incremental consumption of the offering truly necessary, or could the mantra be recited independently of eating?
Does internal mental control guarantee external efficacy of the sacrifice, or is it merely personal discipline?

sanskrit: तदेष श्लोको यदा कर्मसु काम्येषु स्त्रियं स्वप्नेषु पश्यन्ति समृद्धिं तत्र जानीयात्तस्मिन्स्वप्ननिदर्शने तस्मिन्स्वप्ननिदर्शने
transliteration: tadeṣa śloko yadā karmasu kāmyeṣu striyaṃ svapneṣu paśyanti samṛddhiṃ tatra jānīyāttasminsvapnanidarśane tasminsvapnanidarśane
translation: Here is a verse in this connection: When one sees a woman in a dream while performing a rite for the fulfillment of a desire, that means it is successful. One can know this from the dream.
word_meaning: Tat eṣaḥ ślokaḥ, here is a verse on the subject; yadā, when; karmasu kāmyeṣu, in a rite for fulfilling a desire; striyam svapneṣu paśyati, one sees a woman in a dream; samṛddhim tatra, there is success; jānīyāt tasmin svapnanidarśane tasmin svapnanidarśane, one knows from seeing this in a dream, from seeing this in a dream.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty
Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: Seeing a woman in a dream during a desire‑fulfilling rite signifies that the rite will succeed
Dream visions serve as a legitimate means of knowing the outcome of ritual actions
The efficacy of a rite is externally validated by symbolic imagery rather than internal intention alone
Ritual performance aimed at desire fulfillment is subject to omens that can be interpreted to predict material prosperity
objection_hooks: The appearance of a woman in a dream could be a random psychological occurrence, not a reliable indicator of ritual success
The verse assumes a universal symbolism of the woman, but cultural contexts may assign different meanings, undermining its predictive claim
Relying on dream signs may encourage superstition, detracting from the ethical purpose of the rite
The verse does not explain how the dream conveys knowledge, leaving the mechanism ambiguous

sanskrit: श्वेतकेतुर्हारुणेयः पञ्चालानां समितिमेयाय तं ह प्रवाहणो जैवलिरुवाच कुमारानु त्वाशिषत्पितेत्यनु हि भगव इति
transliteration: śvetaketurhāruṇeyaḥ pañcālānāṃ samitimeyāya taṃ ha pravāhaṇo jaivaliruvāca kumārānu tvāśiṣatpitetyanu hi bhagava iti
translation: Once Śvetaketu, the grandson of Aruṇa, went to the court of the Pañcālas . Pravāhaṇa, the son of Jīvala, asked him, ‘Young man, did your father teach you?’ [Śvetaketu replied: ] ‘Yes, revered sir, he did’.
word_meaning: Śvetaketuḥ āruṇeyaḥ ha, once Śvetaketu, the grandson of Aruṇa; pañcālānām samitim eyāya, went to the court of the Pañcālas; tam ha, to him; pravāhaṇaḥ jaivaliḥ uvāca, Pravāhaṇa, the son of Jīvala, said; kumāra, young man; tvā pitā anu-aśiṣat iti, did your father teach you; bhagavaḥ anu hi iti, yes, revered sir, he did.
commentary: Those who want liberation should have a strong spirit of renunciation, and they should know the nature of everything, from Brahmā to a blade of grass. Earlier there was a discussion on prāṇa . Now a discussion on agni, fire, begins. The story of Śvetaketu and his father is being introduced here for that purpose.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Instruction from one's father or guru is a prerequisite for attaining true knowledge of Brahman
The dialogic exchange between student and teacher exemplifies the method required to understand the nature of fire (agni)
Renunciation combined with comprehensive knowledge of all entities, from Brahma to a blade of grass, constitutes a necessary condition for liberation
The transmission of spiritual instruction across generations, as shown by the lineage of Śvetaketu, ensures continuity of authentic teaching
objection_hooks: If self‑inquiry can reveal Brahman, why must paternal instruction be a prerequisite
The emphasis on renunciation seems at odds with the claim that detailed worldly knowledge is required for liberation
Is the narrative about fire merely a story element rather than a methodological requirement for understanding agni
Lineage transmission does not guarantee correctness; errors can be passed down despite familial continuity

sanskrit: वेत्थ यदितोऽधि प्रजाः प्रयन्तीति न भगव इति वेत्थ यथा पुनरावर्तन्त३ इति न भगव इति वेत्थ पथोर्देवयानस्य पितृयाणस्य च व्यावर्तना३ इति न भगव इति
transliteration: vettha yadito'dhi prajāḥ prayantīti na bhagava iti vettha yathā punarāvartanta3 iti na bhagava iti vettha pathordevayānasya pitṛyāṇasya ca vyāvartanā3 iti na bhagava iti
translation: [Pravāhaṇa asked, ] ‘Do you have any idea where, from this world, human beings go in heaven?’ ‘No, sir, I have no idea, ’ [replied Śvetaketu ]. ‘Do you know how they come back?’ ‘No, sir, I don’t.’ ‘Have you any idea where the two paths—the path of the gods and the path of the ancestors—part?’ ‘No, sir, I don’t know’.
word_meaning: Vettha, do you know; yat, where; itaḥ, from this place; adhi, high up; prajāḥ, living beings; prayanti iti, go; na bhagavaḥ iti, no, revered sir, I don’t; vettha, do you know; yathā, the way; punaḥ āvartante iti, they come back; na bhagavaḥ iti, no, revered sir, I don’t; vettha, do you know; pathoḥ, of the two paths; devayānasya, the path of the gods; pitṛyāṇasya ca, and the path of the ancestors; vyāvartanā iti, where they part; na bhagavaḥ iti, no, revered sir, I don’t.
commentary: The path of the gods and the path of the manes both go the same way for some distance. They separate only towards the end. Śvetaketu did not know at what point they separate, nor did he know what path those who are reborn take while coming back to the earth.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The seeker’s ignorance of where the divine and ancestral paths diverge shows that scriptural knowledge of post‑death destinations is not self‑evident
The mention of a ‘path of the gods’ and a ‘path of the ancestors’ implies a differentiated cosmology of after‑life realms
The inability to specify the point of separation suggests that the process of rebirth is concealed and requires revelation
The repeated questioning and admission of not‑knowing reflects a pedagogical method that begins with acknowledged uncertainty
The dialogue presupposes a hierarchy of post‑humous destinations, with the gods’ path distinct from the ancestors’ path
objection_hooks: How can one claim a differentiated after‑life cosmology when the text itself admits that the participants do not know the details?
The assertion that rebirth is concealed may be unwarranted; perhaps the teacher simply has not yet taught that information
The view that the method relies on acknowledged uncertainty overlooks the possibility that the questioning serves a rhetorical rather than instructional purpose

sanskrit: वेत्थ यथासौ लोको न सम्पूर्यत३ इति न भगव इति वेत्थ यथा पञ्चम्यामाहुतावापः पुरुषवचसो भवन्तीति नैव भगव इति
transliteration: vettha yathāsau loko na sampūryata3 iti na bhagava iti vettha yathā pañcamyāmāhutāvāpaḥ puruṣavacaso bhavantīti naiva bhagava iti
translation: [Pravāhaṇa asked, ] ‘Do you know why the other world [the world of the moon] is not filled with people?’ [ Śvetaketu replied, ] ‘No, revered sir, I don’t know.’ ‘Do you know why after the fifth oblation water comes to be called “ puruṣa ” [man]?’ ‘No, sir, I don’t know’.
word_meaning: Vettha yathā, do you know why; asau lokaḥ, that world [i.e., the world of the moon]; na sampūryate iti, is not filled up; na bhagavaḥ iti, no, revered sir; vettha yathā, do you know why; pañcamyām āhutau, after the fifth oblation; āpaḥ puruṣavacasaḥ bhavanti iti, water becomes known as ‘man’; na eva bhagavaḥ iti, no, revered sir, I don’t.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
claim_candidates: The Upanishadic pedagogy utilizes probing questions to expose the disciple’s lack of knowledge about cosmological and ritual symbolism
The verse implies that the lunar world is distinct from the earthly realm, being not filled with people, suggesting a hierarchical cosmology
The identification of water with purusha after the fifth oblation indicates that ritual actions can transform ordinary elements into representations of the human self
The repeated address revered sir reflects a formal epistemic hierarchy where the teacher is regarded as the ultimate source of knowledge
The dialogue demonstrates that knowledge of the underlying reasons for ritual symbolism is not assumed but must be sought through inquiry
objection_hooks: The presence of a single question does not necessarily indicate a systematic pedagogical method; it could be a narrative device
The statement that the lunar world is not filled may be a rhetorical question rather than an assertion of cosmological hierarchy
Equating water with purusha after a ritual may be metaphorical language without ontological implication, so the claim of transformation is overstated
The use of revered sir could be a conventional honorific rather than evidence of a hierarchical epistemic structure

sanskrit: अथानु किमनुशिष्ठोऽवोचथा यो हीमानि न विद्यात्कथं सोऽनुशिष्टो ब्रुवीतेति स हायस्तः पितुरर्धमेयाय तं होवाचाननुशिष्य वाव किल मा भगवानब्रवीदनु त्वाशिषमिति
transliteration: athānu kimanuśiṣṭho'vocathā yo hīmāni na vidyātkathaṃ so'nuśiṣṭo bruvīteti sa hāyastaḥ piturardhameyāya taṃ hovācānanuśiṣya vāva kila mā bhagavānabravīdanu tvāśiṣamiti
translation: [Pravāhaṇa said: ] ‘Why did you say then, “I have been taught”? How can one who does not know these things say, “I have been taught”?’ Śvetaketu was hurt. He went back to his father and said, ‘You have not really taught ṃe, yet you said, “I have taught you.”’.
word_meaning: Atha kim anuśiṣṭaḥ anu avocathāḥ, then why did you say, ‘I have been taught’; yaḥ hi imāni na vidyāt, for he who does not know these things; katham saḥ anuśiṣṭaḥ bruvīta iti, how can he say ‘I have been taught’; saḥ, he [Śvetaketu]; ha āyastaḥ, was hurt; pituḥ ardham eyāya, went back to his father’s place; tam ha uvāca, he said to him [i.e., to his father]; mā ananuśiṣya vāva kila, without really teaching me; bhagavān, revered sir; abravīt tvā anu aśiṣam iti, you said, ‘I have taught you.’
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
claim_candidates: A teacher's claim of having taught is invalid if the student lacks knowledge of the subject
The validity of instruction is judged by the student's comprehension rather than the teacher's declaration
Genuine teaching must result in the student's acquisition of knowledge; otherwise the teaching claim is false
Emotional hurt experienced by a student indicates that false claims of instruction damage the teacher‑student relationship
objection_hooks: A teacher may assert having taught even if the student has not yet internalized the knowledge; teaching can be an act independent of immediate comprehension
Knowledge alone may not be the sole criterion for teaching; disciplined practice (tapas) can precede intellectual understanding
The student's feeling of hurt is a subjective emotional response and does not constitute logical evidence against the teacher's claim
The verse may be employing rhetorical hyperbole, so deriving a universal principle about teaching from it may overextend its intended meaning

sanskrit: पञ्च मा राजन्यबन्धुः प्रश्नानप्राक्षीत्तेषां नैकंचनाशकं विवक्तुमिति स होवाच यथा मा त्वं तदैतानवदो यथाहमेषां नैकंचन वेद यद्यहमिमानवेदिष्यं कथं ते नावक्ष्यमिति
transliteration: pañca mā rājanyabandhuḥ praśnānaprākṣītteṣāṃ naikaṃcanāśakaṃ vivaktumiti sa hovāca yathā mā tvaṃ tadaitānavado yathāhameṣāṃ naikaṃcana veda yadyahamimānavediṣyaṃ kathaṃ te nāvakṣyamiti
translation: [ Śvetaketu said: ] ‘That friend of the princes put five questions to me. I was not able to answer a single one of them.’ [He then told his father the five questions. After pondering over them for some time, his father] said: ‘Those questions you told me about on your return from the court—I am not able to answer even one of them. If I knew the answers, why should I have not told you?’.
word_meaning: Rājanyabandhuḥ, the friend of princes; pañca praśnān mā aprākṣīt, asked me five questions; teṣām na ekañcana aśakam vivaktum iti, I was not able to answer a single one of them; saḥ ha uvāca, he [his father] said; yathā mā tvam tadā, [on your return from the court] as you were then; etān, all these [questions]; avadaḥ, you told [me]; yathā, so; aham eṣām na ekañcana veda, I do not know even one of them; yadi aham imān avediṣyam, if I knew them; katham te na avakṣyam iti, why should I not have told you?
commentary: The word rājanyabandhuḥ, a friend of kings or princes, is not to be taken literally. Here the word is used sarcastically. Actually, the man is a rogue.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The speaker’s admission of total ignorance about the five questions indicates that the subject matter lies beyond ordinary intellectual comprehension
The rhetorical question why should I not have told you if I knew the answers asserts that possessing knowledge entails an obligation to disclose it
The sarcastic description of the questioner as friend of princes demonstrates that social status does not guarantee insight into the ultimate truth
The father’s inability to answer, despite his seniority, suggests that experiential realization is required rather than mere scholarly inquiry
objection_hooks: One might object that the speaker’s ignorance could simply reflect a lack of preparation, not an inherent impossibility of understanding the questions
The claim that knowledge must be disclosed assumes a moral duty that is not explicitly stated in the verse and may not apply to esoteric teachings
Interpreting the sarcastic term friend of princes as a critique of status may overlook the possibility that it is merely a narrative detail without philosophical import
Asserting that experiential realization is necessary may be challenged by the view that systematic study can also lead to answers, which the verse does not preclude

sanskrit: स ह गौतमो राज्ञोऽर्धमेयाय तस्मै ह प्राप्तायार्हां चकार स ह प्रातः सभाग उदेयाय तं होवाच मानुषस्य भगवन्गौतम वित्तस्य वरं वृणीथा इति स होवाच तवैव राजन्मानुषं वित्तं यामेव कुमारस्यान्ते वाचमभाषथास्तामेव मे ब्रूहीति स ह कृच्छ्री बभूव
transliteration: sa ha gautamo rājño'rdhameyāya tasmai ha prāptāyārhāṃ cakāra sa ha prātaḥ sabhāga udeyāya taṃ hovāca mānuṣasya bhagavangautama vittasya varaṃ vṛṇīthā iti sa hovāca tavaiva rājanmānuṣaṃ vittaṃ yāmeva kumārasyānte vācamabhāṣathāstāmeva me brūhīti sa ha kṛcchrī babhūva
translation: Gautama then went to the king’s palace. On his arrival, the king welcomed him respectfully. The next morning, when the king was in his court, Gautama went there to meet him. The king said to him, ‘Revered Gautama, ask for a boon from me—anything a person might wish for.’ Gautama replied: ‘Let those things be with you. Please tell me whatever you said to my son.’ Hearing this, the king turned pale.
word_meaning: Saḥ ha gautamaḥ, then Gautama; rājñaḥ ardham eyāya, went to the king’s palace; prāptāya, when he arrived; tasmai ha arhām cakāra, the king respectfully welcomed him; saḥ, he [Gautama]; ha prātaḥ, the next morning; sabhāge udeyāya, went to see the king in the court; tam ha uvāca, he [the king] said to him [Gautama]; bhagavan gautama, revered Gautama; mānuṣasya vittasya varam vṛṇīthāḥ iti, ask for any precious thing a person may wish for as a boon; saḥ ha uvāca, he [Gautama] said; rājan, O king; tava eva mānuṣam vittam, let the human wealth be yours; yām eva kumārasya ante vācam abhāṣathāḥ, that which you said to my son; tām eva, the same; me brūhi iti, tell me; saḥ ha kṛcchrī babhūva, he [the king] was very depressed.
commentary: It was against the custom for a kṣatriya, a king, to teach a brāhmin. This is why the king became depressed.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: The king's offering of any boon to Gautama reflects the king's duty to honor Brahmins
Gautama's request that the king convey to his son reverses typical hierarchical communication and challenges social norms
The king's depression upon Gautama's request demonstrates that violating the custom of a Kshatriya teaching a Brahmin causes moral distress
The interaction suggests that material wealth is secondary to the transmission of knowledge or instruction
The king's authority is limited when confronted with the higher spiritual authority of a Brahmin
objection_hooks: The text does not explicitly state that the king's depression is caused by the custom violation; his pallor could have other explanations
The commentary's claim about the custom may be a later interpretive addition not directly evident in the verse itself
The assumption that a social custom has sufficient moral weight to cause depression conflates external duty with internal psychological state
The claim presumes the king internalized the custom, which is not demonstrated in the verse

sanskrit: तं ह चिरं वसेत्याज्ञापयांचकार तं होवाच यथा मा त्वं गौतमावदो यथेयं न प्राक्त्वत्तः पुरा विद्या ब्राह्मणान्गच्छति तस्मादु सर्वेषु लोकेषु क्षत्रस्यैव प्रशासनमभूदिति तस्मै होवाच
transliteration: taṃ ha ciraṃ vasetyājñāpayāṃcakāra taṃ hovāca yathā mā tvaṃ gautamāvado yatheyaṃ na prāktvattaḥ purā vidyā brāhmaṇāngacchati tasmādu sarveṣu lokeṣu kṣatrasyaiva praśāsanamabhūditi tasmai hovāca
translation: The king then issued orders that Gautama should stay with him for a long time [as a brahmacari . Gautama did that. One day] the king said to him: ‘O Gautama, regarding the matter which you asked about, no brāhmin before you had access to this knowledge. This is why in the past, in all the worlds, it was only the kṣatriyas who had the right to impart this knowledge.’ Having said this, he proceeded to teach Gautama.
word_meaning: Tam, to him [to Gautama]; ciram vasa ha iti, stay for a long time; ājñāpayāñcakāra, he issued orders; tam ha uvāca, he said to him [to Gautama]; gautama, O Gautama; yathā mā tvam āvadaḥ, as you said to me; yathā iyam vidyā, because this knowledge; prāk tvattaḥ, before you; brāhmaṇān na gacchati, did not go to the brāhmins; purā, in the past; tasmāt u, that is why; sarveṣu lokeṣu, in all the worlds; kṣatrasya eva praśāsanam abhūt iti, only kṣatriyas had the right to teach it; tasmai ha uvāca, he said to him.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: The authority to impart sacred knowledge was historically limited to the Kshatriya class.
No Brahmin before Gautama possessed this particular knowledge, indicating a caste-based epistemic hierarchy.
The king’s decree allowing Gautama to stay long demonstrates that royal patronage can override traditional class restrictions on teaching.
Transmission of this knowledge is linked to the social duty of the Kshatriya rather than solely to spiritual merit.
objection_hooks: Scriptural sources elsewhere describe Brahmins as primary teachers of sacred knowledge, challenging the claim of exclusive Kshatriya authority.
Dharmic principles prescribe immutable varna duties, so the idea that a king can override caste restrictions may contradict established dharma.
Advaita Vedanta holds that knowledge of Brahman is independent of social status, questioning the link between caste duty and spiritual insight.
Historical evidence of Brahmin scholars teaching similar doctrines suggests the claim of no prior Brahmin knowledge may be inaccurate.

sanskrit: इति तृतीयः खण्डः ॥
transliteration: asau vāva loko gautamāgnistasyāditya eva samidraśmayo dhūmo'hararciścandramā aṅgārā nakṣatrāṇi visphuliṅgāḥ
translation: O Gautama, heaven is the [sacrificial] fire; the sun is its fuel; the rays are the smoke; day is the flame; the moon is the embers; and the stars are the sparks.
word_meaning: Gautama, O Gautama; asau vāva lokaḥ agniḥ, that world there [i.e., heaven] is the fire; ādityaḥ eva tasya samit, the sun is its fuel; raśmayaḥ dhūmaḥ, the rays are the smoke; ahaḥ arciḥ, the day is the flame; candramāḥ aṅgārāḥ, the moon is the embers; nakṣatrāṇi visphuliṅgāḥ, the stars are the sparks.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The cosmic order is analogized to a sacrificial fire, implying that the universe functions as a ritual offering
The sun serves as the essential energy (fuel) sustaining the cosmic fire, indicating its role as the primary source of vitality
Day, moon, and stars correspond to different stages or components of the fire (flame, embers, sparks), suggesting a hierarchical structure within the cosmic manifestation
The identification of celestial bodies with elements of fire implies that material phenomena are expressions of a deeper, unifying principle
objection_hooks: The analogy may be metaphorical, not indicating an actual functional equivalence, thus the claim that the universe functions as a ritual offering could be overstated
Assigning the sun as the sole fuel ignores other cosmic forces, questioning the exclusivity implied
The hierarchical mapping of day, moon, stars to fire components may be culturally specific and not reflect an inherent cosmic order
Interpreting material phenomena as expressions of a unifying principle presupposes a metaphysical framework not explicit in the verse

sanskrit: तस्मिन्नेतस्मिन्नग्नौ देवाः श्रद्धां जुह्वति तस्या अहुतेः सोमो राजा संभवति
transliteration: tasminnetasminnagnau devāḥ śraddhāṃ juhvati tasyā ahuteḥ somo rājā saṃbhavati
translation: The gods [i.e., the organs of the sacrificer] offer water as a token of respect to the fire [heaven]. Out of that oblation appears King Soma [the shining moon].
word_meaning: Tasmin etasinin agnau, in that fire [which is also heaven]; devāḥ, the gods [i.e., the organs of the sacrificer]; śraddhām juhvati, offer faith [as water] as the oblation; tasyāḥ āhuteḥ, out of that oblation; rājā somaḥ, King Soma [i.e., the shining moon]; sambhavati, appears.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty
sub_concepts: Brahman as Cosmological and Physical Principle
claim_candidates: The sacrificial fire functions as a cosmic conduit through which the divine Soma manifests
The organs of the sacrificer are metaphorically identified as gods, indicating internal participation in ritual efficacy
Offering water as an expression of faith to the fire transforms the material offering into a celestial phenomenon
The appearance of Soma, the shining moon, from the oblation demonstrates that ritual action generates cosmic order
The fire is equated with heaven, suggesting the altar is a microcosm of the celestial realm
objection_hooks: How can a physical fire literally produce the moon, or is this metaphorical, questioning the literal reading
The identification of bodily organs as gods may be symbolic, but does it imply actual divinity, raising epistemic doubt
If devotion transforms water into celestial phenomena, what mechanism is invoked, and does this rely on unverified metaphysical causation
The notion of fire as heaven could be poetic; does it hold ontological weight or is it merely a rhetorical device

sanskrit: पर्जन्यो वाव गौतमाग्निस्तस्य वायुरेव समिदभ्रं धूमो विद्युदर्चिरशनिरङ्गाराह्रादनयो विस्फुलिङ्गाः
transliteration: parjanyo vāva gautamāgnistasya vāyureva samidabhraṃ dhūmo vidyudarciraśaniraṅgārāhrādanayo visphuliṅgāḥ
translation: O Gautama, the god of rain is the [sacrificial] fire; air is its fuel; the cloud is the smoke; lightning is the flame; the thunderbolt is the embers; and thunder is the sparks.
word_meaning: Gautama, O Gautama; parjanyaḥ vāva agniḥ, the god of rain is the fire; vāyuḥ eva tasya samit, air is its fuel; abhram dhūmaḥ, the cloud is the smoke; vidyut arciḥ, lightning is the flame; aśaniḥ aṅgārāḥ, the thunderbolt is the embers; hrādanayaḥ visphuliṅgāḥ, thunder is the sparks.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The verse equates the god of rain with sacrificial fire, identifying rain as fire.
Air is described as the fuel of fire, linking breath to the sustenance of divine activity.

Cloud, lightning, thunderbolt, and thunder are presented as smoke, flame, embers, and sparks respectively, showing a systematic correspondence between natural phenomena and components of the sacrificial fire.
The passage portrays the sacrificial fire as a symbolic microcosm that reflects the larger cosmic order of elements.
By mapping diverse elements onto the fire ritual, the verse suggests that ritual symbolism mirrors the underlying unity of the cosmos.
objection_hooks: If rain is fire, does the metaphor collapse the distinct qualities of water and fire into a contradictory identity?
The identification may be merely poetic; how can we know whether it asserts literal ontological identity rather than symbolic analogy?
By calling air merely fuel, does the verse diminish the independent agency of wind as a principle of nature?

sanskrit: तस्मिन्नेतस्मिन्नग्नौ देवाः सोमं राजानं जुह्वति तस्या आहुतेर्वर्षं संभवति
transliteration: tasminnetasminnagnau devāḥ somaṃ rājānaṃ juhvati tasyā āhutervarṣaṃ saṃbhavati
translation: The gods offer King Soma [the shining moon] as the oblation to the fire. Out of that oblation appears rain.
word_meaning: Tasmin etasmin agnau, in that fire; devāḥ, the gods; somam rājānam juhvati, offer King Soma [the shining moon] as the oblation; tasyāḥ āhuteḥ, out of that oblation; varṣam, rain; sambhavati, appears.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: The performance of a divine sacrifice to Agni by the gods demonstrates that ritual offerings can directly influence natural phenomena such as rain
The identification of Soma with a king implies that the moon holds sovereign authority among celestial bodies in Vedic cosmology
The fire (Agni) functions as a transformative medium that converts the offering of Soma into rain, indicating a causal link between fire and water in the cosmic order
The verse suggests that the gods themselves rely on material oblations to fulfill their purposes, indicating that divine action operates through material processes
objection_hooks: How can a symbolic ritual performed by deities be said to cause physical rain, given the lack of empirical evidence for such causation
Does personifying the moon as a king merely reflect poetic language rather than an ontological claim about its supremacy
If divine action depends on material offerings, does this imply limitation of the gods, contradicting the notion of their omnipotence

sanskrit: पृथिवी वाव गौतमाग्निस्तस्याः संवत्सर एव समिदाकाशो धूमो रात्रिरर्चिर्दिशोऽङ्गारा अवान्तरदिशो विस्फुलिङ्गाः
transliteration: pṛthivī vāva gautamāgnistasyāḥ saṃvatsara eva samidākāśo dhūmo rātrirarcirdiśo'ṅgārā avāntaradiśo visphuliṅgāḥ
translation: O Gautama, the earth is the [sacrificial] fire; the year is its fuel; the sky is the smoke; night is the flame; the quarters are the embers; and the intermediate directions are the sparks.
word_meaning: Gautama, O Gautama; pṛthivī vāva agniḥ, earth is the fire; saṃvatsaraḥ eva tasyāḥ samit, the year is its fuel; ākāśaḥ dhūmaḥ, the sky is the smoke; rātriḥ arciḥ, night is the flame; diśaḥ aṅgārāḥ, the quarters are the embers; avāṅtaradiśaḥ visphuliṅgāḥ, the intermediate directions are the sparks.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
sub_concepts: Brahman as Cosmological and Physical Principle
claim_candidates: The verse proposes that the entire cosmos functions as a single sacrificial fire, thereby equating material existence with the ritual act of yajna
By identifying the earth with fire and the sky with smoke, the text suggests that the apparent duality of solid and ethereal elements is ultimately a manifestation of one underlying reality
The description of the year as fuel implies that temporal cycles are the energizing principle sustaining the cosmic fire, linking time directly to the sustenance of Brahman
The classification of the intermediate directions as sparks indicates that even the subtle, peripheral aspects of space are integral expressions of the same divine fire
The metaphorical mapping asserts that the sacrificial fire is not an external ritual object but an intrinsic cosmic process, thereby redefining yajna as an internal, universal phenomenon
objection_hooks: If the cosmos is a sacrificial fire, how does the verse account for the existence of non‑fire elements such as water or earth that do not appear as components of the fire metaphor

Equating the year with fuel may conflate metaphorical language with literal causation, raising the question of whether temporal cycles truly energize the divine fire or merely illustrate a poetic analogy
The identification of the sky as smoke could be challenged on ontological grounds, since smoke is a transient by‑product whereas the sky is a vast, enduring expanse
Interpreting the intermediate directions as sparks might overlook the possibility that the verse simply enumerates directional points without implying a deeper metaphysical unity

sanskrit: तस्मिन्नेतस्मिन्नग्नौ देवा वर्षं जुह्वति तस्या आहुतेरन्नं संभवति
transliteration: tasminnetasminnagnau devā varṣaṃ juhvati tasyā āhuterannaṃ saṃbhavati
translation: The gods offer rain as the oblation to the fire. Out of that oblation appears food.
word_meaning: Tasmin etasmin agnau, in that fire; devāḥ, the gods; varṣam juhvati, offer rain as the oblation; tasyāḥ āhuteḥ, out of that oblation; annam, food; sambhavati, appears.
contextual_topics: Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
Progressive Worship of Brahman up to the Universal Self
claim_candidates: The verse asserts that divine rain, when offered to the fire, is causally responsible for the production of food
It conveys that the fire functions as a transformative medium through which celestial elements become material sustenance
The text implies that proper ritual offering to the fire is a prerequisite for material well‑being, linking ethical duty to physical nourishment
By describing gods performing the offering, the verse suggests a reciprocal relationship between deities and sacrificial elements, indicating interdependence among divine forces
The passage presents the sacrificial fire as a conduit that actualizes divine generosity, reflecting a theological principle that worship materializes divine blessings
objection_hooks: The causal link between offering rain to fire and appearance of food may be metaphorical rather than literal, questioning the literal reading of the first claim
The notion that fire transforms celestial rain into food could be challenged as a symbolic representation, not an ontological process, targeting the second claim
Asserting that ritual offering guarantees material well‑being may promote deterministic fatalism, challenging the third claim
The idea of gods needing fire to receive rain anthropomorphizes deities and may not reflect established theological doctrine, targeting the fourth claim

sanskrit: पुरुषो वाव गौतमाग्निस्तस्य वागेव समित्प्राणो धूमो जिह्वार्चिश्चक्षुरङ्गाराः श्रोत्रं विस्फुलिङ्गाः
transliteration: puruṣo vāva gautamāgnistasya vāgeva samitprāṇo dhūmo jihvārciścakṣuraṅgārāḥ śrotraṃ visphuliṅgāḥ
translation: O Gautama, man is the [sacrificial] fire; speech is his fuel; prāṇa is the smoke; the tongue is the flame; the eyes are the embers; and the ears are the sparks.
word_meaning: Gautama, O Gautama; puruṣaḥ vāva agniḥ, man is the fire; vāk eva tasya samit, speech is his fuel; prāṇaḥ dhūmaḥ, prāṇa is the smoke; jihvā arciḥ, the tongue is the flame; cakṣuḥ aṅgārāḥ, the eyes are the embers; śrotram visphuliṅgāḥ, the ears are the sparks.
commentary: Speech is said to be the fuel because it is the source of strength. A person who cannot speak is helpless. Prāṇa is the smoke because the breath comes out of the mouth just as smoke comes out of fire. The tongue is the flame because both are red. The eyes are the embers because both appear to be shining. And the ears are the sparks because both spread out and cover a large area.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
claim_candidates: Speech functions as the essential fuel that sustains the human fire, implying that verbal expression is prerequisite for effective action
Prāṇa, identified as smoke, is a manifestation of the inner fire’s activity, suggesting that breath is a byproduct of the self’s energetic core
The sensory organs—tongue, eyes, ears—are metaphorically equated with flame, embers, and sparks, indicating that perception arises from the activation of the inner fire
The inability to speak renders a person helpless, asserting that speech is indispensable for agency within the human fire metaphor
The overall analogy portrays the human being as a unified sacrificial fire, supporting the view that the individual self is a microcosmic reflection of the universal fire
objection_hooks: The claim that speech is the essential fuel may be challenged as a metaphorical exaggeration that does not account for non‑verbal forms of influence
Equating prāṇa with smoke could be questioned on the basis that breath is vital for life, not merely a byproduct, thus the analogy may invert causal priority
Describing sensory perception as fire elements might be critiqued for overlooking the physiological mechanisms that operate independently of any inner fire
Asserting that a speechless person is helpless may be disputed by examples of mute sages who achieve spiritual mastery without verbal expression

sanskrit: तस्मिन्नेतस्मिन्नग्नौ देवा अन्नं जुह्वति तस्या आहुते रेतः सम्भवति
transliteration: tasminnetasminnagnau devā annaṃ juhvati tasyā āhute retaḥ sambhavati
translation: The gods offer food as the oblation to the fire. Out of that oblation appears semen.
word_meaning: Tasmin etasmin agnau, in that fire; devāḥ, the gods; annam juhvati, offer food as the oblation; tasyāḥ āhuteḥ, out of that oblation; retaḥ, semen; sambhavati, appears.
contextual_topics: Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
The Universal Self
Being as the Source of All
claim_candidates: The sacrificial fire functions as a transformative medium that converts external offerings into the internal creative principle of semen
The emergence of semen from the oblation indicates that divine activity (gods' offering) is intrinsically linked to human procreative power
Ritual offerings are not merely symbolic but are causally effective in generating vital life-force
The verse suggests that the material substance (food) and the vital essence (semen) are ontologically connected through the agency of the fire
The description of semen as a product of the sacrifice implies that the sacred act participates in the process of creation
objection_hooks: How can a physical fire literally produce semen given biological constraints
Does the verse intend a metaphorical reading of semen rather than a literal physiological claim
If ritual alone generates life-force, why does the text not acknowledge natural biological reproduction
Could the claim that offerings transform into semen be an overextension of symbolic language beyond its intended ritual context

sanskrit: योषा वाव गौतमाग्निस्तस्या उपस्थ एव समिद्यदुपमन्त्रयते स धूमो योनिरर्चिर्यदन्तः करोति तेऽङ्गारा अभिनन्दा विस्फुलिङ्गाः
transliteration: yoṣā vāva gautamāgnistasyā upastha eva samidyadupamantrayate sa dhūmo yonirarciryadantaḥ karoti te'ṅgārā abhinandā visphuliṅgāḥ
translation: 1-2. O Gautama, woman is the [sacrificial] fire... The gods offer semen as the oblation to the fire. Out of that oblation appears the foetus.
word_meaning: nothing, here.
contextual_topics: The Cosmic-Egg
sub_concepts: Brahman as Cosmological and Physical Principle
claim_candidates: Woman functions as a sacrificial fire in the process of creation
Divine semen offered to the fire results in the generation of a foetus, implying that procreation is a ritual offering
The emergence of the foetus from the fire symbolizes the transformation of material offerings into a living being, indicating that the material world is a manifestation of the divine principle
The description equates the act of conception with a sacred sacrifice, suggesting that sexual union is a means of realizing cosmic order
objection_hooks: How can a physical process like conception be equated with a sacrificial fire without metaphorical exaggeration
Does the verse imply that the divine semen is literal, raising issues of literalism versus symbolism
The claim that woman is fire may conflict with other Upanishadic depictions of the feminine principle, questioning consistency
If procreation is presented as a ritual, does this diminish the role of personal agency in the act

sanskrit: इति तु पञ्चम्यामाहुतावापः पुरुषवचसो भवन्तीति स उल्बावृतो गर्भो दश वा नव वा मासानन्तः शयित्वा यावद्वाथ जायते
transliteration: iti tu pañcamyāmāhutāvāpaḥ puruṣavacaso bhavantīti sa ulbāvṛto garbho daśa vā nava vā māsānantaḥ śayitvā yāvadvātha jāyate
translation: Thus, after the fifth oblation, water becomes known as ‘man.’ The foetus lies within the mother’s womb, covered with membrane, for about nine or ten months, and then it is born.
word_meaning: Iti tu, thus [the fifth question has been answered]; pañcamyām āhutau, after the fifth oblation; āpaḥ, water; puruṣavacasaḥ bhavanti iti, becomes known as ‘man’; ulbāvṛtaḥ, covered with membrane; saḥ garbhaḥ, that foetus; daśa vā nava vā māsān, for nine or ten months; yāvat vā, or so; antaḥ śayitvā, lying inside [the mother’s womb]; atha jāyate, is then born.
commentary: If all five oblations have been offered, then the water of the first oblation becomes a puruṣa, a human being. It lies in its mother’s womb for nine or ten months and is then born as a child. This is the answer to the last of the five questions that Pravāhaṇa asked Śvetaketu . By answering the last question first, he could answer the others more easily.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The fifth ritual oblation transforms the elemental water into a human being (purusha)
The scriptural description specifies a gestation period of nine or ten months for a human being
The identification of water with the human indicates that the material element serves as a symbolic representation of the individual self
Answering the final of the five questions first provides a methodological key that simplifies resolution of the preceding questions
The covering membrane (ulbāvṛta) of the foetus denotes an intermediate state between elemental water and the fully formed human
objection_hooks: How can a ritual act cause a literal transformation of water into a human being rather than a metaphorical identification
Does the scriptural specification of a nine- or ten‑month gestation period account for natural variations, or is it a symbolic number
Is the equivalence of water and the human self sufficient to infer a broader symbolic representation of Brahman, or does it overextend the textual meaning
Does the claim that answering the last question first simplifies the others assume a logical hierarchy that the text does not explicitly state

sanskrit: स जातो यावदायुषं जीवति तं प्रेतं दिष्टमितोऽग्नय एव हरन्ति यत एवेतो यतः संभूतो भवति
transliteration: sa jāto yāvadāyuṣaṃ jīvati taṃ pretaṃ diṣṭamito'gnaya eva haranti yata eveto yataḥ saṃbhūto bhavati
translation: When a person is born, he lives as long as he is destined to live. Then, when he dies as ordained, they [his sons or disciples] take him from his home to the fire from which he came. It is that same fire from which he was born [and to which he owes his birth].
word_meaning: Saḥ jātaḥ, [when] he is born; yāvat-āyuṣam jīvati, he lives as long as he is destined; diṣṭam pretam, dying as ordained; itaḥ, from here [his home]; taw agnaye eva haranti, they take him to the fire; yataḥ eva itaḥ, from which he came here; yataḥ sambhūtaḥ bhavati, that from which he was born.
commentary: From each oblation, something is born that is offered as the next oblation in the fire. The last thing born is a human being. This is why it is said that a human being is born of fire. In the end, when that person dies, his body also is offered in that same fire.
contextual_topics: Being as the Source of All
sub_concepts: Brahman as Cosmological and Physical Principle
claim_candidates: The fire that births a human is the same fire that receives his body at death
Human existence is cyclically linked to fire, indicating fire as the fundamental medium of life and death
The span of a person's life is predetermined and not dependent on personal actions
Offering the body to fire at death fulfills a cosmic order of returning to the source
objection_hooks: If fire at birth is metaphorical, how can it be literally the same fire that consumes the body at death?
The claim that life span is predetermined ignores evidence of lifestyle influencing longevity
Other elements such as water and air also sustain life, challenging the idea that fire alone is the fundamental medium
Ritual offering to fire may be cultural practice rather than a necessary cosmic requirement

sanskrit: तद्य इत्थं विदुः। ये चेमेऽरण्ये श्रद्धा तप इत्युपासते तेऽर्चिषमभिसंभवन्त्यर्चिषोऽहरह्न आपूर्यमाणपक्षमापूर्यमाणपक्षाद्यान्षडुदङ्ङेति मासांस्तान्
transliteration: tadya itthaṃ viduḥ| ye ceme'raṇye śraddhā tapa ityupāsate te'rciṣamabhisaṃbhavantyarciṣo'harahna āpūryamāṇapakṣamāpūryamāṇapakṣādyānṣaḍudaṅṅeti māsāṃstān
translation: 1-2. Those who know this [about the five fires], and those who live in the forest practising austerities with faith—they go after death to the world of light. From the world of light they go to the world of day; from the world of day to the world of the bright fortnight; from the world of the bright fortnight to the six months when the sun moves northward; from there they go to the year; from the year to the sun; from the sun to the moon; and from the moon to lightning. There someone, not human, receives them and leads them to brahmaloka . This is the path of the gods.
word_meaning: Tat ye viduḥ, those who know this [i.e., about the five fires]; ittham, thus; ye ca ime, and these people who; araṇye, in the forest; śraddhā tapaḥ iti upāsate, practise austerities with faith; te arciṣam abhisambhavanti, they become [attain] light; arciṣaḥ, from light; ahaḥ, to the day; ahnaḥ, from the day; āpūryamāṇapakṣam, to the bright fortnight; āpūryamāṇapakṣāt, from the bright fortnight; yān ṣaṭ māsān, to the six months; udan eti, [when the sun] moves to the north; tān, to that; māsebhyaḥ, from those months; saṃvatsaram, to the year; saṃvatsarāt, from the year; ādityam, to the sun; ādityāt, from the sun; candramasam, to the moon; candramasaḥ, from the moon; vidyutam, to lightning; tat, there; puruṣaḥ, a person [existing there]; amānavaḥ, not human; enān, those [human beings]; saḥ gamayati, leads; brahma, to brahmaloka; eṣaḥ devayānaḥ panthāḥ iti, this is the path of the gods
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: Practising austerities with faith in the forest guarantees ascent through successive cosmic realms after death
The ascent proceeds through the specific stages of light, day, bright fortnight, six months of northward sun, year, sun, moon, and lightning before reaching Brahmaloka
A non‑human being receives the soul at the final stage and leads it to Brahmaloka, indicating divine assistance is required for ultimate liberation
The described sequence is presented as the path of the gods, implying a hierarchical cosmology of post‑mortem progression
objection_hooks: The guarantee of ascent based solely on austerities may be challenged by the possibility of other karmic factors influencing post‑mortem destiny
The literal interpretation of the listed cosmic stages could be symbolic, raising doubt about their ontological reality
The involvement of a non‑human guide appears to conflict with Advaita’s emphasis on self‑realisation as the means to Brahman

translation: 1-2. Those who know this [about the five fires], and those who live in the forest practising austerities with faith—they go after death to the world of light. From the world of light they go to the world of day; from the world of day to the world of the bright fortnight; from the world of the bright fortnight to the six months when the sun moves northward; from there they go to the year; from the year to the sun; from the sun to the moon; and from the moon to lightning.
