translation: ‘You enjoy eating food and you see your dear ones and everything pleasant. He who worships the Vaiśvānara Self thus enjoys eating food and is able to see his dear ones. He also has children in his family who shine with the radiance of Brahman [i.e., they become well known for their good conduct and scholarship]. But water is like the bladder of the Self.’ Then the king said, ‘If you had not come to me your bladder would have burst’.
word_meaning: Annam atsi, [the king said: ] you eat food; priyam paśyasi, you see everything pleasant [i.e., your children, grandchildren, etc.]; yaḥ, he who; etam evam vaiśvānaram ātmānam upāste, worships this Vaiśvānara Ātman thus; annam atti, eats food; priyam paśyati, [and] sees everything pleasant [or, sees his dear ones]; asya kule, in his family; brahmavarcasam bhavati, are born those who shine with the brightness of Brahman; eṣaḥ tu ātmanaḥ bastiḥ itḥ but this [water] is like the bladder of the Self; ha uvāca, he [the king] said; te bastiḥ vyabhetsyat, your bladder would have burst; yat mām na āgamiṣyaḥ iti, if you had not come to me.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: Worship of the Vaiśvānara Self guarantees enjoyment of food and the ability to see dear ones
Children born in the family of one who worships the Vaiśvānara Self shine with the radiance of Brahman
The Self is compared to water, specifically its bladder, indicating a functional similarity in containing vital essence
Neglecting the Self leads to internal rupture, as illustrated by the king's warning about a bursting bladder
objection_hooks: The promise of material enjoyment may be metaphorical rather than literal, questioning the claim of guaranteed pleasure
The description of children shining with Brahman's radiance could be symbolic, not an empirical observation
The analogy of water to the bladder of the Self is ambiguous and may not establish a clear ontological relationship
The king's statement might be hyperbolic, lacking doctrinal support for a causal link between self-neglect and bodily rupture

sanskrit: अथ होवाचोद्दालकमारुणिं गौतम कं त्वमात्मानमुपस्स इति पृथिवीमेव भगवो राजन्निति होवाचैष वै प्रतिष्ठात्मा वैश्वानरो यं त्वमात्मानमुपास्से तस्मात्त्वं प्रतिष्ठितोऽसि प्रजया च पशुभिश्च
transliteration: atha hovācoddālakamāruṇiṃ gautama kaṃ tvamātmānamupassa iti pṛthivīmeva bhagavo rājanniti hovācaiṣa vai pratiṣṭhātmā vaiśvānaro yaṃ tvamātmānamupāsse tasmāttvaṃ pratiṣṭhito'si prajayā ca paśubhiśca
translation: The king then said to Uddālaka Āruṇi, ‘O Gautama, whom do you worship as the Self?’ Uddālaka replied, ‘I worship the earth, revered king.’ The king said: ‘That which you worship as the Vaiśvānara Ātman is named Pratiṣṭhā [the support]. This is why you have so many children and animals to support you’.
word_meaning: Atha, next; ha uvāca, he [the king] said; uddālakam āruṇim, to Uddālaka Āruṇi; gautama, O Gautama; kam, whom; tvam ātmānam upāsse iti, do you worship as the Self; bhagavaḥ rājan, revered king; pṛthivīm eva iti, [I worship] the earth; ha uvāca, [the king] said; yam tvam ātmānam upāsse, the Self which you worship; eṣaḥ, this [earth]; vai, for sure; ātmā vaiśvānaraḥ, is the Vaiśvānara Ātman; pratiṣṭhā, as Pratiṣṭhā [the support]; tasmāt, therefore; tvam, you; pratiṣṭhitaḥ prajayā ca paśubhiḥ ca asi, are supported by children and animals.
commentary: The earth is like the feet of Vaiśvānara Ātman. This is why it is ‘the support.’
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The earth is identified as the Vaiśvānara Ātman, the universal Self that pervades all beings
Worship of the earth as the Self provides material support (pratiṣṭhā) for one’s children and animals
The identification of the earth as the Self functions as a substitute for more elaborate ritual worship of the divine
The concept of Pratiṣṭhā (support) is derived from the relationship between the Self (earth) and the dependent beings (children, animals)
The dialogue implies that the individual Self can be external (earth) and thus identical with the cosmic Self
objection_hooks: How can a material object like the earth be equated with the infinite, non‑material Vaiśvānara Ātman without logical contradiction
Does worship of the earth truly replace ritual practices, or does it merely simplify them while retaining the same metaphysical assumptions
The verse may be stating a pragmatic observation about support rather than a metaphysical causality; is the claim about support literal or metaphorical
If the Self is identified with the earth, how does this account for other elemental aspects of the cosmos such as sky or fire

sanskrit: अत्स्यन्नं पश्यसि प्रियमत्त्यन्नं पश्यति प्रियं भवत्यस्य ब्रह्मवर्चसं कुले य एतमेवमात्मानं वैश्वानरमुपास्ते पादौ त्वेतावात्मन इति होवाच पादौ ते व्यम्लास्येतां यन्मां नागमिष्य इति
transliteration: atsyannaṃ paśyasi priyamattyannaṃ paśyati priyaṃ bhavatyasya brahmavarcasaṃ kule ya etamevamātmānaṃ vaiśvānaramupāste pādau tvetāvātmana iti hovāca pādau te vyamlāsyetāṃ yanmāṃ nāgamiṣya iti
translation: ‘You enjoy eating food and you see your dear ones and everything pleasant. He who worships the Vaiśvānara Self thus enjoys eating food and is able to see his dear ones. He also has children in his family who shine with the radiance of Brahman [i.e., they become well known for their good conduct and scholarship]. But the earth is like the feet of the Self.’ Then the king said, ‘If you had not come to me your feet would have become extremely weak’.
word_meaning: Annam atsi, [the king said: ] you eat food; priyam paśyasi, you see everything pleasant [i.e., your children, grandchildren, etc.]; yaḥ, he who; etam evam vaiśvānaram ātmānam upāste, worships this Vaiśvānara Ātman thus; annam atti, eats food; priyam paśyati, [and] sees everything pleasant [or, sees his dear ones]; asya kule, in his family; brahmavarcasam bhavati, are born those who shine with the brightness of Brahman; eṣaḥ tu ātmanaḥ pādau iti, but this [earth] is like the two feet of the Self; ha uvāca, he [the king] said; te pādau vyamlāsyetām, your feet would have become very weak; yat mām na āgamiṣyaḥ iti, if you had not come to me.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Worship of the Vaiśvānara Atman guarantees material prosperity and pleasant relationships
The progeny of one who worships the Self are described as shining with the brilliance of Brahman
The earth is metaphorically likened to the feet of the Self, indicating that the material world supports the spiritual Self
The king’s statement that the feet would become weak without his presence implies a dependence of material well‑being on worldly authority
objection_hooks: The verse may merely describe a correlation between worship and prosperity, not a causal guarantee
The comparison of earth to the feet of the Self could be poetic symbolism rather than an ontological claim of support
The king’s remark might be a rhetorical boast rather than a doctrinal assertion about dependence on authority

sanskrit: तान्होवाचैते वै खलु यूयं पृथगिवेममात्मानं वैश्वानरं विद्वांसोऽन्नमत्थ यस्त्वेतमेवं प्रादेशमात्रमभिविमानमात्मानं वैश्वानरमुपास्ते स सर्वेषु लोकेषु सर्वेषु भूतेषु सर्वेष्वात्मस्वन्नमत्ति
transliteration: tānhovācaite vai khalu yūyaṃ pṛthagivemamātmānaṃ vaiśvānaraṃ vidvāṃso'nnamattha yastvetamevaṃ prādeśamātramabhivimānamātmānaṃ vaiśvānaramupāste sa sarveṣu lokeṣu sarveṣu bhūteṣu sarveṣvātmasvannamatti
translation: The king said to the brāhmins: ‘Those of you who are here meditate on the Vaiśvānara Self only in part. [That is why when you eat you think you are eating separately.] He who worships the Self as all-pervasive and infinite, enjoys eating through whoever eats in the worlds, through all beings, and through all selves.
word_meaning: Tān, to them [the brāhmins]; ha uvāca, [the king] said; ete yūyam vai khalu, those of you here; imam vaiśvānaram ātmānam vidvāṃsaḥ, have known this [undivided] Vaiśvānara Ātman; pṛthak iva, only in part [and as separate in each individual]; annam attha, [and that is why] you eat food [thinking you are eating separately; yaḥ tu, but he who; etam evam vaiśvānaram ātmānam upāste, worships this Vaiśvānara Ātman thus; prādeśamātram, as all-pervasive [i.e., as covering the various worlds]; abhivimānam, [and] infinite; saḥ, he; sarveṣu lokeṣu, in all the worlds; sarveṣu bhūteṣu, in all beings; sarveṣu ātmasu, in all selves; annam atti, eats food.
commentary: Prādeśamātra means one who covers all the worlds, from heaven to the earth—including everything and every being. Abhivimāna means infinite, beyond measure. Here the principle is that if you worship God as finite, you remain finite; if you worship him as infinite, you become infinite. Another principle suggested is that you are one with all. You are happy if all are happy. You cannot expect anything for yourself to the exclusion of others. Yet another principle is to regard your body as the place of an Agnihotra sacrifice, and the food you eat as the oblation. The six scholars mentioned here worshipped the Vaiśvānara Ātman in part—as either heaven, the sun, air, space, water, or the earth. Aśvapati told them their worship was not complete. They should include their own self also as the Vaiśvānara Ātman. In fact, they should realize that there is but one Self and that Self is in everything and in every being.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Worshipping the Self as finite limits one to finitude, whereas worshipping it as infinite confers infinitude.
The Vaiśvānara Ātman is present in every world, being, and self, so true worship entails seeing oneself as identical with all beings.
Partial meditation on the Self, treating it as separate parts such as heaven or sun, is insufficient for complete realization.
When one truly regards the Self as all-pervasive, the act of eating is experienced as a shared enjoyment with all beings.
The body functions as a sacrificial altar and food as oblation when the Self is worshipped as universal.
objection_hooks: How can worship change one's ontological status from finite to infinite?
The claim that the Self is present in all beings may conflict with observable individuality and diversity.
Equating eating with shared enjoyment presumes a metaphysical unity that is not empirically verifiable.
Treating the body as a sacrificial altar could be seen as metaphorical rather than literal, raising questions of practical applicability.

sanskrit: तस्य ह वा एतस्यात्मनो वैश्वानरस्य मूर्धैव सुतेजाश्चक्षुर्विश्वरूपः प्राणः पृथग्वर्त्मात्मा संदेहो बहुलो बस्तिरेव रयिः पृथिव्येव पादावुर एव वेदिर्लोमानि बर्हिर्हृदयं गार्हपत्यो मनोऽन्वाहार्यपचन आस्यमाहवनीयः
transliteration: tasya ha vā etasyātmano vaiśvānarasya mūrdhaiva sutejāścakṣurviśvarūpaḥ prāṇaḥ pṛthagvartmātmā saṃdeho bahulo bastireva rayiḥ pṛthivyeva pādāvura eva vedirlomāni barhirhṛdayaṃ gārhapatyo mano'nvāhāryapacana āsyamāhavanīyaḥ
translation: Suteja [i.e., ‘the bright and beautiful’—heaven] is the head of this Vaiśvānara Self; Viśvarūpa [‘having many forms’—the sun] is the eye; Pṛthagvartmā [‘one who changes direction’—air] is the prāṇa; Bahula [‘pervasive’—space] is the middle part; Rayi [‘wealth’—water] is the bladder; the earth [ Pratiṣṭhā —‘the support’] is the feet; the sacrificial altar is the chest; the kuśa grass is the hair on the chest; the Gārhapatya fire is the heart; the Anvāhāryapacana [i.e., the Dakṣiṇāgni ] fire is the mind; and the Āhavanīya fire is the mouth.
word_meaning: Tasya etasya ha vai vaiśvānarasya ātmanaḥ, of this Vaiśvānara Ātman; sutejāḥ eva mūrdhā, heaven is the head; viśvarūpaḥ cakṣuḥ, the sun is the eye; pṛthakvartmātmā prāṇaḥ, air is prāṇa; bahulaḥ sandehaḥ, the sky is the middle part of the body; rayiḥ bastiḥ eva, water is the bladder; pṛthivī eva pādau, the earth is the feet; vediḥ, the sacrificial altar; ura eva, is the chest; barhiḥ lomāni, the kuśa grass [used in the sacrifice] is the hair [on the chest]; gārhapatyaḥ hṛdayam, the Gārhapatya fire is the heart; anvāhāryapacana manaḥ, the Anvāhāryapacana fire [i.e., the Dakṣiṇāgni fire] is the mind; āhavanīyaḥ āsyam, the Āhavanīya fire is the mouth.
commentary: The implication is that none of these taken separately can be the Vaiśvānara Self. It is only a part of it.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The verse asserts that no single bodily organ can be identified as the Vaiśvānara Self, indicating that the Self transcends individual parts
By mapping heaven, sun, air, space, water, earth, altar, grass, fire and mind to body parts, the verse establishes a macrocosm‑microcosm correspondence that reflects Advaita’s unity of all reality
The identification of the Gārhapatya fire with the heart implies that inner fire symbolizes the central locus of consciousness within the Self
The enumeration of diverse parts suggests that the Self is a composite whole and that realization involves integrating all aspects rather than focusing on a single element
objection_hooks: If each part is explicitly equated with a cosmic element, how can the Self be said to transcend those parts rather than be literally identical to them
The macrocosm‑microcosm mapping may serve as a ritual teaching tool and not necessarily convey an ontological claim about Atman
Equating the heart with fire could be a symbolic reference to vitality or passion, not proof of a metaphysical central consciousness
The commentary only notes that none of the parts alone is the Self, but it does not explicitly state that integration of all parts is required for realization

sanskrit: तद्यद्भक्तं प्रथममागच्छेत्तद्धोमीयं स यां प्रथमामाहुतिं जुहुयात्तां जुहुयात्प्राणाय स्वाहेति प्राणस्तृप्यति
transliteration: tadyadbhaktaṃ prathamamāgacchettaddhomīyaṃ sa yāṃ prathamāmāhutiṃ juhuyāttāṃ juhuyātprāṇāya svāheti prāṇastṛpyati
translation: The first part of the food is like the first oblation. One who eats should offer it as an oblation to prāṇa, saying, ‘Prāṇāya svāhā ’ [i.e., I offer this as an oblation to prāṇa]. With this, your prāṇa becomes pleased.
word_meaning: Tat, therefore; yat bhaktam, that food which; prathamam āgacchet, comes first; tat, that; homīyam, is meant as an oblation; saḥ, he [who eats]; yām prathamām āhutim, that first oblation; juhuyāt, offers; tām, that; juhuyāt, offers; prāṇāya svāhā iti, [with the mantra ] ‘Prāṇāya svāhā’; prāṇaḥ tṛpyati, [then] prāṇa is pleased.
commentary: Here eating is being compared to performing a sacrifice. Every time you put food into your mouth, it is as if you are offering an oblation. Prāṇa is the deity to whom you offer the first oblation. The word prāṇa in this context means that aspect of the vital force which is responsible for respiration.
contextual_topics: Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Offering the first portion of food to prāṇa constitutes a valid sacrificial act equivalent to a Vedic oblation
The satisfaction of prāṇa through this offering implies that prāṇa functions as a deity who can be pleased by ritualized gratitude
Treating each meal as a sacrificial rite integrates daily life with spiritual practice, thereby blurring the distinction between secular nourishment and sacred duty
The practice of uttering prāṇāya svāhā while offering food demonstrates that mantra recitation is essential for the efficacy of the offering
Since prāṇa is identified with the vital force of respiration, offering to prāṇa symbolically nourishes the life principle itself
objection_hooks: The equivalence of a mundane meal to a Vedic oblation may lack the requisite sanctity prescribed by scriptural injunctions, questioning its validity as a true sacrifice
Assuming prāṇa can experience pleasure anthropomorphizes a physiological process, which may be metaphorical rather than literal, undermining the claim of deity satisfaction
The necessity of the mantra prāṇāya svāhā could be challenged as a later ritual addition not present in the original Upanishadic teaching, thus the claim about mantra efficacy may be unfounded
Integrating daily eating with sacrificial duty might conflict with the principle that sacrificial rites require specific materials and intent, raising logical tension about the scope of duty

sanskrit: प्राणे तृप्यति चक्षुस्तृप्यति चक्षुषि तृप्यत्यादित्यस्तृप्यत्यादित्ये तृप्यति द्यौस्तृप्यति दिवि तृप्यन्त्यां यत्किंच द्यौश्चादित्यश्चाधितिष्ठतस्तत्तृप्यति तस्यानुतृप्तिं तृप्यति प्रजया पशुभिरन्नाद्येन तेजसा ब्रह्मवर्चसेनेति
transliteration: prāṇe tṛpyati cakṣustṛpyati cakṣuṣi tṛpyatyādityastṛpyatyāditye tṛpyati dyaustṛpyati divi tṛpyantyāṃ yatkiṃca dyauścādityaścādhitiṣṭhatastattṛpyati tasyānutṛptiṃ tṛpyati prajayā paśubhirannādyena tejasā brahmavarcaseneti
translation: When prāṇa is pleased, the eye is pleased; when the eye is pleased, the sun is pleased; when the sun is pleased, heaven is pleased; when heaven is pleased, whatever there is ruled by heaven and the sun is pleased. Then when that is pleased, the eater derives pleasure from his children, from his animals, from an abundance of food, from physical strength, and from his good life and scholarship.
word_meaning: Prāṇe tṛpyati, when prāṇa is pleased; cakṣuḥ tṛpyati, the eye is pleased; cakṣuṣi tṛpyati, when the eye is pleased; ādityaḥ tṛpyati, the sun is pleased; āditye tṛpyati, when the sun is pleased; dyauḥ tṛpyati, heaven is pleased; divi tṛpyantyām, when heaven is pleased; yat kiñca, whatever; dyauḥ ca ādityaḥ ca adhitiṣṭhataḥ, is there ruled by heaven and the sun; tat tṛpyati, that is pleased; tasya anu tṛptim, with its being pleased; tṛpyati, he [the eater] is pleased; prajayā, by children; paśubhiḥ, by animals; annādyena, by food; tejasā, by vigour; brahmavarcasena iti, by the radiance of Brahman derived from good character and scholarship.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
claim_candidates: The satisfaction of the vital breath initiates a cascade of pleasure that ultimately pleases Brahman’s radiance
Human well‑being, including offspring, livestock, food, vigor, and scholarly life, depends on the prior satisfaction of cosmic elements such as the sun and heaven
Ethical conduct and scholarship generate the radiance of Brahman, which in turn yields material and familial prosperity
The hierarchical ordering of pleasure (prāṇa → eye → sun → heaven) reflects a principle that microcosmic satisfaction mirrors macrocosmic harmony
Pleasure is presented as the ultimate goal of both natural forces and human activity, indicating a doctrine that joy measures fulfillment
objection_hooks: The causal link between prāṇa’s pleasure and Brahman’s radiance may be metaphorical rather than ontological, questioning the claim of a direct cascade
Attributing human prosperity to the satisfaction of celestial bodies overlooks socioeconomic factors, challenging the claim that cosmic pleasure determines material well‑being
The assertion that ethical conduct produces Brahman’s radiance presumes a theistic reward system not explicitly stated, raising doubt about the claim’s textual basis
Interpreting the sequence as a metaphysical principle may impose a philosophical framework absent from the verse, which could be a simple poetic enumeration

sanskrit: अथ यां द्वितीयां जुहुयात्तां जुहुयाद्व्यानाय स्वाहेति व्यानस्तृप्यति
transliteration: atha yāṃ dvitīyāṃ juhuyāttāṃ juhuyādvyānāya svāheti vyānastṛpyati
translation: When he [the eater] offers the second oblation, he offers it saying, ‘Vyānāya svāhā ’ [I offer this as an oblation to vyāna ]. With this, vyāna becomes pleased.
word_meaning: Atha, next; yām dvitīyām juhuyāt, when he offers the second [oblation]; tām juhuyāt, he offers that; vyānāya svāhā iti, [with the mantra ] ‘Vyānāya svāhā’; vyānaḥ tṛpyati, [then] vyāna is pleased.
commentary: Vyāna is the aspect of the vital force responsible for our speech and for feats requiring great effort. It operates on the nerves.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: Offering an oblation with the mantra Vyānāya svāhā pleases the vital force vyāna
The second oblation in a ritual is directed toward the vital force responsible for speech and effort
The satisfaction of vyāna through ritual indicates that vital forces can be propitiated by mantras
The practice of offering to vyāna reflects a view that internal physiological functions are objects of worship
objection_hooks: How can a non‑sentient physiological function like vyāna experience pleasure
Is the pleasure of vyāna metaphorical rather than literal, thus the claim about propitiation may be symbolic
Does the verse imply that all vital forces require oblations, or is this specific to vyāna

sanskrit: व्याने तृप्यति श्रोत्रं तृप्यति श्रोत्रे तृप्यति चन्द्रमास्तृप्यति चन्द्रमसि तृप्यति दिशस्तृप्यन्ति दिक्षु तृप्यन्तीषु यत्किंच दिशश्च चन्द्रमाश्चाधितिष्ठन्ति तत्तृप्यति तस्यानु तृप्तिं तृप्यति प्रजया पशुभिरन्नाद्येन तेजसा ब्रह्मवर्चसेनेति
transliteration: vyāne tṛpyati śrotraṃ tṛpyati śrotre tṛpyati candramāstṛpyati candramasi tṛpyati diśastṛpyanti dikṣu tṛpyantīṣu yatkiṃca diśaśca candramāścādhitiṣṭhanti tattṛpyati tasyānu tṛptiṃ tṛpyati prajayā paśubhirannādyena tejasā brahmavarcaseneti
translation: When vyāna is pleased, the ear is pleased; when the ear is pleased, the moon is pleased; when the moon is pleased, the quarters are pleased; with the quarters being pleased, whatever there is ruled by the quarters and the moon is pleased. Then when that is pleased, the eater derives pleasure from his children, from his animals, from an abundance of food, from physical strength, and from his good life and scholarship.
word_meaning: Vyāne tṛpyati, when vyāna is pleased; śrotram tṛpyati, the ear is pleased; śrotre tṛpyati, when the ear is pleased; candramāḥ tṛpyati, the moon is pleased; candramasi tṛpyati, when the moon is pleased; diśaḥ tṛpyanti, the quarters are pleased; dikṣu tṛpyantīṣu, if the quarters are pleased; yat kiñca, whatever; diśaḥ ca candramāḥ ca adhitiṣṭhanti, there is ruled by the quarters and the moon; tat tṛpyati, that is pleased; tasya anu tṛptim, with its being pleased; tṛpyati, he [the eater] is pleased; prajayā, by children; paśubhiḥ, by animals; annādyena, by food; tejasā, by vigour; brahmavarcasena iti, by the radiance of Brahman derived from good character and scholarship.
commentary: Section Twenty-One
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
claim_candidates: The verse asserts that the satisfaction of the subtle body (vyāna) ultimately leads to pleasure derived from Brahman's radiance
It implies that worldly pleasures such as children, animals, food and vigor are manifestations of the underlying satisfaction of the cosmic order represented by the quarters and the moon
The text suggests that Brahman's radiance is contingent upon good character and scholarship, indicating an ethical prerequisite for experiencing Brahman's joy

The verse presents a symbolic hierarchy where sensory experience (ear, moon, directions) reflects cosmic principles, supporting a non‑dual identification of individual experience with universal Brahman
The verse claims that the eater's material satisfaction is ultimately derived from Brahman, indicating that material pleasure is subsumed under the divine
objection_hooks: The causal link between vyāna's pleasure and Brahman's radiance may be metaphorical rather than ontological, questioning the claim that Brahman's radiance depends on personal virtue
The identification of sensory pleasures with the cosmic order could conflate empirical experiences with metaphysical realities, leading to a category error
The assertion that ethical conduct is a prerequisite for Brahman's joy appears to conflict with Advaita's view of Brahman's unconditional reality, creating logical tension
The claim that material satisfaction is subsumed under Brahman might be seen as undermining the distinction between samsara and moksha

sanskrit: अथ यां तृतीयां जुहुयात्तां जुहुयादपानाय स्वाहेत्यपानस्तृप्यति
transliteration: atha yāṃ tṛtīyāṃ juhuyāttāṃ juhuyādapānāya svāhetyapānastṛpyati
translation: When he [the eater] offers the third oblation, he offers it saying, ‘Apānāya svāhā ’ [I offer this as an oblation to apāna ]. With this, apāna becomes pleased.
word_meaning: Atha, next; yām tṛtīyām juhuyāt, when he offers the third [oblation]; tām juhuyāt, he offers that; apānāya svāhā iti, [with the mantra ] ‘Apānāya svāhā’; apānaḥ tṛpyati, [then] apāna is pleased.
commentary: Apāna is the aspect of the vital force responsible for elimination of waste from the body.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: Offering the third oblation with the mantra ‘Apānāya svāhā’ pleases the apāna vital force
The satisfaction of apāna through ritual indicates that bodily vital forces can be influenced by sacred utterances
The third oblation functions as a substitute for direct physical purification of waste, aligning ritual with physiological processes
The use of the specific mantra ‘Apānāya svāhā’ reflects a symbolic representation of the vital force within the sacrificial act
Repeating the offering until apāna is pleased suggests that ritual efficacy depends on the response of the targeted subtle element
objection_hooks: How can a spoken mantra affect a physiological process like waste elimination?
Is the pleasure of apāna merely metaphorical, not an actual change in bodily function?
Does the ritual truly substitute for physical purification, or is it merely symbolic without practical effect?
Could the specific mantra be arbitrary, lacking intrinsic connection to apāna?

sanskrit: अपाने तृप्यति वाक्तृप्यति वाचि तृप्यन्त्यामग्निस्तृप्यत्यग्नौ तृप्यति पृथिवी तृप्यति पृथिव्यां तृप्यन्त्यां यत्किंच पृथिवी चाग्निश्चाधितिष्ठतस्तत्तृप्यति तस्यानु तृप्तिं तृप्यति प्रजया पशुभिरन्नाद्येन तेजसा ब्रह्मवर्चसेनेति
transliteration: apāne tṛpyati vāktṛpyati vāci tṛpyantyāmagnistṛpyatyagnau tṛpyati pṛthivī tṛpyati pṛthivyāṃ tṛpyantyāṃ yatkiṃca pṛthivī cāgniścādhitiṣṭhatastattṛpyati tasyānu tṛptiṃ tṛpyati prajayā paśubhirannādyena tejasā brahmavarcaseneti
translation: When apāna is pleased, the organ of speech is pleased; the organ of speech being pleased, fire is pleased; when fire is pleased, the earth is pleased; the earth being pleased, whatever is under the control of the earth and fire is pleased. Then when that is pleased, the eater derives pleasure from his children, from his animals, from an abundance of food, from physical strength, and from his good -life and scholarship.
word_meaning: Apāne tṛpyati, when apāna is pleased; vāk tṛpyati, the organ of speech is pleased; vāci tṛpyantyām, the organ of speech being pleased; agniḥ tṛpyati, fire is pleased; agnau tṛpyati, when fire is pleased; pṛthivī tṛpyati, the earth is pleased; pṛthivyām tṛpyantyām, the earth being pleased; yat kiñca, whatever; pṛthivī ca agniḥ ca adhitiṣṭhataḥ, is under the control of the earth and fire; tat tṛpyati, that is pleased; tasya anu tṛptim, with its being pleased; tṛpyāti, he [the eater] is pleased; prajayā, by children; paśubhiḥ, by animals; annādyena, by food; tejasā, by vigour; brahmavarcasena iti, by the radiance of Brahman derived from good character and scholarship.
commentary: Section Twenty-Two
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: The satisfaction of the internal vital force apāna leads to the satisfaction of speech, fire, earth, and ultimately the eater's pleasure
The pleasure derived from children, animals, food, vigor, and a good life is ultimately due to the radiance of Brahman
Good character and scholarship generate the radiance of Brahman, which in turn pleases the eater
External material happiness is dependent on internal spiritual satisfaction
objection_hooks: The causal link between apāna's satisfaction and the eater's pleasure may be metaphorical rather than literal, questioning the direct causation claim
Asserting that Brahman's radiance is the source of material pleasures conflates spiritual and material realms, challenging the claim of Brahman as the ultimate cause of worldly joy
The proposition that good character and scholarship produce Brahman's radiance assumes a direct correlation that may not be universally accepted
The idea that external happiness depends solely on internal spiritual satisfaction overlooks external circumstances and other factors

sanskrit: अथ यां चतुर्थीं जुहुयात्तां जुहुयात्समानाय स्वाहेति समानस्तृप्यति
transliteration: atha yāṃ caturthīṃ juhuyāttāṃ juhuyātsamānāya svāheti samānastṛpyati
translation: When he [the eater] offers the fourth oblation, he offers it saying, ‘Samānāya svāhā ’ [I offer this as an oblation to samāna ]. With this, samāna becomes pleased.
word_meaning: Atha, next; yām caturthīm juhuyāt, when he offers the fourth [oblation]; tām juhuyāt, he offers that; samānāya svāhā iti, [with the mantra ] ‘Samānāya svāhā’; samānaḥ tṛpyati, [then] samāna is pleased.
commentary: Samāna is the aspect of the vital force responsible for digestion and assimilation of food.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: The ritual offering of the fourth oblation, accompanied by the mantra samānāya svāhā, is intended to satisfy the samāna aspect of the vital force
The satisfaction of samāna through proper oblation indicates that bodily functions are integrated into Vedic sacrificial practice
The use of the specific mantra samānāya svāhā demonstrates that each oblation is directed toward a particular internal principle
The pleasure of samāna upon receiving the oblation suggests that the vital force responds to ritual actions as a conscious entity
objection_hooks: How can a non-sentient physiological process like digestion be said to experience pleasure, making the claim anthropomorphic
Is the association of a specific mantra with the digestion aspect historically attested, or is this an interpretive extrapolation beyond the verse
Could the verse simply be prescribing a ritual formula without implying any real effect on bodily functions, thus undermining the claim that bodily functions are integrated into sacrificial practice

sanskrit: समाने तृप्यति मनस्तृप्यति मनसि तृप्यति पर्जन्यस्तृप्यति पर्जन्ये तृप्यति विद्युत्तृप्यति विद्युति तृप्यन्त्यां यत्किंच विद्युच्च पर्जन्यश्चाधितिष्ठतस्तत्तृप्यति तस्यानु तृप्तिं तृप्यति प्रजया पशुभिरन्नाद्येन तेजसा ब्रह्मवर्चसेनेति
transliteration: samāne tṛpyati manastṛpyati manasi tṛpyati parjanyastṛpyati parjanye tṛpyati vidyuttṛpyati vidyuti tṛpyantyāṃ yatkiṃca vidyucca parjanyaścādhitiṣṭhatastattṛpyati tasyānu tṛptiṃ tṛpyati prajayā paśubhirannādyena tejasā brahmavarcaseneti
translation: When samāna is pleased, the mind is pleased; when the mind is pleased, the cloud is pleased; when the cloud is pleased, lightning is pleased; lightning being pleased, whatever is under the control of lightning and the cloud is pleased. Then when that is pleased, the eater derives pleasure from his children, from his animals, from an abundance of food, from physical strength, and from his good life and scholarship.
word_meaning: Samāne tṛpyati, when samāna is pleased; manaḥ tṛpyati, the mind is pleased; manasi tṛpyati, when the mind is pleased; parjanyaḥ tṛpyati, the cloud is pleased; parjanye tṛpyati, when the cloud is pleased; vidyut tṛpyati, lightning is pleased; vidyuti tṛpyantyām, lightning being pleased; yat kiñca, whatever; vidyut ca parjanyaḥ ca adhitiṣṭhataḥ, is under the control of lightning and the cloud; tat tṛpyati, that is pleased; tasya am tṛptim, with its being pleased; tṛpyati, he [the eater] is pleased; prajayā, by children; paśubhiḥ, by animals; annādyena, by food; tejasā, by vigour; brahmavarcasena iti, by the radiance of Brahman derived from good character and scholarship.
commentary: Section Twenty-Three
contextual_topics: Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
claim_candidates: The verse asserts that the satisfaction of the mind leads to the satisfaction of the cloud and lightning, indicating that worldly pleasures are dependent on a hierarchical cosmic order
It claims that the ultimate source of lasting pleasure is the radiance of Brahman, which is attained through good character and scholarship
The verse suggests that the control exercised by lightning and cloud over natural elements symbolizes the governing power of Brahman over material existence
It implies that ethical conduct and learning are prerequisites for experiencing Brahman's radiance, linking moral effort to spiritual fulfillment
objection_hooks: The causal chain from mind to cloud to lightning may be metaphorical rather than literal, so the claim that worldly pleasures depend on cosmic order could be overextended
Identifying Brahman's radiance as the ultimate source of pleasure might conflate material vigor with the transcendent Brahman, creating ontological confusion
Other Upanishadic passages assert that Brahman is self‑evident and not contingent on moral actions, challenging the claim that ethical conduct is a prerequisite for Brahman's radiance
Equating the control of lightning and cloud with Brahman's governance may be an anthropomorphic projection lacking explicit textual support

sanskrit: अथ यां पञ्चमीं जुहुयात्तां जुहुयादुदानाय स्वाहेत्युदानस्तृप्यति
transliteration: atha yāṃ pañcamīṃ juhuyāttāṃ juhuyādudānāya svāhetyudānastṛpyati
translation: When he [the eater] offers the fifth oblation, he offers it saying, ‘Udānāya svāhā ’ [I offer this as an oblation to udāna ]. With this, udāna becomes pleased.
word_meaning: Atha, next; yām pañcamīm juhuyāṭ when he offers the fifth [oblation]; tām juhuyāt, he offers that; udānāya svāhā iti, [with the mantra ] ‘Udānāya svāhā’; udānaḥ tṛpyati, [then] udāna is pleased.
commentary: Udāna is the aspect of the vital force responsible for helping the individual self leave the body at the time of death.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: Performing the fifth oblation Udānāya svāhā pleases the udāna, the vital force that enables the self to leave the body at death
The satisfaction of udāna through ritual offering shows that ritual actions can influence subtle vital forces that determine the soul’s exit from the body
The designation of a fifth oblation implies a hierarchical structure of sacrifices where each has distinct metaphysical effects
The utterance svāhā functions as a binding affirmation that activates udāna’s capacity to aid the self’s liberation at death
The pleasure of udāna upon receiving the offering indicates a reciprocal relationship between devotee and vital principle
objection_hooks: How can a material ritual offering affect an internal subtle force like udāna that is not directly perceptible
Does describing udāna as ‘pleased’ attribute literal agency to it, creating ontological confusion
Could the influence of the fifth oblation on the soul’s departure be explained by psychological conditioning rather than a metaphysical effect
If each oblation has distinct effects, why is the fifth singled out for udāna and does the text justify this hierarchy

sanskrit: उदाने तृप्यति त्वक्तृप्यति त्वचि तृप्यन्त्यां वायुस्तृप्यति वायौ तृप्यत्याकाशस्तृप्यत्याकाशे तृप्यति यत्किंच वायुश्चाकाशश्चाधितिष्ठतस्तत्तृप्यति तस्यानु तृप्तिं तृप्यति प्रजया पशुभिरन्नाद्येन तेजसा ब्रह्मवर्चसेन
transliteration: udāne tṛpyati tvaktṛpyati tvaci tṛpyantyāṃ vāyustṛpyati vāyau tṛpyatyākāśastṛpyatyākāśe tṛpyati yatkiṃca vāyuścākāśaścādhitiṣṭhatastattṛpyati tasyānu tṛptiṃ tṛpyati prajayā paśubhirannādyena tejasā brahmavarcasena
translation: When udāna is pleased, the organ of touch is pleased; the organ of touch being pleased, air is pleased; when air is pleased, space is pleased; when space is pleased, whatever is under the control of air and space is pleased. Then when that is pleased, the eater derives pleasure from his children, from his animals, from an abundance of food, from physical strength, and from his good life and scholarship.
word_meaning: Udāne tṛpyati, when udāna is pleased; tvak tṛpyati, the organ of touch [i.e., the skin] is pleased; tvaci tṛpyantyām, the organ of touch being pleased; vāyuḥ tṛpyati, air is pleased; vāyau tṛpyati, when air is pleased; ākāśaḥ tṛpyati, space is pleased; ākāśe tṛpyati, when space is pleased; yat kiñca, whatever; vāyuḥ ca ākāśaḥ ca adhitiṣṭhataḥ, is under the control of air and space; tat tṛpyati, that is pleased; tasya anu tṛptim, with its being pleased; tṛpyati, he [the eater] is pleased; prajayā, by children; paśubhiḥ, by animals; annādyena, by food; tejasā, by vigour; brahmavarcasena iti, by the radiance of Brahman derived from good character and scholarship.
contextual_topics: Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: The satisfaction of the skin (tvak) directly causes the satisfaction of the air (vāyu)
When space (ākāśa) is pleased, all entities governed by air and space become pleased
The eater’s ultimate pleasure is contingent upon his offspring, livestock, food, vigor, and the radiance of Brahman
The radiance of Brahman is described as being derived from good character and scholarship
The verse presents a hierarchical causal chain from udāna through subtle elements to material well‑being and spiritual radiance
objection_hooks: The text may only describe a correlation between skin and air, not a causal relationship
The statement that all things under air and space are pleased could be an overgeneralization beyond the verse’s scope
Linking the eater’s pleasure to Brahman’s radiance might be metaphorical rather than a doctrinal claim
The hierarchical model inferred may impose a philosophical structure not explicitly stated in the verse

sanskrit: स य इदमविद्वाग्निहोत्रं जुहोति यथाङ्गारानपोह्य भस्मनि जुहुयात्तादृक्तत्स्यात्
transliteration: sa ya idamavidvāgnihotraṃ juhoti yathāṅgārānapohya bhasmani juhuyāttādṛktatsyāt
translation: If a person performs the Agnihotra sacrifice without knowing anything about the Vaiśvānara Self, it will be like offering oblations into ashes instead of the fire.
word_meaning: Saḥ yaḥ, he who; agnihotram juhoti, performs the Agnihotra sacrifice; idam avidvān, without knowing this [i.e., about the Vaiśvānara Ātman ]; yathā, just
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: Performing the Agnihotra sacrifice without knowledge of the Vaiśvānara Self renders the ritual ineffective
Knowledge of the universal Self is a necessary condition for the efficacy of Agnihotra
The verse equates a ritual performed in ignorance to offering oblations into ashes, implying that ignorance nullifies the intended spiritual benefit
The true fire of sacrifice is the realization of the Self rather than the physical fire
The ritual performed without proper understanding is merely a material act lacking spiritual transformation
objection_hooks: The physical fire still consumes the oblations, so the ritual may retain some efficacy regardless of knowledge
Other Vedic texts emphasize ritual purity and correct performance over intellectual knowledge, challenging the necessity of knowledge for efficacy
The comparison to ashes might be metaphorical, not indicating a total loss of merit
The statement could be context‑specific to certain Vedic practices and not a universal principle

sanskrit: अथ य एतदेवं विद्वानग्निहोत्रं जुहोति तस्य सर्वेषु लोकेषु सर्वेषु भूतेषु सर्वेष्वात्मसु हुतं भवति
transliteration: atha ya etadevaṃ vidvānagnihotraṃ juhoti tasya sarveṣu lokeṣu sarveṣu bhūteṣu sarveṣvātmasu hutaṃ bhavati
translation: But he who performs the Agnihotra sacrifice with full knowledge of the Vaiśvānara Self is deemed to have offered oblations to all the worlds, to all beings, and to all selves.
word_meaning: Atha, but; yaḥ, he who; agnihotram juhoti, performs the Agnihotra sacrifice; etat evam vidvān, knowing it accordingly; tasya, his; hutam bhavati, oblation is offered; sarveṣu lokeṣu, to all the worlds; sarveṣu bhūteṣu, to all beings; sarveṣu ātmasu, to all selves.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: Performing Agnihotra with true knowledge of the universal Self makes the sacrifice equivalent to offering to all worlds, beings, and selves
Knowledge of the Vaiśvānara Self transforms a particular ritual into a universal act of worship
The efficacy of a sacrifice is determined by the sacrificer's understanding of the Self rather than the material aspects of the rite
The verse implies that the ultimate object of sacrifice is the universal Self, encompassing all entities
objection_hooks: How can a finite ritual act be said to reach all beings without actual physical offerings to each
Does the verse imply that knowledge alone suffices for the merit of sacrifice, thereby undermining the importance of ritual precision
Could the claim that the sacrifice is offered to all selves be metaphorical rather than literal, questioning its ontological status

sanskrit: तद्यथेषीकातूलमग्नौ प्रोतं प्रदूयेतैवंहास्य सर्वे पाप्मानः प्रदूयन्ते य एतदेवं विद्वानग्निहोत्रं जुहोति
transliteration: tadyatheṣīkātūlamagnau protaṃ pradūyetaivaṃhāsya sarve pāpmānaḥ pradūyante ya etadevaṃ vidvānagnihotraṃ juhoti
translation: Just as the cotton fibres of the iṣīkā grass are totally consumed when thrown into the fire, similarly all sins are consumed of one who performs the Agnihotra sacrifice with the knowledge of the Vaiśvānara Self.
word_meaning: Tat yathā, just as; iṣīkā-tūlam, the cotton-like fibre of the iṣīkā grass; agnau, into the fire; protam, on being thrown; pradūyeta, is totally consumed; evam, like this; asya ha, his; sarve pāpmānaḥ, all sins; pradūyante, are burnt up; yaḥ, he who; etat evam vidvān, having known this in this way; agnihotram juhoti, performs the Agnihotra sacrifice.
commentary: Iṣīkā is a kind of grass that grows very tall and has a cotton-like substance coming from it which is easily consumed when thrown into fire. Similarly, the knowledge that a person is one with all easily consumes the fruits of his sañcita (accumulated) karma and his āgāmī (future) karma. But a person may have to suffer from prārabdha karma, which is already in the process of bearing fruit. Prārabdha karma is like an arrow that has already been shot.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Performing Agnihotra with self‑knowledge results in the complete destruction of all past and future sins
The knowledge that the individual self is identical with the universal Self functions as a catalyst that burns accumulated karma similarly to cotton fibres in fire
Prārabdha karma, already set in motion, cannot be eliminated by the sacrifice even when performed with correct knowledge
The efficacy of the sacrifice depends on the purity of the self‑knowledge rather than on the external ritual alone
objection_hooks: How can a single ritual eradicate all future sins if future actions are yet undetermined
If prārabdha karma cannot be burned, does the claim of total sin consumption contradict the statement that all sins are consumed
Does the analogy of cotton fibres oversimplify the complex moral consequences of actions, making the claim metaphorically weak
Is reliance on self‑knowledge sufficient, or does it ignore the necessity of ethical conduct in preventing new karma

sanskrit: तस्मादु हैवंविद्यद्यपि चण्डालायोच्छिष्टं प्रयच्छेदात्मनि हैवास्य तद्वैश्वानरे हुतं स्यादिति तदेष श्लोकः
transliteration: tasmādu haivaṃvidyadyapi caṇḍālāyocchiṣṭaṃ prayacchedātmani haivāsya tadvaiśvānare hutaṃ syāditi tadeṣa ślokaḥ
translation: Therefore, even if a person who knows the Vaiśvānara Ātman gives the remnants of his food after eating to a person who has no caste, that will be like his oblation offered to his own Vaiśvānara Self. Here is a verse on the subject:
word_meaning: Tasmāt, therefore; u ha evam vit, one who knows [the Vaiśvānara Self]; yadi api, even if; caṇḍālāya, to a caṇḍāla [an outcaste]; ucchiṣṭam, part of the food left after eating; prayacchet, one gives; tat, that [leftover food]; asya ha eva hutam syāt, will be his oblation offered; vaiśvānare ātmani iti, to the Vaiśvānara Ātman; tat eṣaḥ ślokaḥ, here is a verse on the subject.
commentary: Normally food that is left over after eating should not be given to anyone. But suppose a person has realized his Vaiśvānara Self and he gives such food to an outcaste. That is not a breach of any rule. Rather, it will be like an oblation offered to his own Self, for it is the same Self who is giving and who is receiving.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
claim_candidates: Realization of the Vaiśvānara Self nullifies caste‑based restrictions on food sharing
Offering leftover food to an outcaste, when one knows the universal Self, is equivalent to offering it to one's own Self
The act of giving food in this context constitutes a valid oblation despite conventional ritual prohibitions
Knowledge of the universal Self transforms external actions into internal worship
objection_hooks: How can a personal realization override socially established dharma without causing disorder?
If the outcaste is considered the same Self, why does the text still distinguish him as caṇḍāla?
Does equating a mundane act like sharing leftovers with a sacred oblation dilute the significance of true yajna?
Could this teaching be misused to justify any transgression of caste rules under the pretext of self‑knowledge?

sanskrit: यथेह क्षुधिता बाला मातरं पर्युपासत एवं सर्वाणि भूतान्यग्निहोत्रमुपासत इत्यग्निहोत्रमुपासत इति
transliteration: yatheha kṣudhitā bālā mātaraṃ paryupāsata evaṃ sarvāṇi bhūtānyagnihotramupāsata ityagnihotramupāsata iti
translation: Just as here in this world, when children are hungry they go to their mother and beg for food, in the same way, all living beings beg that the Agnihotra sacrifice may be performed without any delay.
word_meaning: Yathā, just as; iha, in this world; kṣudhitāḥ bālāḥ, hungry children; mātaram paryupāsate, go to their mother [for food]; evam, in the same way; sarvāṇi bhūtāni, all living beings; agnihotram upāsate iti, wait for the Agnihotra sacrifice to begin; agnihotram upāsate iti, wait for the Agnihotra sacrifice to begin.
commentary: Here the reference is to a person who has attained Self-knowledge. When such a person performs his Agnihotra sacrifice as described before, by taking his meal, it is as if all living beings are eating. This happens because he is one with all.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self

sanskrit: श्वेतकेतुर्हारुणेय आस तं ह पितोवाच श्वेतकेतो वस ब्रह्मचर्यं न वै सोम्यास्मत्कुलीनोऽननूच्य ब्रह्मबन्धुरिव भवतीति
transliteration: śvetaketurhāruṇeya āsa taṃ ha pitovāca śvetaketo vasa brahmacaryaṃ na vai somyāsmatkulīno'nanūcya brahmabandhuriva bhavatīti
translation: Āruṇi had a son named Śvetaketu . Once Āruṇi told him: ‘Śvetaketu, you should now live as a brahmacārin . No one in our family has not studied the scriptures and has not been a good brāhmin’.
word_meaning: Śvetaketuḥ ha Āruṇeyaḥ āsa, Āruṇi had a son named Śvetaketu; tam ha pita uvāca, his father said to him [to Śvetaketu]; śvetaketo, O Śvetaketu; vasa brahmacaryam, live as a brahmacārin [i.e., a celibate student]; na vai somya asmat kulīnaḥ, no one in our family, my child; ananūcya, has not studied the scriptures; brahma - bandhuḥ iva bhavati iti, and has not been a good brāhmin.
commentary: Om. The word brahma- bandhu literally means a relative or friend of a brāhmin—in other words, one who is a brāhmin in name only. The question arises here, why did Āruṇi himself not invest his son with the sacred thread, initiating him into the life of a brahmacārin? Why did he suggest that his son go to another brāhmin for his sacred thread and for his education and training? Śaṅkara says, it is likely that Āruṇi was about to start on a journey and would be away from home for some time, and that is why he decided to send his son to another brāhmin.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty

sanskrit: स ह द्वादशवर्ष उपेत्य चतुर्विंशतिवर्षः सर्वान्वेदानधीत्य महामना अनूचानमानी स्तब्ध एयाय तंह पितोवाच
transliteration: sa ha dvādaśavarṣa upetya caturviṃśativarṣaḥ sarvānvedānadhītya mahāmanā anūcānamānī stabdha eyāya taṃha pitovāca
translation: Śvetaketu went to his teacher’s house at the age of twelve. After studying all the Vedas, he returned home when he was twenty-four, having become very serious and vain, and thinking himself to be a great scholar. [Noticing this, ] his father said to him: ‘O Śvetaketu, you have now become very serious and vain, and you think you are a great scholar. But did you ask your teacher for that teaching [about Brahman ]—
word_meaning: Saḥ ha, he [Śvetaketu]; dvādaśa- varṣaḥ, at the age of twelve; upetya, having gone [to his teacher as directed by his father]; caturviṃśati-varṣaḥ, till he was twenty-four; sarvān vedān adhītya, having studied all the Vedas; eyāya, returned home; mahāmanāḥ, very serious; anūcānamānī, vain; stabdhaḥ, having a high opinion of his scholarship; tam ha pita uvāca, his father said to him; śvetaketo, O Śvetaketu; yat nu idam somya, now young man; mahāmanāḥ asi, you have become very serious; anūcānamānī, vain; stabdhaḥ, thinking yourself to be a great scholar; tam ādeśam, that teaching; aprākṣyaḥ uta, did you ask [your teacher].
commentary: Āruṇi must have been disappointed to see Śvetaketu’s manners when he returned home. In order to instil into Śvetaketu the spirit of humility, Āruṇi put a question to him. He wanted to remind his son that scholarship was not the same as Self-knowledge. He also wanted Śvetaketu to understand that unless he knew the secret of Self-knowledge, his education was pointless. This secret of Self-knowledge is ādeśa .

sanskrit: श्वेतकेतो यन्नु सोम्येदं महामना अनूचानमानी स्तब्धोऽस्युत तमादेशमप्राक्ष्यः येनाश्रुतं श्रुतं भवत्यमतं मतमविज्ञातं विज्ञातमिति कथं नु भगवः स आदेशो भवतीति
transliteration: śvetaketo yannu somyedaṃ mahāmanā anūcānamānī stabdho'syuta tamādeśamaprākṣyaḥ yenāśrutaṃ śrutaṃ bhavatyamataṃ matamavijñātaṃ vijñātamiti kathaṃ nu bhagavaḥ sa ādeśo bhavatīti
translation: ‘—that teaching by which what is never heard becomes heard, what is never thought of becomes thought of, what is never known becomes known?’ [ Śvetaketu asked, ] ‘Sir, what is that teaching?’.
word_meaning: Yena, [that teaching] by which; aśrutam, what is never heard; śrutam bhavati, becomes heard; amatam matam, what is never thought of [becomes] thought of; avijñātam vijñātam iti, what is never known [becomes] known; bhagavaḥ, O lord; katham nu saḥ ādeśaḥ bhavati iti, what is that teaching?
commentary: How can there be such a thing by knowing which you know everything else? This is what is puzzling Śvetaketu. Is it possible that by knowing one thing you also know something else? Separate things are to be known separately. But the claim is being made here that unless you know the Self you know nothing. And if you know the Self you know everything. This sounds like an absurd proposition. This ādeśa, or teaching, that Āruṇi is talking about is the secret that opens up one’s eyes, that makes one conscious of the fact that until and unless one knows the Self, one knows nothing.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman

sanskrit: यथा सोम्यैकेन मृत्पिण्डेन सर्वं मृन्मयं विज्ञातं स्याद्वाचारम्भणं विकारो नामधेयं मृत्तिकेत्येव सत्यम्
transliteration: yathā somyaikena mṛtpiṇḍena sarvaṃ mṛnmayaṃ vijñātaṃ syādvācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ mṛttiketyeva satyam
translation: O Somya, it is like this: By knowing a single lump of earth you know all objects made of earth. All changes are mere words, in name only. But earth is the reality.
word_meaning: Somya, young man; yathā, just as; ekena mṛtpiṇḍena, from one single lump of earth; sarvam mṛnmayam vijñātam, all objects made of earth are known; vācārambhaṇam nāmadheyam vikāraḥ, all changes are mere words, in name only; mṛttika iti eva satyam, the earth is the reality.
commentary: What is this ādeśa that Śvetaketu ’s father wanted him to learn from his teacher? It is that there is only one single reality in this world, and that reality appears to be many because of the different names and forms superimposed on it. Here he is using earth as an example. If you know a single thing made of earth—for instance, a pot—then you know all things made of earth. How? The word ‘pot’ is merely a name; the real object is earth. Earth may assume different names and forms, but it remains the same earth.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man

transliteration: yathā somyikena nakhanikṛntanena sarvaṃ kārṣṇāyasaṃ vijñātaṃ syādvācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ kṛṣṇāyasamityeva satyamevaṃsomya sa ādeśo bhavatīti

transliteration: na vai nūnaṃ bhagavantasta etadavediṣuryaddhyetadavediṣyankathaṃ me nāvakṣyanniti bhagavāṃstveva me tadbravītviti tathā somyeti hovāca

sanskrit: ब्रह्मणश्च ते पादं ब्रवाणीति ब्रवीतु मे भगवानिति तस्मै होवाच प्राची दिक्कला प्रतीची दिक्कला दक्षिणा दिक्कलोदीची दिक्कलैष वै सोम्य चतुष्कलः पादो ब्रह्मणः प्रकाशवान्नाम
transliteration: brahmaṇaśca te pādaṃ bravāṇīti bravītu me bhagavāniti tasmai hovāca prācī dikkalā pratīcī dikkalā dakṣiṇā dikkalodīcī dikkalaiṣa vai somya catuṣkalaḥ pādo brahmaṇaḥ prakāśavānnāma
translation: The bull said, ‘Let me also tell you about one foot of Brahman .’ Satyakāma replied, ’Yes, lord, please tell me.’ Then the bull said to him: ‘The east is one part of Brahman, the west is another, the south is another, and the north is yet another. O Somya, this is one foot of Brahman, consisting of four parts. This foot is called Prakāśavān, the shining’.
word_meaning: Brahmaṇaḥ ca te pādam bravāṇi iti, [the bull said, ] let me also tell you about a foot [a quarter] of Brahman; bravītu me bhagavān iti, yes, lord, please tell me; tasmai ha uvāca, [the bull] said to him; prācī dik kalā, the east is one part [i.e., one sixteenth—a quarter of a quarter]; pratīcī dik kalā, the west is one part; dakṣiṇā dik kalā, the south is one part; udīcī dik kalā, the north is one part; eṣaḥ vai somya catuṣkalaḥ pādaḥ brahmaṇaḥ, O Somya, this is one foot of Brahman having four parts; prakāśavān nāma, it is called Prakāśavān [the shining].

sanskrit: अथ यदि महज्जिगमिषेदमावास्यायां दीक्षित्वा पौर्णमास्यां रात्रौ सर्वौषधस्य मन्थं दधिमधुनोरुपमथ्य ज्येष्ठाय श्रेष्ठाय स्वाहेत्यग्नावाज्यस्य हुत्वा मन्थे सम्पातमवनयेत्
transliteration: atha yadi mahajjigamiṣedamāvāsyāyāṃ dīkṣitvā paurṇamāsyāṃ rātrau sarvauṣadhasya manthaṃ dadhimadhunorupamathya jyeṣṭhāya śreṣṭhāya svāhetyagnāvājyasya hutvā manthe sampātamavanayet
translation: Then if anyone wishes to attain greatness, he should first become initiated on a new moon day, and after that, on the night of a full moon, he should prepare a paste of various herbs and mix them together with curd and honey. He should then offer this oblation to the fire saying, ‘Jyeṣṭhāya śreṣṭhāya svāhā, ’ [i.e., Svāhā to the oldest and to the best]. Whatever is left over in the offering spoon he should put into the homa pot.
word_meaning: Atha yadi, then if; mahat jigamiṣet, a person wants to attain greatness; amāvāsyāyām dīkṣitvā, having been initiated on the day of a new moon; paurṇamāsyām rātrau, on the night of the full moon; sarvauṣadhyasya mantham, a paste of various herbs; dadhi -madhunoḥ upamathya, [and] mixing with curd and honey; jyeṣṭhāya śreṣṭhāya svāhā iti, say ‘Svāhā to the oldest and the best’; agnau ājyasya hutvā, offer this as oblations to the fire; manthe sampātam avanayet, put the residue from the offering spoon in the pot.
commentary: If a person wants to attain greatness, it should not be for worldly gain, but for his spiritual benefit. Here, some instructions are given concerning the sacrifices he should perform. Prior to those sacrifices, however, he should practise strict self-control for some time. This whole discipline is intended to take him to a higher world after death, but the over-all result is that he becomes a better person spiritually.

sanskrit: सदेव सोम्येदमग्र आसीदेकमेवाद्वितीयम् । तद्धैक आहुरसदेवेदमग्र आसीदेकमेवाद्वितीयं तस्मादसतः सज्जायत
transliteration: sadeva somyedamagra āsīdekamevādvitīyam | taddhaika āhurasadevedamagra āsīdekamevādvitīyaṃ tasmādasataḥ sajjāyata
translation: Somya, before this world was manifest there was only existence, one without a second. On this subject, some maintain that before this world was manifest there was only non-existence, one without a second. Out of that non-existence, existence emerged.
word_meaning: Somya, young man; idam, this [world as we see it, with its names and forms]; agre, before [its manifestation]; sat eva, was existence only; ekam eva advitīyam, one without a second; āsīt, existed; tat, about that; eke, some [Buddhists and others]; āhuḥ, say; idam, this [world]; agre, first [before its manifestation]; asat eva, nothingness only; ekam eva advitīyam, one without a second; āsīt, existed; tasmāt, from that; asataḥ, nothingness; sat jāyata, existence emerged.
commentary: ‘Something out of nothing’ is an absurd idea. If there is a tree, it must have come out of a seed, whether the seed was seen by anyone or not. Sometimes you see a tree sprouting from a crack on the roof of a building. Where did it come from? From a seed which the wind must have blown on to the roof. A tree can only grow from a seed. Similarly, existence can only come from existence. This is what the Upaniṣad is suggesting when it says that before the world was manifest there was existence, one without a second. The word means ‘existence.’ The Vedānta scriptures describe this existence as a state of being. It is one without a second. It is pure, all-pervasive, beyond thought and speech, and formless. It is consciousness. Some philosophers maintain, however, that before the world originated there was nothing, one without a second. They claim that the world emerged from this nothing. Vedānta says, suppose you are passing by a potter’s house and you see him with a huge lump of clay. Then you return that same way a few hours later, and you are surprised to see that the nameless and formless lump of clay is transformed into a number of pots, plates, bowls, cups, etc.—each distinct with a name and a form. Similarly, existence becomes manifest as this world, but it remains existence. It The Naiyāyikas, the Buddhists, and others think just the opposite—that existence has come out of non-existence. But how can they know anything about a past non-existence? And how can they know, in particular, that it is one only without a second? In fact, the concept of non-existence is being introduced here only to make a stronger foundation for the concept of existence. In order to know what to avoid, one must be able to see it. Similarly, the concept of non-existence is added only to make it clear what is meant by existence.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
Being as the Source of All
claim_candidates: The Upanishadic teaching asserts that existence (sat) is the only reality prior to manifestation and cannot arise from non‑existence (asat).

The manifested world emerges as a transformation of the underlying existence, not as a creation ex nihilo.
Philosophical schools that claim the world emerged from non‑existence lack epistemic justification for knowing a past non‑existence.
The ultimate reality (Brahman) is described as pure, formless, all‑pervasive consciousness, identical with the singular existence before creation.
objection_hooks: How can we rule out the possibility that non‑existence is a valid ontological state preceding existence, given that the Upanishadic text may be using metaphorical language?
The argument that we cannot know past non‑existence presumes a linear temporal framework; could the concept of non‑existence be beyond time, making the critique irrelevant?
The analogy of clay to pots may not adequately capture the metaphysical nature of Brahman; does the transformation metaphor oversimplify the relationship between sat and the world?
If non‑existence is only a pedagogical tool, does that not imply it has some ontological significance, contradicting the claim that it is merely conceptual?

sanskrit: कुतस्तु खलु सोम्यैवंस्यादिति होवाच कथमसतः सज्जायेतेति। सत्त्वेव सोम्येदमग्र आसीदेकमेवाद्वितीयम्
transliteration: kutastu khalu somyaivaṃsyāditi hovāca kathamasataḥ sajjāyeteti| sattveva somyedamagra āsīdekamevādvitīyam
translation: The father said: ‘O Somya, what proof is there for this—that from nothing something has emerged? Rather, before this world came into being, O Somya, there was only existence, one without a second’.
word_meaning: Somya, O Somya; kutaḥ tu, but what [proof is there]; khalu, indeed; evam syāt, could this be so; iti ha uvāca, he [ Āruṇi ] said; katham, in what way; asataḥ, from non-existence; sat, existence; jāyata iti, will come; tu, on the other hand; somya, O Somya; idam agre, before this [world]; sat eva āsīt, there
commentary: Let us say the world was not here before, but it came into existence at a certain point of time. What does this mean? Does this mean that there was a void and out of that void the world as we now see it emerged? As has been stated already, the idea of something coming out of nothing is absurd. Yet some Buddhist scholars, who believe that existence comes from non-existence, argue that unless a seed is destroyed, a tree cannot grow from it. So according to them something comes out of nothing. Śaṅkara argues that it is only the form of the seed that is destroyed. The material that makes up the seed goes on to produce the tree. There is no example anywhere of something coming from nothing. A potter makes pots out of clay. Can he make a pot out of nothing? No. But then the Buddhists argue, can a pot produce another pot? Vedānta says, no, but a pot can change its form. It can become potsherds or it can go back to the form of clay. Vedānta says, the world always existed, but it did not always exist in the form we see it now. A snake is always a snake, whether it is lying like a long rope or it is coiled up. The world is Sat (Existence), and it is nameless and formless. But how it does come to have names and forms? The answer is that Existence is the only reality, but if it seems to have different names and forms, they are merely superimpositions and are not real.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
Being as the Source of All
sub_concepts: Brahman as Cosmological and Physical Principle
claim_candidates: The world is not created ex nihilo; existence (Sat) is eternal and singular

The assertion that before the world there was only Sat implies that Brahman is the sole reality preceding all phenomena
objection_hooks: How can we verify that existence is singular without empirical evidence?

Equating Sat with Brahman may ignore distinctions made in other Upanishadic passages; is this identification universally valid?

sanskrit: तदैक्षत बहु स्यां प्रजायेयेति तत्तेजोऽसृजत तत्तेज ऐक्षत बहु स्यां प्रजायेयेति तदपोऽसृजत । तस्माद्यत्र क्वच शोचति स्वेदते वा पुरुषस्तेजस एव तदध्यापो जायन्ते
transliteration: tadaikṣata bahu syāṃ prajāyeyeti tattejo'sṛjata tatteja aikṣata bahu syāṃ prajāyeyeti tadapo'sṛjata | tasmādyatra kvaca śocati svedate vā puruṣastejasa eva tadadhyāpo jāyante
translation: That Existence decided: ‘I shall be many. I shall be born.’ He then created fire. That fire also decided: ‘I shall be many. I shall be born.’ Then fire produced water. That is why whenever or wherever a person mourns or perspires, he produces water.
word_meaning: Tat, that [existence]; aikṣata, decided; bahu syām, I shall be many; prajāyeya iti, I shall be born; tat, that [existence]; asṛjata, created; tejaḥ, fire; tat tejaḥ, that [existence as] fire; aikṣata, decided; bahu syām, I shall be many; prajāyeya iti, I shall be born; tat, that [fire]; apaḥ, water; asṛjata, created; tasmāt, that is why; yatra kva ca, whenever and wherever; puruṣaḥ, a person; śocati, grieves; svedate vā, or perspires; tat, [it happens] that; tejasaḥ eva, from fire; āpaḥ adhijāyante, water comes.
commentary: The word aikṣata means ‘saw, ’ ‘thought, ’ or ‘decided.’ It can only apply to a conscious principle, because only a conscious principle can decide or think or see. And only a conscious being can say that he will be many. The scriptures say that this Existence, or Brahman, is one without a second, always the same, unchanging, and unchangeable. So how can it at the same time be many? Vedānta says that it is like a lump of earth sometimes taking different forms of pots, cups, etc. Or it is like a rope which sometimes looks like a snake. The change is only in names and forms. It is not a real change. Vedānta says, this applies to all that we see in this world. Underlying the seeming diversity there is unity. This unity—this One—supports the diversity. It is this One that has become many, but only in appearance. To go back to the example of the earth, the earth remains earth, though in appearance it may take the form of a lump or of some pots or of some other things. An apt description of this is ‘unity in diversity.’ It is Brahman that has become everything—space, air, fire, water, earth. Then the question arises, how can fire, which is inanimate, think? The answer is that here fire stands for Brahman. Brahman as fire is making things happen. Brahman is the source of everything. It is the base, the reality. Just as earth can be in the form of a lump or a pot, similarly, Brahman can be in the form of fire, water, or something else. It is not that Brahman undergoes any change. Brahman remains Brahman. It is Sat, eternal Existence. It is the Absolute. It is never conditioned by anything. When it says it will be ‘many, ’ it means it will appear in many forms, just as earth or gold can be in many forms. But it must be borne in mind that this Existence is also pure consciousness.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
Being as the Source of All

sanskrit: ता आप ऐक्षन्त बह्व्यः स्याम प्रजायेमहीति ता अन्नमसृजन्त तस्माद्यत्र क्व च वर्षति तदेव भूयिष्ठमन्नं भवत्यद्भ्य एव तदध्यन्नाद्यं जायते
transliteration: tā āpa aikṣanta bahvyaḥ syāma prajāyemahīti tā annamasṛjanta tasmādyatra kva ca varṣati tadeva bhūyiṣṭhamannaṃ bhavatyadbhya eva tadadhyannādyaṃ jāyate
translation: That water decided: ‘I shall be many; I shall be born.’ That water then created food. This is why whenever and wherever there is rain, at once food grows in great abundance. It is from water that food is produced.
word_meaning: Tāḥ āpaḥ, that water; aikṣanta, decided; bahvyaḥ syāma, I shall be many; prajāyemahi iti, I shall be born; tāḥ, that [water]; annam asṛjanta, produced food; tasmāt, that is why; yatra kva ca, whenever and wherever; varṣati, it rains; taṭ at once; bhūyiṣṭham, in great abundance; annam bhavati, food grows; adbhyaḥ eva, it is from water; tat, then; annādyam adhijāyate, food is produced.
commentary: Here, food represents earth.

sanskrit: तेषां खल्वेषां भूतानां त्रीण्येव बीजानि भवन्त्याण्डजं जीवजमुद्भिज्जमिति
transliteration: teṣāṃ khalveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ trīṇyeva bījāni bhavantyāṇḍajaṃ jīvajamudbhijjamiti
translation: Living beings have their origin in three ways: from eggs, from parents, and from plants.
word_meaning: Teṣām khalu eṣām bhūtānām, of these living beings; trīṇi eva bījāni bhavanti, there are three kinds of origin; āṇḍajam, birth from eggs; jīvajam, from parents; udbhijjam iti, from plants.

sub_concepts: Brahman as Cosmological and Physical Principle

sanskrit: सेयं देवतैक्षत हन्ताहमिमास्तिस्रो देवता अनेन जीवेनात्मनानुप्रविश्य नामरूपे व्याकरवाणीति
transliteration: seyaṃ devataikṣata hantāhamimāstisro devatā anena jīvenātmanānupraviśya nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇīti
translation: That god [Existence] decided: ‘Entering into these three deities [fire, water, and earth], as the individual self, I shall manifest myself in many names and forms’.
word_meaning: Sā iyam devatā, that deity [i.e., Sat, Existence]; aikṣata, decided; hanta, so; aham, I; imāḥ tisraḥ devatāḥ, these three gods [i.e., fire, water, and earth]; anena jīvena ātmanā, as the jīvātman [i.e., the individual self]; anupraviśya, having entered; nāmarūpe, as names and forms; vyākaravāṇi iti, I shall manifest.
commentary: The Self (Sat) is within fire, water, and earth, but that is not to say that it is in any way affected by them. If you stand before a mirror, you see your reflection. The reflection may be good or it may not be good, but does that affect the mirror? The sun gives light to the eyes, but if there is anything wrong with the eyes, does that affect the sun? Similarly, the Self is everywhere and in everything. But wherever it is, it is the same. Names and forms, apart from the Self, are false. But there is, in reality, nothing apart from the Self. Everything is the Self. In that sense, the names and forms are also the Self and therefore real.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man

sanskrit: तासां त्रिवृतं त्रिवृतमेकैकां करवाणीति सेयं देवतेमास्तिस्रो देवता अनेनैव जीवेनात्मनानुप्रविश्य नामरूपे व्याकरोत्
transliteration: tāsāṃ trivṛtaṃ trivṛtamekaikāṃ karavāṇīti seyaṃ devatemāstisro devatā anenaiva jīvenātmanānupraviśya nāmarūpe vyākarot
translation: Sat [Existence] thought, ‘I shall divide each of these three deities threefold.’ Then, having entered into these three deities as the individual self, he manifested himself as names and forms.
word_meaning: Tāsām, of these [three deities]; trivṛtam trivṛtam, dividing them threefold; ekaikām, each of them; karavāṇi iti, I shall make; sā iyam devatā, that deity [Existence]; imāḥ tisraḥ devatā, these three deities; anena jīvena eva ātmanā, as the individual self; anupraviśya, having entered; nāmarūpe vyākarot, manifested himself as names and forms.
commentary: Trivṛtam is applied in the case of fire, water, and earth as follows: gross fire = 1/2 subtle fire + 1/4 subtle water + 1/4 subtle earth gross water = 1/2 subtle water + 1/4 subtle fire + 1/4 subtle earth gross earth = 1/2 subtle earth + 1/4 subtle fire + 1/4 subtle water This mixture turns the subtle elements into gross elements. It makes them separate and yet one. A similar process, called pañcikaraṇa, is applied in the case of the five elements—space, air, fire, water, and earth. Sat, or Brahman, is present in all the elements as their Self. First he is manifest as their sum total, called Virāṭ He then manifests himself as names and forms.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man

sanskrit: तासां त्रिवृतं त्रिवृतमेकैकामकरोद्यथा तु खलु सोम्येमास्तिस्रो देवतास्त्रिवृत्त्रिवृदेकैका भवति तन्मे विजानीहीति
transliteration: tāsāṃ trivṛtaṃ trivṛtamekaikāmakarodyathā tu khalu somyemāstisro devatāstrivṛttrivṛdekaikā bhavati tanme vijānīhīti
translation: [Having so decided, ] he made each of these three elements threefold. But as to how each of these three deities becomes threefold, O Somya, learn this from me.
word_meaning: Tāsām of those [three elements]; ekaikām, each one of them; trivṛtam trivṛtam akarot, he made threefold; somya, O Somya; yathā tu khalu, but as to how; imāḥ tisraḥ devatā, these three deities; trivṛt trivṛt ekaikā bhavati, each becomes threefold; tat me vijānīhi iti, learn this from me.

sanskrit: यदग्ने रोहितंरूपं तेजसस्तद्रूपं यच्छुक्लं तदपां यत्कृष्णं तदन्नस्यापागादग्नेरग्नित्वं वाचारम्भणं विकारो नामधेयं त्रीणि रूपाणीत्येव सत्यम्
transliteration: yadagne rohitaṃrūpaṃ tejasastadrūpaṃ yacchuklaṃ tadapāṃ yatkṛṣṇaṃ tadannasyāpāgādagneragnitvaṃ vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ trīṇi rūpāṇītyeva satyam
translation: The red colour of gross fire is from subtle fire, the white colour is from subtle water, and the dark colour is from subtle earth. Thus that which constitutes the ‘fire’-ness of fire is gone. All changes are mere words, in name only [i.e., fire is only a name indicating a certain condition]. The three colours are the reality.
word_meaning: Yat agneḥ rohitam rūpam, that red colour of [gross] fire; tat rūpam tejasaḥ, that colour is from [subtle] fire; yat śuklam, that which is white; tat apām, that is from [subtle] water; yat kṛṣṇam, that which is dark; tat annasya, that is from [subtle] earth [lit., food]; agneḥ agnitvam apāgāt, [thus] the ‘fire’-ness of fire is gone; vācārambhaṇam nāmadheyam vikāraḥ, all changes are mere words, in name only; trīṇi rūpāṇi iti eva satyam, only the three colours are the reality [i.e., outside of the three colours, there is no fire].
commentary: When fire is gross it has a red colour which comes from its subtle aspect. But there is also a white colour in it which comes from the subtle water element. Similarly, sometimes it has a dark colour which comes from the subtle earth element. The Upaniṣad says, in reality, fire is nothing beyond these three colours—red, white, and black. This proves the falsity of the idea of gross fire.

sanskrit: यदादित्यस्य रोहितंरूपं तेजसस्तद्रूपं यच्छुक्लं तदपां यत्कृष्णं तदन्नस्यापागादादित्यादादित्यत्वं वाचारम्भणं विकारो नामधेयं त्रीणि रूपाणीत्येव सत्यम्
transliteration: yadādityasya rohitaṃrūpaṃ tejasastadrūpaṃ yacchuklaṃ tadapāṃ yatkṛṣṇaṃ tadannasyāpāgādādityādādityatvaṃ vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ trīṇi rūpāṇītyeva satyam

sanskrit: यच्छन्द्रमसो रोहितंरूपं तेजसस्तद्रूपं यच्छुक्लं तदपां यत्कृष्णं तदन्नस्यापागाच्चन्द्राच्चन्द्रत्वं वाचारम्भणं विकारो नामधेयं त्रीणि रूपाणीत्येव सत्यम्

sanskrit: यद्विद्युतो रोहितंरूपं तेजसस्तद्रूपं यच्छुक्लं तदपां यत्कृष्णं तदन्नस्यापागाद्विद्युतो विद्युत्त्वं वाचारम्भणं विकारो नामधेयं त्रीणि रूपाणीत्येव सत्यम्
transliteration: yadvidyuto rohitaṃrūpaṃ tejasastadrūpaṃ yacchuklaṃ tadapāṃ yatkṛṣṇaṃ tadannasyāpāgādvidyuto vidyuttvaṃ vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ trīṇi rūpāṇītyeva satyam
translation: The red colour of lightning is from fire, the white colour is from water, and the dark colour is from earth. Thus that which constitutes the ‘lightning’-ness of lightning is gone. All changes are mere words, in name only. The three colours are the reality.
word_meaning: Yat vidyutaḥ rohitam rūpam, that red colour of lightning; tat rūpam tejasaḥ, that colour is from fire; yat śuklam, that which is white; tat apām, that is from water; yat kṛṣṇam, that which is dark; tat annasya, that is from earth [lit., food]; vidyutaḥ vidyuttvam apāgāt, [thus] the ‘lightning’-ness of lightning is gone; vācārambhaṇam nāmadheyam vikāraḥ, all changes are mere words, in name only; trīṇi rūpāṇi iti eva satyam, only the three colours are the reality [i.e., outside of the three colours, there is no lightning].

The Universal Self

sanskrit: एतद्ध स्म वै तद्विद्वांस आहुः पूर्वे महाशाला महाश्रोत्रिया न नोऽद्य कश्चनाश्रुतममतमविज्ञातमुदाहरिष्यतीति ह्येभ्यो विदांचक्रुः
transliteration: etaddha sma vai tadvidvāṃsa āhuḥ pūrve mahāśālā mahāśrotriyā na no'dya kaścanāśrutamamatamavijñātamudāhariṣyatīti hyebhyo vidāṃcakruḥ
translation: The earlier great householders, who were well read in the Vedas, knew this. They said, ‘There is nothing anyone can mention that is not heard of or thought of or already known to us.’ I his is because they came to know about the three colours.

sanskrit: यदु रोहितमिवाभूदिति तेजसस्तद्रूपमिति तद्विदांचक्रुर्यदु शुक्लमिवाभूदित्यपांरूपमिति तद्विदांचक्रुर्यदु कृष्णमिवाभूदित्यन्नस्य रूपमिति तद्विदांचक्रुः
transliteration: yadu rohitamivābhūditi tejasastadrūpamiti tadvidāṃcakruryadu śuklamivābhūdityapāṃrūpamiti tadvidāṃcakruryadu kṛṣṇamivābhūdityannasya rūpamiti tadvidāṃcakruḥ
translation: They knew that whatever else was seen as red was the colour of fire; whatever else was seen as white was the colour of water; and whatever else was seen as dark was the colour of earth.

sanskrit: यद्वविज्ञातमिवाभूदित्येतासामेव देवतानांसमास इति तद्विदांचक्रुर्यथा तु खलु सोम्येमास्तिस्रो देवताः पुरुषं प्राप्य त्रिवृत्त्रिवृदेकैका भवति तन्मे विजानीहीति
transliteration: yadvavijñātamivābhūdityetāsāmeva devatānāṃsamāsa iti tadvidāṃcakruryathā tu khalu somyemāstisro devatāḥ puruṣaṃ prāpya trivṛttrivṛdekaikā bhavati tanme vijānīhīti
translation: And whatever else was not properly known they understood was the combination of those three deities [fire, water, and earth]. O Somya, now learn from me how these three deities enter into a person and become threefold.
word_meaning: Yat u avijñātam iva abhūt iti, and whatever they saw that was not properly known; samāsaḥ iti, the combination; etāsām eva devatānām, of these deities [fire, water, and earth]; tat vidāñcakruḥ, that they knew; somya, my son; yathā, as to how; imāḥ khalu nu, these very; tisraḥ devatāḥ, three deities; puruṣam, a living being; prāpya, entering [as food]; trivṛt trivṛt ekaikā bhavati, each one becomes threefold; tat me vijānīhi iti, learn that from me.

sanskrit: अन्नमशितं त्रेधा विधीयते तस्य यः स्थविष्ठो धातुस्तत्पुरीषं भवति यो मध्यमस्तन्मांसं योऽणिष्ठस्तन्मनः
transliteration: annamaśitaṃ tredhā vidhīyate tasya yaḥ sthaviṣṭho dhātustatpurīṣaṃ bhavati yo madhyamastanmāṃsaṃ yo'ṇiṣṭhastanmanaḥ
translation: When we eat food, it divides itself into three parts. The grossest part of it becomes excreta; that which is less gross becomes our flesh; and the finest part becomes our mind.
word_meaning: Annam aśitam, when food is eaten; tredhā, in three ways; vidhīyate, is divided; tasya, of it; yaḥ sthaviṣṭhaḥ, that which is the grossest; dhātuḥ, part; tat purīṣam bhavati, that becomes excreta; yaḥ madhyamaḥ, that which is less gross [lit., middle]; tat māṃsam, that [becomes] flesh; yaḥ aṇiṣṭhaḥ, that which is the subtlest; tat manaḥ, that [becomes] the mind.
commentary: When we eat, the food nourishes the body in different ways. How? First, the grossest part of the food is rejected by the body. Then that which is less gross, a bit finer, becomes our flesh. And finally the finest part becomes the mind. According to Vedānta, the mind is material. It functions through the nervous system, which is called hitā . How does this food get transformed into the mind? Śaṅkara says that the subtlest part of the food becomes blood and enters into the heart. From there it goes through the veins and nerves, nourishing the mind. The term mind refers here to the phenomena of our thinking, feeling, willing, etc., plus the aggregate of our sense organs—our seeing, hearing, and so forth. Suppose you do not eat anything. What happens? Slowly you will feel that your mind is becoming more and more feeble. Your memory starts failing, and you cannot concentrate. The finest part of your system is affected. Then the body begins to shrink. You become thinner and thinner, and finally you die. Food nourishes all these. This is why Vedānta says that the mind is material.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
